briefs.title: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court
briefs.citation: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court, 592 U.S. 351, 141 S. Ct. 1017 (2021), consolidated with Ford Motor Co. v. Bandemer, Nos. 19-368 and 19-369. The United States Supreme Court heard argument on October 7, 2020, and decided the cases on March 25, 2021. Justice Kagan wrote the five-Justice majority opinion, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kav

sections.Parties:
Ford Motor Company was the defendant in both underlying damages actions and the petitioner in both
Supreme Court proceedings. It was incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Michigan. In Montana,
Charles Lucero, the personal representative of Markkaya Gullett's estate, brought the underlying action on behalf of Gullett and her heirs. In Minnesota, Adam Bandemer was the injured plaintiff and the respondent opposing Ford's jurisdictional challenge. Bandemer also sued Eric Hanson, the driver, and Hanson's father, who owned the vehicle, for negligence. Their alleged responsibility was separate from the defect claims against Ford. Majority, slip op. at 2-3; Montana opinion ¶ 2; Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d 744, 747-48 (Minn.
2019).
The Montana trial court appears in the Supreme Court caption because Ford had sought supervisory control over that court's exercise of jurisdiction. The underlying tort action was Lucero v. Ford Motor Co.; the jurisdictional proceeding challenged the Montana Eighth Judicial District Court's authority to continue hearing it. The caption therefore reflects the route of review. Ford was seeking dismissal of Lucero's claims against it, and the trial court was the object of the requested supervisory relief. Montana opinion ¶¶ 3-7;
majority, slip op. at 3 n.1.
sections.Material Facts:
In 2015, Montana resident Markkaya Gullett was driving a 1996 Ford Explorer on a Montana interstate near her home. A rear tire experienced tread separation. The Explorer lost stability, rolled into a ditch, and came to rest upside down; Gullett died at the scene. Lucero alleged strict liability for a design defect, strict liability for failure to warn, and negligence, and sought compensatory and punitive damages. The jurisdictional decision treated the claimed defect and Ford's responsibility as allegations. It did not establish why the tire failed or adjudicate the merits of the Explorer's design. Montana opinion ¶ 2; majority, slip op. at 2.
Ford Motor Co.
Ford designed the Explorer in Michigan, assembled it in Kentucky, and initially sold it to a dealer in
Washington. More than ten years later, the vehicle was resold and registered in Montana. Its eventual presence in Montana followed later consumer transactions and relocation, rather than Ford's original sale of that particular Explorer into Montana. The place of initial sale supplied the factual basis for Ford's argument that its own Montana business had not generated this claim. Montana opinion ¶ 2; majority, slip op. at 3.
In January 2015, Minnesota resident Adam Bandemer rode as a passenger in a 1994 Ford Crown Victoria driven by his friend Eric Hanson on a rural Minnesota road. They were traveling to an ice-fishing location when Hanson rear-ended a county snowplow and the car went into a ditch. Bandemer alleged that the passenger-side airbag failed to deploy and that he suffered severe brain injury as a result. Minnesota officers responded, and Minnesota physicians treated him. His complaint asserted products-liability, negligence, and breach-of-warranty claims against Ford and negligence claims against Hanson and Hanson's father. The complaint attributed the collision to Hanson's negligence and the airbag's failure to a defect. These were distinct alleged causes of the accident and resulting injury. Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 747-48; majority, slip op. at 2-3.
Ford designed the Crown Victoria in Michigan, manufactured it in Canada, and originally sold the particular vehicle in North Dakota. Later transactions brought it into Minnesota, where it was registered. Thus, as in
Montana, the state of the accident was also the injured person's home, but differed from the places where
Ford had designed, manufactured, and initially sold the individual car. Bandemer's status as a passenger also shows why a jurisdictional rule framed around the injured person's own purchase would fit the underlying litigation poorly. Majority, slip op. at 3; Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 754.
Ford deliberately and repeatedly served both states' automobile markets. It advertised through television, radio, billboards, print media, and direct mail, including promotion of Explorers and Crown Victorias at the relevant times. Those models were available through its dealership network, which included 36 dealerships in Montana and 84 in Minnesota. Minnesota's record included sales of more than 2,000 model-year 1994
Crown Victorias and approximately 200,000 vehicles of all types during 2013-2015. The Supreme Court relied on the substantial business Ford conducted in each particular forum. Its national size supplied context, while its state-specific conduct supplied the relevant contacts. Majority, slip op. at 3-4, 11-12; Bandemer,
931 N.W.2d at 748, 751.
Ford's relationship with those markets continued after a vehicle's first sale. Its dealers sold used Fords, maintained and repaired vehicles after their warranties expired, and supplied continuing services to owners.
Ford distributed replacement parts to both authorized dealers and independent repair shops. These activities made long-term ownership practical and supported the resale market through which the older vehicles could reach local residents. Ford earned money from those activities and encouraged residents to continue driving its vehicles. Minnesota's court also considered Ford's collection of vehicle-performance information through local dealerships for design and repair purposes. The Supreme Court's own explanation centered on advertising, sales, service, parts, and the resulting market for the relevant models. Majority, slip op. at 2,
11-14; Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 751, 754.
Ford Motor Co.
sections.Procedural History:
Lucero filed the action in Montana's Eighth Judicial District Court, Cascade County, No. DV-18-247. Ford moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, arguing that its Montana contacts lacked the necessary connection to Lucero's claims. The district court rejected the objection. Ford then petitioned the Montana
Supreme Court to exercise supervisory control, overturn the jurisdictional ruling, and direct dismissal. This was review of a threshold ruling while the tort litigation remained pending. Montana opinion ¶¶ 2-4;
majority, slip op. at 3 n.1.
The Montana Supreme Court accepted supervisory control under its state constitutional authority and
Montana Rule of Appellate Procedure 14(3). It described supervisory control as an extraordinary remedy and concluded that ordinary appellate review was inadequate because of the urgency of deciding the trial court's power over the parties. The petition presented a purely legal question of statewide constitutional importance concerning Ford's due-process rights. The court reviewed the personal-jurisdiction ruling de novo, meaning that it independently decided the legal issue rather than deferring to the district court's legal conclusion.
Accepting the petition gave Ford immediate review; it did not mean that Ford was entitled to dismissal.
Montana opinion ¶¶ 5-7.
On May 21, 2019, the Montana Supreme Court upheld jurisdiction. It first found authorization under
Montana Rule of Civil Procedure 4(b)(1)(B), which covers claims arising from an act resulting in the accrual of a tort action within Montana. The alleged misconduct had resulted in an accident and injury there. It then separately addressed federal due process and concluded that Ford deliberately served Montana's market and that the local accident sufficiently related to those activities. Its published decision is Ford Motor Co. v.
Montana Eighth Judicial District Court, 2019 MT 115, 395 Mont. 478, 443 P.3d 407. Montana opinion ¶¶
7-12; majority, slip op. at 3-4.
Bandemer filed his action in Minnesota's Seventh Judicial District Court, Todd County, No. 77-cv-16-1025.
Ford moved to dismiss under Minnesota Rule of Civil Procedure 12.02(b), which permits an objection to personal jurisdiction. The district court denied the motion. Ford appealed, and the Minnesota Court of
Appeals affirmed in Bandemer v. Ford Motor Co., 913 N.W.2d 710 (Minn. Ct. App. 2018). Applying
Minnesota precedent, that court found Ford's directed advertising and marketing sufficiently related to the claims. Ford then obtained review by the Minnesota Supreme Court. Majority, slip op. at 3 n.1; Bandemer,
931 N.W.2d at 747-49.
On July 31, 2019, the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed. It reviewed personal jurisdiction as a question of law de novo. Under the state's approach at the motion-to-dismiss stage, Bandemer had to make a prima facie showing of jurisdiction: allegations and supporting materials sufficient to establish jurisdiction if accepted.
The court accepted the complaint's allegations and supporting affidavits as true under the applicable standard and discussed Ford's discovery responses when evaluating the claimed contacts. Its footnote concerning vehicle-performance data explains that an allegation remained accepted unless Ford's discovery response directly contradicted it. This procedural treatment of allegations supported the jurisdictional inquiry; it did not establish a defect or entitlement to damages at trial. Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 749, 751 n.3.
Ford Motor Co.
Minnesota's long-arm statute extended jurisdiction to the limits of federal due process, so the constitutional inquiry governed. Ford conceded the quantity and quality of its Minnesota contacts and the reasonableness of litigating there; it contested the connection between those contacts and Bandemer's claims. The court found that Ford's sales of the relevant model, marketing, and collection of performance information were sufficiently connected to the alleged defect and local accident. Justice Anderson dissented, joined by Chief
Justice Gildea, because he considered Ford's Minnesota activities unrelated to this particular vehicle and claim. Bandemer also advanced a consent theory based on Ford's registered agent. Both Minnesota appellate courts left that alternative undecided because specific jurisdiction resolved the dispute. Bandemer, 931
N.W.2d at 748-55 & n.1; id. at 755 (Anderson, J., dissenting).
Ford petitioned for certiorari from both state supreme court judgments. The Supreme Court granted review and consolidated the cases, then affirmed on March 25, 2021. The Court reviewed a federal constitutional limit on state adjudicatory authority. These cases reached it through the state courts; they did not begin as federal district court diversity actions. The immediate relief Ford sought was dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction, which would have required the plaintiffs to pursue Ford in another available forum. Majority, slip op. at 1-4, 18.
The affirmance preserved the denials of Ford's dismissal motions. The Supreme Court issued no damages award, found no product defect, and imposed no tort liability. Nor did consolidation turn the two separate accidents into a single underlying tort action. It allowed the Court to resolve the common jurisdictional question in one decision while each state's litigation retained its own plaintiff, claims, evidence, and procedural history. Majority, slip op. at 1-4, 18.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment permit a state court to exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a manufacturer when the manufacturer extensively markets, sells, and services the relevant vehicle model in the state, and that model allegedly injures a resident in a local accident, although the manufacturer designed, manufactured, and first sold the particular vehicle elsewhere? More specifically, must the plaintiff prove that the manufacturer's conduct in the forum caused the claim, or can a sufficiently close relationship between that conduct and the local controversy satisfy the requirement that the claim arise out of or relate to the defendant's forum contacts? Majority, slip op. at 1, 7-9.
sections.Holding:
A court first needs authorization under the applicable state jurisdictional law and must then remain within the Fourteenth Amendment's limits. Montana examined those steps separately; Minnesota interpreted its statute to reach the constitutional boundary. International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, 316-19 (1945), supplies the constitutional framework: the defendant must have sufficient contacts with the forum for the exercise of jurisdiction to comport with traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. A state rule authorizing jurisdiction does not by itself resolve that constitutional question. Montana opinion ¶¶ 10-12;
Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 749; majority, slip op. at 4-7.
Ford Motor Co.
General jurisdiction permits adjudication of claims regardless of their relationship to the forum. For a corporation, its place of incorporation and principal place of business are the ordinary places where it is at home; exceptional circumstances can establish another home. The parties agreed that Ford was subject to general jurisdiction in Delaware and Michigan and was not at home in Montana or Minnesota. The Court therefore needed to determine whether these particular claims supported specific jurisdiction. Extensive local sales mattered to that inquiry without turning either forum into a place where Ford could be sued on every claim. Majority, slip op. at 5-6, 9 n.3.
Specific jurisdiction requires the defendant's own purposeful contact with the state and a sufficient connection between those contacts and the particular claims. Purposeful availment means that the defendant deliberately takes advantage of opportunities to conduct activities in the forum, such as serving its market or undertaking a relationship centered there. A third party's unilateral movement cannot supply the defendant's own conduct. The claims must then "arise out of or relate to" the relevant contacts. Finally, the exercise of jurisdiction must be reasonable in light of the defendant's position and the interests at stake. In Ford, purposeful availment was conceded, so the disputed issue was the required relationship between Ford's admitted local activities and the suits. Majority, slip op. at 5-9, 14-15.
Montana and Minnesota could exercise specific personal jurisdiction over Ford in these two products-liability suits. Ford extensively advertised, sold, and serviced the same vehicle models in each state; each accident occurred there and injured a state resident. Those facts sufficiently connected Ford, the forum, and the particular litigation even though Ford had designed, manufactured, and initially sold the individual vehicles elsewhere.
sections.Judgment:
The Supreme Court affirmed both state supreme court judgments. Ford's motions to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction remained denied, and the underlying damages actions could proceed in Montana and
Minnesota. The Court did not determine whether either vehicle was defective, whether Ford caused the injuries, or the amount of damages. Its decision resolved the challenged constitutional basis for jurisdiction, leaving the merits for the trial courts. Majority, slip op. at 18.
sections.Reasoning:
Ford proposed a causation requirement focused on the individual vehicle. In its account, the state could exercise specific jurisdiction only if Ford's conduct there gave rise to the plaintiff's claim. The relevant places would therefore be the state where Ford initially sold the car, or the places where it designed or manufactured it. Later consumer resales could not transform unrelated advertising and sales of other vehicles into conduct causing these injuries. Ford emphasized that, even if it had never operated in Montana or
Minnesota, the particular vehicles could have arrived through the same resale transactions and produced the same claims. It invoked Bristol-Myers Squibb and Walden to argue that substantial business and the plaintiff's local injury could not replace a connection to the defendant's own conduct. Majority, slip op. at 3,
7-9, 13, 15-18.
Ford Motor Co.
The plaintiffs defended jurisdiction based on Ford's sustained efforts to develop and support the local market for the very models alleged to be defective. The relevant relationship included Ford's promotion of local ownership, sales of the models, repair and parts networks, and an accident injuring a resident within that market. They opposed making jurisdiction depend on tracing an older car back to Ford's first sale or proving that a particular advertisement induced a particular purchase. Their position treated the local accident as related to Ford's ongoing business in that state. The majority accepted that connection. Majority, slip op. at
11-15; Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 751-54.
Kagan gave independent significance to both parts of the established phrase "arise out of or relate to." The first part concerns causation. The second permits some relationships to support jurisdiction without proof that the defendant's forum conduct caused the plaintiff's claim. Ford's proposed rule would eliminate that second route by demanding causation in every case. The majority found no basis in its precedents for that universal requirement. It nevertheless insisted that relatedness has real limits: the defendant's activities, the state, and the specific litigation must remain sufficiently connected. Majority, slip op. at 8-9.
The distinction concerns jurisdictional causation. It addresses whether Ford's Montana or Minnesota activities must have caused these particular claims to arise. The plaintiffs' substantive claims still required whatever proof of defect, breach, injury, and causal responsibility the governing law demanded. A decision that a forum can adjudicate a negligence or products-liability claim does not establish that Ford caused the collision or enhanced the injuries. This separation follows from the motions the Court reviewed and the limited jurisdictional judgments it affirmed. Majority, slip op. at 2-4, 8-9, 18.
The Court connected Ford's activities to the claims at the level of the relevant vehicle models and the market
Ford systematically served. Explorers and Crown Victorias were among the products it advertised, sold, serviced, and supported in these states. The suits alleged that those models malfunctioned while being used there and injured local residents. That combination supplied a concrete connection to the controversy. Ford's other business elsewhere, its overall wealth, or the mere existence of some unrelated local enterprise would not describe the relationship on which the Court relied. Majority, slip op. at 11-12.
The movement of these individual vehicles through the used-car market was compatible with Ford's own business strategy. Ford encouraged resale, stocked replacement parts, and supported repairs long after the first sale. A purchaser could therefore choose an older Ford bought elsewhere partly because of services and parts available at home. The majority identified that possibility to explain why the litigation fit Ford's local activities, while expressly acknowledging that the plaintiffs had neither alleged nor established such individual causal links. The decision does not rest on a finding that Gullett, Bandemer, or the Crown
Victoria's owner actually relied on an advertisement or repair network. Majority, slip op. at 12-14.
Ford Motor Co.
The Court also rejected requiring proof of the particular reasons for a purchase. Its footnote explains that jurisdiction should remain available on these facts even if a plaintiff recently moved into the forum with a car purchased without the move in mind. Ford's independent, established relationship with the destination state's market remains relevant when the vehicle injures a resident there. That observation preserves the defendant-contact requirement: the move changes where the product is used, while Ford's own market activities supply the purposeful forum contacts. Majority, slip op. at 14 & n.5.
World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286 (1980), involved an automobile sold in New York that later caused an alleged injury in Oklahoma. The regional distributor and retailer challenging jurisdiction had not served Oklahoma's market, so the consumer's trip did not establish jurisdiction over them. That opinion also explained that a manufacturer or distributor deliberately serving a state's market could face suit there when its product caused local injury. Audi and the nationwide Volkswagen importer had not challenged jurisdiction in that litigation. Ford's extensive Montana and Minnesota operations placed it within the manufacturer-and-market situation discussed in World-Wide Volkswagen. Majority, slip op. at 9-11.
Ford correctly observed that the earlier opinion's discussion of the nonchallenging manufacturers was dictum. Kagan acknowledged that status and explained that later decisions repeatedly endorsed the same principle, including Keeton, Burger King, Goodyear, the O'Connor opinion in Asahi, and Daimler. Ford applied that principle to actual jurisdictional challenges by the manufacturer. The warning relevant to due process came from Ford's deliberate market activities and the possibility of suits concerning local failures of its vehicles. Mere foreseeability that a movable car might cross a state line would not supply that relationship. Majority, slip op. at 9-11, 14-15.
Ford benefited from the states' enforcement of contracts, protection of property, and maintenance of markets in which it sold and supported vehicles. The Court viewed adjudication of related local product injuries as a reciprocal responsibility accompanying those benefits. Ford could anticipate those suits and account for litigation costs through insurance, pricing, or changes to its forum activities. This reasoning connected fairness to Ford's deliberate conduct and the nature of the claims. It did not announce that a defendant's size or ability to afford litigation independently supplies jurisdiction. Majority, slip op. at 6-7, 10, 14-15.
Montana and Minnesota had direct interests in providing remedies for injured residents and regulating the safety of products used on their roads. The states of initial sale, Washington and North Dakota, had a more remote connection to these particular disputes: an earlier owner had purchased a car there many years before an accident elsewhere involving other residents. Ford's proposed rule would channel the suits toward those states despite the accident states' substantial interests. The majority used that comparison to support jurisdiction in Montana and Minnesota. It did not hold that the initial-sale states necessarily lacked jurisdiction; the availability of other forums was not the question decided. Majority, slip op. at 15; Gorsuch concurrence at 3-4.
Ford Motor Co.
For the familiar fairness analysis, these facts support attention to Ford's litigation burden, the forum's regulatory and remedial interests, the plaintiffs' access to relief, and the efficient resolution of a local accident dispute. Minnesota's opinion expressly noted local treatment, the local accident, and two resident codefendants, and recorded Ford's concession on reasonableness. The United States Supreme Court did not resolve a disputed five-factor balance in a separate checklist; it explained fairness and federalism as reasons supporting the jurisdictional connection established by the facts. Convenience alone could not supply missing purposeful contacts or a missing relationship to the claim. Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 754-55;
majority, slip op. at 6-7, 14-15.
In Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court, 582 U.S. 255 (2017), nonresident plaintiffs sued in
California over Plavix prescribed, obtained, used, and alleged to have caused injury elsewhere. The defendant's California sales and the presence of similar claims by Californians did not connect those nonresidents' own claims to California. Ford read that result as making an out-of-state sale fatal to jurisdiction. Kagan instead emphasized the absence of a forum connection to those plaintiffs' particular injuries. Here, the relevant products were used in the forum, the accidents and injuries occurred there, the injured people were residents, and Ford served the local market for those products. Majority, slip op. at
15-17.
The two decisions consequently require a claim-specific inquiry even when the defendant does substantial business throughout the country. Ford's Montana sales could support the local Explorer suit on these facts without supporting an Ohio resident's suit over a purchase, use, and accident occurring entirely in Ohio. The majority expressly rejected eliminating the connection requirement for nationwide companies. The volume of unrelated local business does not compensate for an absent connection between the forum and the particular controversy. Majority, slip op. at 9 n.3, 15-17.
In Walden v. Fiore, 571 U.S. 277 (2014), a Georgia officer seized money from Nevada residents at an
Atlanta airport. Their later experience of the alleged loss in Nevada could not create the officer's own contact with Nevada; he had directed no relevant activity there. Ford, by contrast, conceded extensive purposeful activity in each forum. Once those defendant-created contacts existed, the location of the accident, injury, and injured person's residence helped assess the claims' relationship to them. Walden prevents the plaintiff's connections from substituting for the defendant's contacts. It does not make the plaintiff's place of injury irrelevant to determining whether an existing defendant-forum relationship encompasses the suit. Majority, slip op. at 17-18.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Alito agreed that existing precedent plainly allowed these suits. Ford maintained a substantial presence in the states, sold and serviced vehicles there, and supplied parts; residents suffered local injuries involving vehicles purchased within those states through the later market. In his view, World-Wide Volkswagen already supplied the answer. He rejected Ford's demand for the strict proof of but-for causation described in its position and agreed with the main thrust of the majority's application. Alito concurrence at 1-3.
Ford Motor Co.
His objection concerned treating "arise out of" and "relate to" as two discrete grounds for jurisdiction. He thought the Court parsed language from judicial opinions as though it were statutory text. Alito would understand the phrases together through a practical, broad conception of causation. Ford's promotion, sales, parts, and service made it reasonable to infer that vehicles of this brand were on local roads because of Ford's efforts to create and support that market. That rough causal connection was enough without proof tracing an individual purchase to a particular forum act. Alito concurrence at 3-4.
Alito worried that an independent category of noncausal relatedness would be difficult to administer. Almost any two matters can be described as related at some level, and the majority's assurance that limits existed did not clearly define them. His approach would preserve a causal idea broad enough to decide Ford while constraining remote claims. The disagreement is therefore substantive: Kagan permitted jurisdiction without a causal showing on these facts, while Alito preferred to explain the same facts as sufficiently causal in a commonsense sense. His concurrence agreed with the judgment but did not narrow the five-Justice majority's holding. Alito concurrence at 3-4; majority, slip op. at 8-9, 14.
Gorsuch also accepted jurisdiction over Ford but questioned both the majority's new formulation and the broader structure of the Court's doctrine. He viewed many lower courts as having understood the connection requirement to include at least but-for causation. Replacing that inquiry with terms such as affiliation or relationship left him uncertain about what facts would count and how much connection would suffice. He also thought evidence that local advertising or service availability induced vehicle purchases might establish a causal connection in these cases, making a new verbal formula unnecessary. The majority responded that those individualized causal facts had not been established and should not be required. Gorsuch concurrence at 1-5; majority, slip op. at 14.
He used two examples to expose uncertainty. First, he questioned whether the majority's comparison of the initial-sale states with the accident states implied that the former could not hear a suit, even though selling the defective car there might satisfy a causation test. That was his criticism of a possible implication, rather than a holding of the majority. Second, he discussed an individual Maine craftsperson who sells a defective duck decoy online to an out-of-state buyer. A sale might directly cause an injury, yet the majority distinguished isolated transactions from Ford's sustained market activity. Gorsuch asked whether the new relatedness formulation would sometimes expand jurisdiction and sometimes restrict it, and where courts should draw the line between those situations. Gorsuch concurrence at 3-5.
Gorsuch then examined the history of jurisdiction based on presence and consent, the development of rules for corporations operating across state lines, and International Shoe's replacement of much of that framework with minimum contacts. He questioned why individuals can ordinarily be served while physically present in a state and sued there on unrelated claims, while large corporations often receive general jurisdiction protection outside one or two home states despite extensive operations elsewhere. He also asked whether rules devised for companies sending agents and goods into states fit an economy in which a small online seller can reach customers nationwide. These were reasons to reconsider the doctrine through constitutional text and history. They did not produce a replacement test adopted by the Court. Gorsuch concurrence at 5-10.
Ford Motor Co.
Gorsuch concluded that Ford had deliberately entered these states to conduct business and had identified no constitutional or historical reason to avoid answering these claims there. He left broader doctrinal reconstruction for future litigation. Kagan defended deciding the cases under International Shoe and its successors, and expressly rejected a rule allowing every claim against a nationwide corporation wherever it conducts business. The controlling decision therefore retains the distinction between general and specific jurisdiction and the requirement of a connection to the particular litigation. Gorsuch concurrence at 10-11;
majority, slip op. at 7 n.2, 9 n.3.
sections.Notes:
The established result concerns a manufacturer that systematically served the forum's market for the same models that allegedly injured local residents in local accidents. The Court expressly reserved a case in which
Ford marketed the model only in a different state or region. It also distinguished isolated or sporadic transactions and reserved the questions posed by internet sales. The decision establishes no minimum number of dealerships, sales, or advertisements, and it does not resolve every question about how narrowly to define the relevant product category. The safe use of the holding is to identify the particular market, the manufacturer's deliberate activities in that market, and the claim's connection to local use and injury.
Majority, slip op. at 11-13 & n.4.
Plaintiff residence strengthens the factual pattern the Court decided, but Ford does not establish a universal residency requirement for specific jurisdiction. A nonresident injured in the forum would require analysis of that person's particular claim and the defendant's relevant contacts; the majority did not decide that variation.
Conversely, moving to the forum after an entirely out-of-state accident would not reproduce Ford's combination of local product use, local malfunction, and local injury. Residence cannot create a missing contact by the defendant. Majority, slip op. at 12-18.
The opinion also does not make Montana or Minnesota the exclusive permissible forum, settle the substantive law governing the claims, decide venue, or resolve the registered-agent consent theory. Those questions have their own requirements. The significance of the judgment is that the Fourteenth Amendment permitted these state courts to hear these claims against Ford on the specific-jurisdiction ground actually litigated. Majority, slip op. at 5-6, 18; Bandemer, 931 N.W.2d at 748 n.1.
The relationship among these cases depends on the basis of jurisdiction asserted. Goodyear, Daimler, and
BNSF restrict all-purpose jurisdiction based on a corporation's business contacts. Ford concerns jurisdiction over particular claims connected to the defendant's forum business. Extensive local business therefore may be insufficient for general jurisdiction while supporting specific jurisdiction over an appropriately related local injury. Consent supplies a separate possible basis; the Minnesota courts did not need to resolve
Bandemer's registration-based consent argument.
Minnesota Supreme Court opinion, 931 N.W.2d 744 (2019). The Montana procedural discussion draws on
Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court, 2019 MT 115, 443 P.3d 407, especially paragraphs 2-12.
Ford Motor Co.

briefs.title: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown
briefs.citation: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915 (2011). United States Supreme Court, decided June 27, 2011. Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court. The Court reviewed a North Carolina Court of Appeals judgment sustaining personal jurisdiction over three foreign subsidiaries in a wrongful-death action. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
The plaintiffs were the parents of Julian Brown and Matthew Helms, acting as administrators of their sons' estates. The boys and their parents were North Carolina residents. The defendants included The Goodyear
Tire and Rubber Company, an Ohio corporation, and three indirect subsidiaries organized and operating in
Luxembourg, Turkey, and France. Only the three foreign subsidiaries contested personal jurisdiction and petitioned for Supreme Court review. The American parent operated in North Carolina and did not challenge the state courts' authority over it. Its participation did not itself establish jurisdiction over each separately incorporated subsidiary.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 2004, Julian and Matthew, thirteen-year-old soccer players, died in a bus accident outside Paris while traveling toward the airport. Their parents alleged that a defective tire manufactured at the Turkish subsidiary's plant caused the crash. The claims challenged the tire's design, construction, testing, and inspection. The accident, manufacture of the allegedly defective tire, and the tire's sale occurred outside
North Carolina. The particular tire was a type not distributed in that state.
The subsidiaries manufactured tires primarily for European and Asian markets. They had no North Carolina place of business, employees, bank accounts, or registration to do business. They did not design or manufacture tires there, solicit business there, or directly sell or ship tires to North Carolina customers. Some of their other tires nevertheless reached North Carolina through distribution by other Goodyear affiliates.
Those shipments comprised a small fraction of the subsidiaries' production: tens of thousands of tires out of tens of millions manufactured during the relevant period. Many were specialized tires obtained by special order. The jurisdictional question concerned what those indirect sales established about the subsidiaries themselves. 564 U.S. at 918-22.
sections.Procedural History:
The parents filed wrongful-death claims in the North Carolina Superior Court for Onslow County. The foreign subsidiaries moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The trial court denied the motions, allowing the claims against them to proceed despite the absence of a connection between their North
Carolina tire sales and the accident.
The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed, 199 N.C. App. 50, 681 S.E.2d 382 (2009). It recognized that specific jurisdiction was unavailable because the alleged injury did not arise from or relate to the subsidiaries' North Carolina contacts. It instead found general jurisdiction, reasoning that the subsidiaries had placed tires into an organized distribution system that carried them to North Carolina and had not taken affirmative steps to prevent distribution there. The court also emphasized the state's interest in providing its residents a forum and the difficulty of litigating abroad. These considerations allowed the intermediate court to treat product distribution as support for adjudicating an unrelated foreign accident.
The North Carolina Supreme Court denied discretionary review, 364 N.C. 128, 695 S.E.2d 756 (2010). The
United States Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the intermediate appellate judgment. The issue was the constitutionality of general jurisdiction; neither liability for the accident nor damages had been adjudicated. Before the Supreme Court, the parents also urged that all Goodyear entities should be treated as one enterprise. The Court declined to consider that argument because they had not timely raised it below or in their opposition to certiorari. 564 U.S. at 922-23, 930-31.
sections.Issue: Does a foreign subsidiary become subject to general personal jurisdiction in North Carolina because some tires that it manufactures abroad enter the state through affiliated distribution channels, when the lawsuit concerns a different tire and a fatal accident in France? May contacts potentially relevant to specific jurisdiction support adjudication of any claim against the manufacturer?
sections.Holding: A state may exercise general, or all-purpose, jurisdiction over a corporation when its affiliations with the state are so continuous and systematic that the corporation is essentially at home there. Specific jurisdiction instead requires an affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy. The subsidiaries' limited, indirect tire distribution did not make them at home in North Carolina and could not support jurisdiction over these unrelated claims. The Court identified a corporation's place of incorporation and principal place of business as paradigm corporate homes, while using Perkins to illustrate sufficiently substantial operations elsewhere. 564 U.S. at 919, 923-29.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court reversed the North Carolina Court of Appeals. North Carolina could not exercise general jurisdiction over the three petitioning subsidiaries on this record. The ruling removed the asserted basis for keeping those subsidiaries in this lawsuit. It did not adjudicate the negligence claims or decide the American parent's liability, and it did not hold that the parents lacked any other forum.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began with the difference between a forum's power over a particular dispute and its power to hear every dispute against a defendant. Product distribution can create a contact relevant to a claim arising from the product's presence or use in the forum. It does not automatically create a corporate home. Treating the circulation of products as sufficient for general jurisdiction would make a substantial manufacturer answerable on any claim wherever its products were sold. That result would erase the more demanding connection required for all-purpose authority.
The North Carolina courts had imported stream-of-commerce reasoning into the wrong jurisdictional inquiry. Whether a defendant directed or expected products to reach a state may matter to specific jurisdiction. Here the plaintiffs had already conceded the missing link between the forum transactions and the accident. Their sons' residence supplied a strong reason for wanting to litigate locally, but it supplied no additional connection between the foreign subsidiaries and North Carolina. A state's interest in its residents could not independently establish the necessary defendant-forum relationship.
The Court compared the subsidiaries with the defendants in Perkins and Helicopteros. In Perkins, the corporation's president actually managed the company's affairs from Ohio while wartime conditions interrupted operations abroad. Ohio functioned as the center of its activities. In Helicopteros, substantial purchases and related training visits in Texas did not support general jurisdiction. The subsidiaries' North
Carolina contacts were far removed from the management activities in Perkins and insufficient even though some actual sales reached the forum.
Finally, jurisdiction had to be assessed over the parties before the Court. The parent company's North
Carolina operations did not eliminate the subsidiaries' distinct legal identities. Because the parents' enterprise theory was forfeited, the Court did not decide the circumstances in which corporate separateness might properly be disregarded. The result therefore cannot be read as a categorical ruling that affiliates' contacts can never be attributed to one another; it rejects these subsidiaries' amenability to unrelated suits on the theory actually preserved. 564 U.S. at 927-31.
sections.Separate Opinions: There were no concurrences or dissents. All nine Justices joined Justice Ginsburg's opinion.
sections.Notes: The case's use of “foreign” includes both corporations from another state and corporations from another country. General jurisdiction turns on the corporation's relationship to the particular forum, rather than foreign nationality alone. Daimler develops the at-home limitation further, while Ford illustrates why a manufacturer may still face specific jurisdiction when its extensive local market activities relate to the models involved in local injuries. The foreign accident here lacked that relationship. The forfeited enterprise argument also shows why preserving an alternative jurisdictional basis in the trial and appellate proceedings matters.

briefs.title: Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co.
briefs.citation: Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co., 342 U.S. 437 (1952). United States Supreme Court, decided March 3, 1952. Justice Burton delivered the Court's opinion. Justice Black concurred in the result. Justice Minton dissented, joined by Chief Justice Vinson. This is the Benguet decision discussed in Goodyear and later general-jurisdiction cases. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
Idonah Slade Perkins, the plaintiff and Supreme Court petitioner, claimed rights as a shareholder of Benguet
Consolidated Mining Company. The Supreme Court described her as a nonresident of Ohio. Benguet, the defendant and respondent, was a Philippine mining corporation organized as a sociedad anonima. Its president was also its general manager and principal stockholder. His activities in Ohio were the corporate activities on which the jurisdictional question turned.
sections.Material Facts:
Benguet owned and operated gold and silver mines in the Philippines. During the Japanese occupation in
World War II, mining operations stopped. The company's president returned to his home in Clermont
County, Ohio, where he conducted the company's business during the wartime interruption and the period immediately afterward. The company's connection to Ohio involved management of its affairs, rather than sales to customers or purchases of supplies alone.
The president maintained an office in Ohio, kept corporate files there, and carried on company correspondence. He drew and distributed salary checks for himself and two secretaries, maintained substantial corporate bank accounts, used an Ohio bank as a stock-transfer agent, and held directors' meetings. He supervised policies for rehabilitating the Philippine mining properties and directed purchases of machinery and the use of funds necessary for that purpose. Although the mines and the underlying assets remained abroad, Ohio was the place from which this continuing corporate activity was directed. The president was personally served in Ohio while acting there for the corporation; the adequacy of the company's actual notice was not disputed.
Perkins sought approximately $68,400 in allegedly unpaid dividends in one action and approximately $2.5 million in damages for an alleged failure to issue 120,000 shares in another. Her claims did not arise from
Benguet's Ohio activities. That absence of a claim-forum connection made the extent and nature of the company's Ohio operations decisive. 342 U.S. at 439-40, 447-48.
sections.Procedural History:
Perkins brought two actions in the Court of Common Pleas of Clermont County, Ohio. Benguet challenged the court's jurisdiction, and the trial court quashed service in each case. The Ohio Court of Appeals affirmed.
The Ohio Supreme Court consolidated the cases and affirmed as well, 155 Ohio St. 116, 98 N.E.2d 33 (1951).
The basis of the Ohio Supreme Court's judgment was important to federal review. Its syllabus stated that the company could not be sued in Ohio on the unrelated claims, but did not clearly establish whether the conclusion rested on Ohio law or on the Federal Constitution. Justice Taft's explanatory opinion understood federal due process to forbid jurisdiction. It was uncertain whether all the judges supporting the judgment agreed with that rationale. If Ohio independently chose not to entertain the actions as a matter of state law, the United States Supreme Court would not require it to do so. If Ohio refused jurisdiction because it believed the Federal Constitution compelled that refusal, the premise was reviewable and incorrect.
The Supreme Court therefore addressed the federal limit while leaving Ohio's own choice of jurisdictional policy for the state courts. Its review did not decide the shareholder claims or resolve whether state law ultimately authorized the suits. The jurisdictional record also presented actual service on the company's president during the very activities supporting jurisdiction, avoiding a separate problem of ineffective or unauthorized notice. 342 U.S. at 440-45.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment prevent Ohio from exercising personal jurisdiction over a Philippine corporation on claims unrelated to Ohio when the corporation's president continuously conducts its business from an Ohio office during the suspension of its Philippine operations? If the Constitution permits jurisdiction, must Ohio exercise it?
sections.Holding: Due process permitted Ohio to entertain these unrelated claims because Benguet's continuous and systematic corporate activities in Ohio were sufficiently substantial. The Constitution did not compel Ohio to provide that forum. The state remained free to permit or withhold jurisdiction under its own law, subject to other applicable constitutional requirements. Later cases treat Perkins as an example of general jurisdiction outside the ordinary places of incorporation and principal place of business, because the forum functioned as the corporation's temporary center of operations. 342 U.S. at 445-49.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court vacated the Ohio Supreme Court's judgment and remanded for further proceedings. The state court had to reconsider the cases with the correct understanding that federal due process did not prohibit jurisdiction on these facts. Perkins did not receive a damages judgment or a federal command that the Ohio courts hear her claims. The disposition preserved a possible independent state-law reason for declining jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court applied International Shoe's focus on the quality and nature of corporate activity. The relevant question was whether the company's connection to Ohio made it fair to require a defense there, even though these claims arose elsewhere. Service on a corporate official could give notice, but notice alone did not establish the substantive authority to adjudicate. Both the official's actual role and the corporation's business in the forum mattered.
The corporate work conducted in Ohio was extensive and central. The president managed corporate correspondence, finances, directors' meetings, compensation, and rehabilitation of the mines. His Ohio office carried on the company's affairs while wartime conditions prevented its normal overseas operations. Those functions gave the corporation a sustained relationship with the state and made this more than the occasional presence of an officer or a series of isolated purchases. The Court therefore found no federal due-process obstacle to a suit unrelated to the Ohio work.
Benguet's lack of an Ohio business license or specially designated statutory service agent did not determine the constitutional question. The company was actually carrying on sufficient business there, and the president's service supplied proper notice. Earlier decisions involving service on public officers without an adequate basis for binding an absent corporation did not control this situation. The Court's reasoning looked to actual corporate activity and notice rather than treating registration as the sole source of adjudicatory authority.
The Court carefully separated a federal permission from a state obligation. The Fourteenth Amendment limits state power; it does not invariably require a state to use every measure of jurisdiction the Constitution would allow. Because the Ohio judgment might have rested on a mistaken view of that limit, vacatur allowed the Ohio courts to decide what their own law required without the mistaken federal premise. This procedural distinction is central to the holding. 342 U.S. at 444-49.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Justice Black concurred in the result without a separate explanation. Justice Minton, joined by Chief Justice
Vinson, would have dismissed the writ of certiorari as improvidently granted. He regarded the Ohio Supreme
Court's authoritative syllabus as a state-law ground adequate to support the judgment, and considered Justice
Taft's federal analysis insufficient to establish that the court itself had rested on federal law. On that view, the Supreme Court's constitutional discussion answered a question that could not change the state judgment.
The disagreement concerned the basis for federal appellate review as well as the practical effect of the remand.
sections.Notes: The modern significance of Perkins is the unusual nature of the forum's role in the corporation's affairs. It does not mean that every corporation with an office, executive, or bank account in a state is subject to unrelated suits there. Goodyear and Daimler use it as the exceptional case in which operations outside the ordinary corporate homes are sufficiently central to support all-purpose jurisdiction. Keep the decision's permissive holding separate from its disposition: the Supreme Court removed a supposed federal prohibition and returned the state-law question to Ohio.

briefs.title: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall
briefs.citation: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall, 466 U.S. 408 (1984). United States Supreme Court, decided April 24, 1984. Justice Blackmun wrote for eight Justices. Justice Brennan dissented. The Court reviewed a Texas Supreme Court judgment sustaining jurisdiction after a wrongful-death trial. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A., usually called Helicol, was a Colombian corporation headquartered in Bogota and engaged in helicopter transportation in South America. It was a defendant below and the Supreme Court petitioner. The respondents were survivors or representatives of four United
States citizens killed in a helicopter crash in Peru. The decedents worked for a Peruvian consortium associated with Williams-Sedco-Horn, a joint venture headquartered in Houston. Other defendants included
Bell Helicopter and the related consortium or joint-venture entities. The Supreme Court's ruling concerned jurisdiction over Helicol, rather than the liability of every defendant.
sections.Material Facts:
On January 26, 1976, a Helicol helicopter crashed in Peru while transporting workers connected to a pipeline project, killing four American passengers. Neither the decedents nor the plaintiffs were domiciled in Texas, although the workers had been hired in Houston. The alleged wrongful deaths arose from the operation of a helicopter abroad.
Helicol's chief executive had made a trip to Houston in 1974 to discuss transportation services with representatives of the consortium. The negotiations concerned matters including prices, fuel, and housing.
The resulting contract was executed in Peru, written in Spanish, and provided for disputes in Peruvian courts.
Payments to Helicol were drawn on a Houston bank, but were received in accounts in New York or Panama
City, Florida. Helicol had not selected the bank on which its customer's checks were drawn.
Between 1970 and 1977, Helicol purchased more than $4 million in helicopters, parts, and accessories from
Bell in Texas. These purchases represented about 80 percent of its helicopter fleet. It sent prospective pilots to Texas for training and to ferry purchased helicopters to South America; maintenance and management personnel also visited for training or consultation. Helicol had no Texas office, employees, operations, bank account, real estate, or regular sales activity. It was not licensed to do business there and had not appointed a
Texas agent for service. Its Texas contacts thus consisted principally of purchases, associated visits, one negotiation trip, and its customer's payment arrangements. 466 U.S. at 409-12.
sections.Procedural History:
The plaintiffs brought wrongful-death suits in a Texas state district court in Harris County. Helicol made special appearances and moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The trial court overruled the objections. The cases were consolidated and tried to a jury, which returned a verdict against Helicol totaling
$1,141,200. The procedural posture therefore involved review of a jurisdictional objection preserved before an actual merits judgment.
The Texas Court of Civil Appeals reversed, concluding that Texas lacked personal jurisdiction over Helicol,
616 S.W.2d 247 (1981). The Texas Supreme Court initially affirmed that decision, over three dissents. On rehearing seven months later, it withdrew its earlier opinion and reversed the intermediate appellate court, again with three dissenters. The rehearing decision, 638 S.W.2d 870 (Tex. 1982), treated the Texas long-arm statute as reaching as far as federal due process permitted and held Helicol's contacts sufficient for jurisdiction.
The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari. A critical limitation on review came from the parties:
both treated the claims as neither arising out of nor relating to Helicol's Texas activities. The Court therefore considered only whether Texas had general jurisdiction over an unrelated controversy. It expressly declined to decide whether “arise out of” and “relate to” describe different connections or whether a sufficiently related claim might support specific jurisdiction. Those issues were not the basis on which the parties had presented the case. 466 U.S. at 412-16 & n.10.
sections.Issue: Can Texas exercise general personal jurisdiction over a Colombian helicopter operator in wrongful-death actions arising from a Peruvian crash when the company's Texas contacts consist of substantial purchases, related training trips, one negotiation visit, and acceptance of checks drawn on a Texas bank, and the parties treat the claims as unrelated to those contacts?
sections.Holding:
The company's contacts did not constitute the continuous and systematic general business contacts necessary to support jurisdiction over an unrelated cause of action. Purchases from a forum seller, even in substantial amounts and accompanied by training trips, do not alone authorize general jurisdiction. The Court decided this as a general-jurisdiction case because of the parties' concession about relatedness. Goodyear and
Daimler later articulate the general-jurisdiction standard as whether the corporation is essentially at home in the forum. 466 U.S. at 416-18.
sections.Judgment:
The Supreme Court reversed the Texas Supreme Court. Texas could not sustain the judgment against Helicol on the asserted general-jurisdiction basis. The decision did not find the helicopter safe, reject the wrongful-death allegations on their merits, or determine the liability of the other defendants. It held that this
Texas court lacked the asserted adjudicatory authority over Helicol.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court compared Helicol's activities with the extensive Ohio management operations in Perkins. Helicol had no comparable office or corporate center in Texas. The single Houston negotiation trip did not resemble continuing management of its business from the forum. Nor did the place where its customer banked materially establish purposeful corporate activity by Helicol. The customer's unilateral choice of a Texas bank could not be attributed to Helicol as a meaningful jurisdictional contact.
The purchases were substantial, but their commercial importance did not make Texas a forum for all claims against the buyer. Relying on Rosenberg Bros. & Co. v. Curtis Brown Co., the Court reasoned that purchasing goods and sending representatives to the seller's state did not establish the kind of corporate presence needed for an unrelated action. The training visits were connected to the purchases and did not independently transform that relationship. Helicol conducted transportation operations in South America; it did not provide those services in Texas.
The plaintiffs' interest in a common forum for all defendants also did not establish jurisdiction. The Court rejected a suggested necessity rationale because the record did not show that all defendants could not be sued together in Peru or Colombia. It did not decide whether jurisdiction by necessity might ever be constitutionally permissible. The absence of proof was enough to reject its use here.
The distinction between purchasing helicopters and litigating claims connected to a helicopter matters because the majority did not resolve the latter as a specific-jurisdiction question. Its holding cannot be expanded into a conclusion that these same transactions would be legally irrelevant to every possible claim.
The parties' concession defined the issue, and the Court confined the controlling ruling to general jurisdiction. 466 U.S. at 415-18 & nn.10, 13.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Justice Brennan dissented. He believed Helicol's Texas dealings, considered together, were sufficiently substantial for jurisdiction. More importantly, he argued that the dispute was sufficiently related to those dealings to permit specific jurisdiction even if it did not technically arise from them. The transportation arrangement was negotiated in Houston; the helicopter involved had been purchased in Texas, and the pilot had trained there. In his view, those links made Texas a fair and foreseeable forum for claims arising from the transportation relationship. He criticized treating relatedness as identical to strict causation and regarded the majority as overlooking the actual relationship between the forum transactions and the accident. 466 U.S.
at 418-28.
sections.Notes:
The procedural concession explains why a case with seemingly relevant Texas transactions became a leading restriction on general jurisdiction. Brennan's distinction between claims that arise from and claims that relate to forum contacts anticipates the issue later resolved in Ford, but his proposed application in this case was a dissent. Ford does not retroactively turn the majority in Helicopteros into a specific-jurisdiction decision.
The proper comparison is between the different grounds presented and decided in the two cases.

briefs.title: Daimler AG v. Bauman
briefs.citation: Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117 (2014). United States Supreme Court, decided January 14, 2014. Justice Ginsburg wrote the opinion of the Court, joined by seven other Justices. Justice Sotomayor concurred in the judgment. All nine agreed that the California litigation could not proceed against Daimler on the jurisdictional theory sustained below, but they disagreed about the reason. Full judicia

sections.Parties:
Twenty-two Argentinian residents sued DaimlerChrysler Aktiengesellschaft, later known as Daimler AG, a
German company headquartered in Stuttgart. They were the plaintiffs below and respondents in the Supreme
Court; Daimler was the defendant and petitioner. Plaintiffs sought to hold Daimler responsible for conduct of
Mercedes-Benz Argentina, an Argentinian subsidiary. The forum contacts relied upon belonged principally to a different indirect subsidiary, Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC, or MBUSA. MBUSA was organized in
Delaware and had its principal place of business in New Jersey. The operative complaint named Daimler as the sole corporate defendant.
sections.Material Facts:
Plaintiffs alleged that Mercedes-Benz Argentina collaborated with Argentinian security forces during the
1976-1983 Dirty War to kidnap, detain, torture, or kill workers and their relatives. The relevant conduct, victims, and perpetrators had no California connection. Plaintiffs asserted claims under the Alien Tort
Statute, the Torture Victim Protection Act, and California and Argentinian law, including wrongful death and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
MBUSA imported Daimler vehicles from Germany and distributed them to independent American dealerships. It operated several California facilities, including a regional office, a vehicle preparation center, and a classic-car center. Its California sales represented about 2.4 percent of Daimler's worldwide sales. The distributor agreement characterized MBUSA as an independent contractor buying and selling vehicles for its own account and disclaimed authority to bind Daimler. Plaintiffs nevertheless contended that MBUSA acted as Daimler's agent because its distribution work was essential to Daimler's business. Their theory sought to make California a forum for any claim against Daimler, despite the absence of a relationship between
California and the alleged abuses in Argentina. 571 U.S. at 120-25.
sections.Procedural History:
Plaintiffs filed in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in 2004. Daimler moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Plaintiffs presented declarations and exhibits about
Daimler's own California connections and alternatively relied on MBUSA's activities. After permitting jurisdictional discovery on the agency theory, the district court dismissed. It found Daimler's own contacts insufficient for general jurisdiction and declined to attribute MBUSA's contacts to Daimler.
A Ninth Circuit panel initially affirmed in 2009, with Judge Reinhardt dissenting. On plaintiffs' petition for rehearing, the panel withdrew that opinion and issued a new decision written by Reinhardt, 644 F.3d 909 (2011). The new opinion treated MBUSA as an agent for jurisdictional purposes because the services it performed were sufficiently important that Daimler would undertake them itself if MBUSA did not. The court also found the exercise of jurisdiction reasonable. Rehearing and rehearing en banc were denied over the dissent of eight judges.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari. Plaintiffs did not pursue specific jurisdiction, did not challenge the insufficiency of Daimler's own contacts, and did not rely on an alter-ego theory. Daimler had not disputed below that MBUSA itself was subject to general jurisdiction in California. The Supreme Court therefore assumed, for purposes of decision, both that MBUSA was at home there and that its contacts could be attributed to Daimler. Those assumptions let the Court resolve the case without definitively deciding the proper agency test or whether MBUSA truly qualified for general jurisdiction under the standard being articulated. Federal Rule 4(k)(1)(A) and California's long-arm provision made the state-law reach, extending to constitutional limits, the relevant jurisdictional framework. 571 U.S. at 124-26, 134-36.
sections.Issue:
May California exercise general jurisdiction over a German parent corporation for alleged misconduct in
Argentina merely because an American subsidiary conducts substantial business in California, even assuming that the subsidiary's contacts are attributable to the parent? Is substantial, continuous local business enough to make the parent answerable there on every claim?
sections.Holding: General jurisdiction ordinarily exists over a corporation in its state of incorporation and principal place of business. Another forum may qualify in an exceptional case when the corporation's operations there are so substantial and of such a nature that it is essentially at home. A substantial volume of business, considered in isolation, is insufficient. Even crediting all MBUSA California contacts to Daimler, Daimler was not at home in California. The relevant assessment considers the corporation's activities in their entirety, nationwide and worldwide. 571 U.S. at 137-39 & nn.19-20.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit. The asserted general-jurisdiction theory could not sustain the action against Daimler in California. The Court did not enter judgment on whether the alleged human-rights abuses occurred or whether Daimler bore substantive responsibility. Its comments on other obstacles to the federal claims did not change the jurisdictional ground of decision.
sections.Reasoning:
The Ninth Circuit's agency formulation was too broad. Almost any subsidiary performs work important enough that a parent would need some way to perform it if the subsidiary disappeared. The formulation could attribute the activities of numerous separately incorporated entities to a parent and expose it to general jurisdiction wherever an affiliate operated. The Supreme Court expressed concern about that consequence but did not need to settle every possible attribution theory. Even the assumed attribution failed to show that
Daimler was at home in California.
The at-home standard gives all-purpose jurisdiction a more definite scope than a rule allowing suit wherever a corporation carries on a substantial, continuous course of business. Incorporation and principal place of business generally identify readily ascertainable places in which a company can anticipate suit on any claim.
They also leave room for an exceptional situation such as Perkins, where Ohio functioned as a corporation's temporary center of operations. The Court did not announce an absolute rule that only two states can ever exercise general jurisdiction.
California was a significant market, but the same could be said of many states and countries in which
Daimler sold vehicles. Evaluating the company's entire operation showed why these commercial activities did not make California its home. The analysis does not establish a numerical percentage threshold: the character of the operation, including whether it is a corporate center, matters along with its place in the company's overall business. Treating every substantial market as a home would undermine predictability and effectively restore jurisdiction over unrelated claims everywhere a large enterprise operates.
The international setting reinforced the problem. Foreign plaintiffs sought to litigate foreign conduct by foreign entities through a California connection supplied by automobile distribution. Broad jurisdiction of that kind could produce friction with other nations and expose American companies to similarly expansive rules abroad. The Court's constitutional holding nevertheless rested on Daimler's lack of an at-home relationship, rather than a categorical rule excluding foreign plaintiffs or international claims. 571 U.S. at
135-42.
sections.Separate Opinions: Justice Sotomayor would have assumed the contacts sufficient and rejected jurisdiction as unreasonable given the foreign plaintiffs, German defendant, Argentinian events, and availability of a more appropriate foreign forum. She objected that the Court decided a question not properly developed below and effectively penalized plaintiffs because Daimler had extensive activities elsewhere. In her view, the comparative approach allowed a larger corporation to avoid jurisdiction that similar local activity might support over a smaller company. She also questioned resolving such a fact-sensitive issue after Daimler had conceded the sufficiency of MBUSA's California contacts, limiting development of the record. Her concurrence supports the judgment, not the majority's at-home rationale. 571 U.S. at 142 (Sotomayor, J., concurring in the judgment).
sections.Notes: Two assumptions must remain distinct from holdings: the Court assumed MBUSA was subject to general jurisdiction and assumed its contacts were attributable to Daimler. It did not decide either proposition. The decision also concerns jurisdiction based on corporate contacts. Mallory later addresses consent under an explicit registration statute as a separate basis, leaving the at-home rule applicable when jurisdiction is asserted over a nonconsenting corporation because of its business operations.

briefs.title: BNSF Railway Co. v. Tyrrell
briefs.citation: BNSF Railway Co. v. Tyrrell, 581 U.S. 402 (2017). United States Supreme Court, decided May 30, 2017. Justice Ginsburg wrote for eight Justices. Justice Sotomayor concurred in the statutory analysis and dissented from the due-process analysis and judgment. The case consolidated two Montana actions under the Federal Employers' Liability Act, or FELA. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
BNSF Railway Company was the defendant in both actions and petitioner in the Supreme Court. It was incorporated in Delaware and had its principal place of business in Texas. Robert Nelson, a North Dakota resident, was one plaintiff. Kelli Tyrrell, a South Dakota resident acting as administrator of the estate of
Brent Tyrrell, was the other. Both opposed BNSF's effort to obtain dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
Nelson alleged knee injuries sustained during his work for BNSF as a fuel-truck driver. Tyrrell alleged that her husband developed fatal kidney cancer from exposure to carcinogenic chemicals while working for
BNSF. Neither plaintiff alleged an injury connected to BNSF's Montana operations, and neither injured employee appeared to have worked for BNSF in Montana. The claims were therefore unrelated to the business contacts relied upon in that state.
BNSF nevertheless had a substantial physical operation in Montana: approximately 2,061 miles of track, about 2,100 employees, and an automotive facility. The railroad operated in twenty-eight states. Montana accounted for roughly 6 percent of its total track, less than 5 percent of its employees, and less than 10 percent of its revenue. Those facts supplied the plaintiffs' argument that BNSF was sufficiently present in
Montana. The Court had to determine whether that operating presence authorized all-purpose jurisdiction, given BNSF's incorporation and headquarters elsewhere. 581 U.S. at 405-07.
sections.Procedural History:
Nelson filed his Montana state-court action in March 2011. Tyrrell filed hers in May 2014. BNSF moved to dismiss both actions for lack of personal jurisdiction. The trial court granted the motion in Nelson's case but denied it in Tyrrell's case. The Montana Supreme Court consolidated the ensuing appeals and held that both actions could proceed, reversing the dismissal in Nelson and affirming the denial in Tyrrell. Its decision was reported at 2016 MT 126, 383 Mont. 417, 373 P.3d 1.
The state supreme court offered two grounds. It interpreted 45 U.S.C. §56 as authorizing jurisdiction over a railroad wherever it did business. It also relied on Montana Rule of Civil Procedure 4(b)(1), which authorizes jurisdiction over persons found within the state. The court treated Daimler as distinguishable because that case concerned foreign corporations and foreign claims, whereas these cases concerned an
American railroad sued under FELA. Justice McKinnon dissented.
The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari to address both the federal statute and the constitutional sufficiency of the Montana contacts. BNSF did not contest that its business satisfied the state rule's “found within” language. That concession established the state-law authorization assumed for decision, but left the federal constitutional objection intact. The employees also advanced consent as an alternative jurisdictional basis. Because the Montana Supreme Court had not addressed that theory, the Supreme Court left it open on remand. The litigation remained at the jurisdictional stage; there had been no trial establishing injury, negligence, or damages. 581 U.S. at 407-09, 415.
sections.Issue: Does FELA authorize a state court to exercise personal jurisdiction over any railroad doing business in the state? If the statute does not do so, do BNSF's extensive Montana tracks and employees make it subject to general jurisdiction there for employment claims unrelated to Montana?
sections.Holding:
FELA's provision specifying federal districts in which an action may be brought is a venue provision. Its statement that federal and state courts have concurrent jurisdiction addresses subject-matter jurisdiction.
Neither provision establishes personal jurisdiction over a railroad in a particular state. Separately, Daimler's at-home requirement applies to domestic railroads and FELA claims as well as foreign corporations and other causes of action. BNSF's Montana operations did not make it at home there. 581 U.S. at 409-15.
sections.Judgment: The Court reversed the Montana Supreme Court and remanded. Neither FELA nor BNSF's Montana business operations supported the grounds for jurisdiction upheld below. The consent theory remained for consideration because it had not been resolved by the state supreme court. The Supreme Court therefore did not order a final rejection of every possible jurisdictional basis or adjudicate the merits of either employee's claim.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court separated three legal questions that the Montana opinion had combined. Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns the court's authority to hear the category of dispute; venue identifies a permissible geographic location within the judicial system; personal jurisdiction concerns the court's authority over the particular defendant. Section 56's statement that an action may be brought in certain federal districts uses the language of venue. Its provision for concurrent state and federal jurisdiction ensures that state courts can hear FELA claims as a class. Neither provision supplies authority over every railroad defendant in every state where it does business.
The Court also distinguished earlier railroad cases that had addressed venue, the Commerce Clause, or injunctions restraining parallel litigation. Those decisions did not settle the due-process question presented here. When Congress intends to confer broad personal jurisdiction, it commonly addresses service of process. The FELA language on which the plaintiffs relied lacked such a grant. A federal substantive right to compensation for negligence does not itself identify every court that may adjudicate that right against a given employer.
Turning to due process, the Court applied the same at-home framework used in Goodyear and Daimler.
Delaware and Texas were BNSF's ordinary corporate homes. Montana hosted real and substantial business, but it was one part of a much broader railroad system. The record did not present an exceptional circumstance resembling the relocation of central corporate operations in Perkins. A company does not become at home in every state in which it lays track or employs a substantial workforce.
Those same operations could support specific jurisdiction over a claim arising from or relating to activity in
Montana. The difficulty here was that these plaintiffs' claims had no such relationship. The Court also rejected the state court's attempt to limit Daimler to multinational corporations or particular kinds of claims.
Constitutional limits on all-purpose adjudicatory authority do not disappear when the defendant is a domestic railroad or the plaintiff invokes FELA. 581 U.S. at 409-15.
sections.Separate Opinions: Justice Sotomayor agreed that FELA did not confer personal jurisdiction and that the type of claim did not eliminate the constitutional inquiry. She continued to object to Daimler's restrictive conception of corporate homes, particularly its comparison of forum contacts with operations elsewhere. She regarded that approach as giving large multistate companies an advantage despite their substantial enjoyment of a forum's protections. Even accepting the at-home test, she would have returned the case for a fact-intensive assessment under the proper standard rather than having the Supreme Court itself reject exceptional-case jurisdiction. She warned that limiting the exception to facts almost identical to Perkins would deprive it of practical meaning. 581 U.S. at 415 (Sotomayor, J., concurring in part and dissenting in part).
sections.Notes:
The remand matters when reading this case with Mallory. BNSF rejects general jurisdiction based on the railroad's ordinary business contacts but expressly leaves alleged consent unresolved. Mallory later addresses consent under Pennsylvania's express registration scheme. The cases concern separate grounds for authority.
A state's permission to hear FELA claims and a railroad's substantial local operations do not, by themselves, answer whether that particular defendant can be sued there on an unrelated claim.

briefs.title: Insurance Corp. of Ireland, Ltd. v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée
briefs.citation: Insurance Corp. of Ireland, Ltd. v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée, 456 U.S. 694 (1982). United States Supreme Court, decided June 1, 1982. Justice White wrote for eight Justices. Justice Powell concurred in the judgment. The Court reviewed whether a district court could deem jurisdictional facts established as a sanction for disobeying discovery orders. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée, or CBG, was the plaintiff and Supreme Court respondent. It was incorporated in Delaware, maintained its principal place of business in Guinea, and operated bauxite mines and processing facilities there. Fourteen foreign excess insurers, including Insurance Corporation of Ireland, were the Supreme Court petitioners. Other insurers had participated below, but four did not contest personal jurisdiction and three obtained dismissal in the court of appeals. The primary insurer, Insurance Company of
North America, or INA, did not challenge the district court's personal or subject-matter jurisdiction.
sections.Material Facts:
CBG was 49 percent owned by the Republic of Guinea and 51 percent by Halco, which operated in
