Governing structure: The Fourteenth Amendment requires a forum connection created through the defendant's own purposeful conduct and a jurisdictional result consistent with fair play and substantial justice. World-Wide Volkswagen identifies the relationship among the defendant, forum, and litigation and supplies five fairness considerations: the defendant's burden, the forum's interest, the plaintiff's interest in effective relief, systemic efficiency, and the shared substantive policies of the sovereigns concerned.
Justice O'Connor's stream-of-commerce-plus approach - four votes: A substantial forum connection must arise from conduct purposefully directed toward that State. Placing a product into a distribution stream while aware that it may arrive in the forum establishes a distribution fact. Purposeful direction appears through additional conduct such as forum-specific product design, forum advertising, regular customer-advice channels, or use of a distributor obligated to serve the forum. Asahi's conduct contained none of those forum-directed features.
Justice Brennan's regular-flow approach - four votes: The stream of commerce is the regular and anticipated movement of products from manufacture through distribution to retail sale. A participant who knows that the final product is marketed in the forum obtains economic benefit from those sales and indirect benefit from the forum's commercial laws. Asahi's repeated, high-volume sales to Cheng Shin, combined with its knowledge of regular
California sales, therefore established minimum contacts under this approach.
Justice Stevens's volume-value-hazard approach - three votes: Justice Stevens found the fairness holding sufficient to decide the case and left the minimum-contacts question open. He added that purposeful availment may depend on the volume, value, and hazardous character of the component. Deliveries exceeding 100,000 units annually over several years could amount to purposeful availment even for a standard product sold worldwide.
Fairness holding: The burden required Asahi to travel from Japan and defend in a foreign legal system. Cheng Shin was a Taiwanese corporation seeking indemnity based on transactions and shipments in Taiwan and Japan. It supplied no concrete reason why California offered a more effective forum than Taiwan or Japan. California's consumer-protection interest had largely been served through the original tort case, and its remaining interest in a foreign indemnity dispute was slight. The interests of Japan and Taiwan and the Federal Government's foreign-relations concerns called for caution.
Doctrinal status: Part II-B is a holding of the Court because eight Justices joined it. The competing minimum-contacts formulations are separate opinions. A court can resolve an Asahi-type case by identifying the governing approach in its jurisdiction or by showing the result under each formulation.
Exam rule: Identify the defendant's distribution conduct, knowledge, sales pattern, control, design, advertising, advice channels, and distributor mandate. Apply O'Connor's additional-conduct test, Brennan's regular-and-anticipated-flow test, and Stevens's volume-value-hazard factors. Then conduct the fairness analysis independently, giving international burdens and foreign sovereign interests their full weight.

briefs.title: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro
briefs.citation: 564 U.S. 873 (2011). Supreme Court of the United States. No. 09-1343; argued January 11, 2011; decided June 27, 2011. Certiorari to the Supreme Court of New Jersey. Kennedy, J., announced the judgment; 4-Justice plurality, 2-Justice concurrence in the judgment, and 3-Justice dissent.

sections.Parties:
Petitioner / defendant: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. (McIntyre UK), a corporation organized and operating in England that designed and manufactured metal-recycling machinery. Respondent / plaintiff: Robert Nicastro, individually and as administrator of the estate of Roseanne Nicastro, a New Jersey worker injured by a McIntyre Model 640 Shear.
Other entities below: McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd., the independent exclusive U.S. distributor, and Curcio
Scrap Metal, Nicastro's New Jersey employer and the machine's purchaser. McIntyre UK and the distributor were separately owned and controlled corporations.
sections.Procedural History:
In September 2003, Nicastro filed a product-liability action in the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen
County, alleging defective design and inadequate warnings. McIntyre UK moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The trial court granted the motion, finding insufficient New Jersey contacts under both conventional minimum-contacts doctrine and the most expansive stream-of-commerce approach it considered.
In an unpublished first appeal, the New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division, reversed and permitted jurisdictional discovery addressing traditional minimum contacts, New Jersey's Charles Gendler stream-of-commerce rule, and
Justice O'Connor's Asahi approach. After discovery, the trial court again dismissed. It found that the machine's arrival was McIntyre UK's sole New Jersey connection and that the evidence showed no expectation that its products would be purchased and used there.
The Appellate Division reversed a second time in a published opinion, 399 N.J. Super. 539 (App. Div. 2008). It found
Justice O'Connor's stream-of-commerce-plus standard satisfied by the exclusive national distributorship, U.S.
trade-show activity, a product designed for U.S. standards, and the sale produced by that distribution arrangement. It also relied on New Jersey's interest in workplace injuries and the location of witnesses and evidence.
The New Jersey Supreme Court granted certification, 196 N.J. 344 (2008), affirmed, and remanded for merits proceedings. 201 N.J. 48, 987 A.2d 575 (2010). Its rule subjected a foreign manufacturer to jurisdiction when the manufacturer knew or reasonably should have known that a nationwide distribution system might produce sales in any
State and took no reasonable step to exclude New Jersey. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed, 6-3.
Justice Kennedy wrote for four Justices. Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Alito, supplied the two additional votes for reversal through a narrower concurrence in the judgment. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented. Because no rationale commanded five votes, the Court's judgment binds the parties while the separate opinions define the competing doctrinal paths. Justice Breyer's fact-specific rationale is commonly treated as the narrowest ground supporting the judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 11, 2001, a three-ton Model 640 Shear severed four fingers from Nicastro's right hand while he operated it at Curcio Scrap Metal in Saddle Brook, New Jersey. Nicastro alleged that the shear lacked a safety guard and sought damages for medical expenses, lost wages, pain, and other injuries. Curcio had encountered the machine at a 1994 or
1995 Las Vegas scrap-recycling convention and purchased it from McIntyre America in 1995 for $24,900. The distributor shipped it from Ohio to New Jersey.
McIntyre UK appointed McIntyre America as its exclusive U.S. distributor. The distributor agreed to promote and sell the machines throughout the United States. McIntyre UK officials attended annual industry conventions with the distributor in Chicago, Las Vegas, New Orleans, Orlando, San Diego, and San Francisco. They attended no New Jersey convention. The distributor shaped advertising and sales efforts according to McIntyre UK's direction and guidance when possible; correspondence also suggested that some inventory remained McIntyre UK's property until sale, functioning as consigned stock.
McIntyre UK held U.S. and European patents. Its product materials described worldwide use, incorporated hydraulic parts available through international outlets, and directed operators to U.S. safety standards. The company sought sales across the national U.S. market. The record established up to four New Jersey machines and suggested that the accident machine was the only confirmed New Jersey sale.
McIntyre UK maintained no New Jersey office, property, tax obligation, advertising, employees, or direct shipment.
The independent distributor made the sale to Curcio. Jurisdictional discovery produced no list of New Jersey prospects, no New Jersey trade-show attendance, and no recurring flow of machines into the State.
sections.Issue: May New Jersey exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a British manufacturer in a products-liability action arising from a machine sold and causing injury in New Jersey when the manufacturer cultivated the United States market through an independent national distributor and trade shows, while the record showed one confirmed New Jersey sale and no conduct directed specifically at New Jersey?
sections.Holding:
The Supreme Court reversed New Jersey's assertion of jurisdiction. Justice Breyer's narrower concurrence resolved the case on the jurisdictional record: one isolated sale, national marketing activity outside New Jersey, and the absence of a regular New Jersey sales flow or forum-specific sales effort failed to establish purposeful availment under existing precedents. The four-Justice plurality would require conduct showing an intention to invoke or benefit from New
Jersey's sovereign authority. The three dissenters found jurisdiction because McIntyre UK deliberately developed the entire U.S. market through a distributor and its product reached and injured a New Jersey user through that arrangement.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Kennedy's plurality - four votes: Personal jurisdiction concerns the lawful authority of a sovereign to bind a defendant. In an ordinary products case, authority rests on the defendant's purposeful availment of that sovereign's benefits and protections. The relevant sovereign was New Jersey because the suit was in state court. McIntyre UK's efforts toward the United States as a national market did not themselves establish submission to New Jersey's authority.
Plurality application: The distributor's nationwide mandate, conventions in other States, and up to four New Jersey machines showed a desire for U.S. sales. The evidence showed no New Jersey advertisement, employee visit, shipment, office, property, tax payment, or other act invoking New Jersey law. The plurality reserved whether Congress could authorize federal jurisdiction based on aggregate national contacts under the Fifth Amendment.
Justice Breyer's concurrence - two votes: Existing precedent resolved this limited record. World-Wide Volkswagen rejected jurisdiction based on one product's isolated arrival. The separate Asahi opinions identified a regular sales flow, additional forum-related conduct, or significant volume, value, and hazard as facts supporting jurisdiction. Nicastro carried the burden of establishing jurisdiction and proved one confirmed sale, no regular New Jersey flow, and no specific New Jersey effort.
Questions left open by the concurrence: Justice Breyer declined to adopt the plurality's broader sovereignty and forum-targeting theory. He also rejected New Jersey's automatic nationwide-distribution rule. The record offered no occasion to decide jurisdiction for high-volume nationwide sales, direct internet sales, fulfillment through a large intermediary, geographically targeted digital advertising, or other modern distribution practices.
Justice Ginsburg's dissent - three votes: McIntyre UK retained an exclusive distributor to develop the whole United
States, joined the distributor at trade shows, designed for U.S. use, and sought revenue wherever U.S. customers lived.
New Jersey formed part of that deliberately cultivated market. The distributor brought the shear to New Jersey through the commercial system the manufacturer created, and the shear caused the forum injury underlying the suit.
Dissent's distinction from precedent: World-Wide Volkswagen involved a consumer who carried a locally sold car into Oklahoma, while the dealer and regional distributor had directed no conduct there. Here, a national distribution system produced the New Jersey sale. Asahi involved a component seller with limited control and a surviving foreign indemnity dispute; McIntyre UK actively sought U.S. customers and faced a local worker's product claim at the place of sale and injury.
Precedential rule: Six Justices agreed that this record failed to support jurisdiction. Five Justices rejected the plurality's broad reasoning: Justices Breyer and Alito withheld assent from it, and the three dissenters opposed it. For class and exam analysis, state the fractured vote, apply Justice Breyer's isolated-sale rationale as the narrow ground, and analyze unresolved distribution patterns under the competing opinions and other binding precedents.
Exam rule: Begin with the forum sovereign and identify every act attributable to the manufacturer. Trace how the product reached the forum. Quantify forum sales, distinguish an isolated occurrence from a regular flow, identify forum targeting or additional conduct, allocate the jurisdictional burden to the plaintiff, and state which opinion supplies each proposed rule.

briefs.title: Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz
briefs.citation: 471 U.S. 462 (1985). Supreme Court of the United States. No. 83-2097; argued January 8, 1985; decided May 20, 1985. Brennan, J., for a six-Justice majority; Stevens, J., joined by White, J., dissenting; Powell, J., took no part. Review of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

sections.Parties:
Appellant / plaintiff: Burger King Corporation, a Florida corporation with principal offices in Miami that licensed and supervised restaurant franchises. Appellee / defendant: John Rudzewicz, a Michigan resident and senior partner in a
Detroit accounting firm who supplied investment capital and personally assumed a twenty-year franchise obligation.
Other defendant below: Brian MacShara, a Michigan resident who proposed the venture and managed the restaurant.
MacShara allowed his judgment to become final and did not participate in the Supreme Court appeal.
sections.Procedural History:
In May 1981, Burger King sued Rudzewicz and MacShara in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of
Florida. Federal subject-matter jurisdiction rested on diversity, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a), and the federal trademark grant, §
1338(a). Burger King alleged breach through failure to send required payments to Miami and trademark infringement through continued operation after termination. It sought damages, an injunction, possession, fees, and costs. The defendants were served in Michigan under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4 and entered special appearances challenging personal jurisdiction.
After a hearing, the district court denied the jurisdictional motions. It applied Florida Statutes § 48.193(1)(g), which reaches a person who breaches a contract in Florida by failing to perform acts required there. The defendants answered, and they counterclaimed under the Michigan Franchise Investment Law. Following a three-day bench trial, the court reaffirmed jurisdiction, found breach and trademark infringement, rejected the counterclaim, entered $228,875 in joint and several contract damages, ordered closure or surrender of the restaurant, and awarded fees and costs.
MacShara took no appeal. Rudzewicz compromised with Burger King and waived appellate review of the trademark-infringement finding and injunction. A divided Eleventh Circuit panel reversed the remaining judgment.
Burger King Corp. v. MacShara, 724 F.2d 1505 (11th Cir. 1984). The parties had stipulated that Florida's long-arm statute reached Rudzewicz, so the panel decided federal due process and held Florida litigation fundamentally unfair.
Rehearing en banc was denied, 729 F.2d 1468.
Burger King sought a direct Supreme Court appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1254(2), a former provision allowing appeal when a court of appeals held a state statute unconstitutional. The Supreme Court dismissed that route because the
Eleventh Circuit had accepted a statutory stipulation and had not clearly adjudged the Florida statute unconstitutional.
Using 28 U.S.C. § 2103, the Court treated the jurisdictional statement as a certiorari petition, granted it, reversed 6-2, and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
Burger King granted twenty-year trademark licenses, leased standardized facilities, and provided market research, advertising assistance, management training, accounting guidance, and operational systems. Franchisees paid a $40,000 initial fee, monthly royalties and advertising charges, and rent tied partly to gross sales. They accepted detailed standards governing food, service, premises, staffing, insurance, accounting, default, and termination.
Burger King's structure divided functions between Miami headquarters and ten district offices. The agreements established the franchise relationship in Miami, selected Florida law, and required fees and notices to be sent to Miami.
Headquarters set policy and controlled major disputes; the Michigan district office handled routine monitoring and relayed matters beyond its authority.
Rudzewicz and MacShara applied through the Birmingham, Michigan, office in autumn 1978. Miami approved a preliminary agreement in February 1979. MacShara attended management training in Miami, and the franchisees bought $165,000 in equipment from Burger King's Miami division. During five months of negotiation, disputes arose over development fees, building design, rent, and personal liability. The franchisees negotiated through both Michigan and Miami, obtained limited concessions from Miami, and began operating in Drayton Plains in June 1979. Rudzewicz personally assumed obligations exceeding $1 million over twenty years.
A late-1979 recession reduced patronage, and the franchisees fell behind on payments due in Miami. Headquarters sent default notices and conducted extended negotiations by telephone and mail, handled credit and refinancing discussions, imposed cost-cutting measures, terminated the franchise, and ordered surrender of the premises. Rudzewicz and
MacShara continued operating under Burger King's marks. Rudzewicz maintained his residence, restaurant, staff, and ordinary business operations in Michigan and personally never visited Florida.
sections.Issue: Does Florida's exercise of specific personal jurisdiction satisfy the Fourteenth Amendment when a Michigan franchisee formed a carefully structured twenty-year relationship with a Florida corporation, accepted continuing supervision and obligations centered in Miami, sent payments and communications there, and allegedly caused forum-related injury through breach, while conducting the restaurant's physical operations in Michigan?
sections.Holding: Yes. Rudzewicz deliberately created a substantial and continuing relationship with Burger King's Miami headquarters, and Burger King's claims arose from that relationship. The negotiations, contemplated future consequences, contract terms, and actual course of dealing established purposeful Florida contacts. Those contacts made jurisdiction presumptively reasonable, and Rudzewicz presented no compelling fairness showing sufficient to overcome that conclusion. The Court reversed the Eleventh Circuit and remanded.
sections.Reasoning:
Constitutional function: Personal jurisdiction protects an individual liberty interest by ensuring fair warning about the sovereigns capable of entering binding judgments. That warning lets a potential defendant structure primary conduct, insure, price risk, choose contractual protections, and anticipate where suit may occur. The right is waivable through consent and other legal arrangements.
Stage one - purposeful minimum contacts and relatedness: Specific jurisdiction requires forum contacts created by the defendant's own purposeful conduct and a claim arising out of or relating to those contacts. Purposeful availment identifies deliberate affiliation that invokes the forum's benefits and protections. Mail, telephone, and continuing interstate obligations can create that affiliation because modern commercial activity routinely operates across state lines.
Contract analysis: The existence of an interstate contract begins the inquiry. Courts evaluate prior negotiations, contemplated future consequences, contract terms, and the parties' actual course of dealing. These features reveal the relationship the defendant chose to create. A contract often records earlier negotiations and organizes future performance, so its jurisdictional significance comes from the full commercial relationship.
Application to Rudzewicz: He reached from Michigan to obtain a long-term affiliation with a Florida enterprise, negotiated contested terms with Miami, accepted a twenty-year regulated relationship, promised payments and notices to Miami, communicated repeatedly with headquarters, and depended on Miami for major decisions. The breach claims arose directly from payments due there and continuing use of a relationship governed from there. These were substantial, deliberate contacts.
Choice of law: The Florida choice-of-law clause selected the governing substantive law and stated that the agreement became valid upon acceptance in Miami. It did not select an exclusive litigation forum and could not create jurisdiction by itself. Combined with the long-term relationship and course of dealing, it reinforced Rudzewicz's deliberate affiliation with Florida and notice that Florida law would protect and regulate the relationship.
Stage two - fair play and substantial justice: After purposeful contacts are established, courts consider the defendant's litigation burden, forum interest, plaintiff's convenient and effective relief, interstate efficiency, and shared substantive policies. Strong fairness considerations can make jurisdiction reasonable on a comparatively modest contact showing. A defendant with purposeful contacts must present a compelling case that the factors make jurisdiction unconstitutional.
Fairness application: Florida had a legitimate interest in claims concerning obligations deliberately centered there.
Michigan's franchise policy could be accommodated through choice-of-law rules. The record supplied no concrete witness or evidence burden of constitutional magnitude; ordinary inconvenience could be addressed through transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Disparity in resources alone did not defeat the consequences of Rudzewicz's purposeful commercial affiliation.
Trial findings and Rule 52(a): The district court found after trial that Burger King made no misrepresentations, that the franchisees were experienced and sophisticated, and that they acted free of economic duress imposed by Burger
King. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a)'s clear-error standard governed those findings. The appellate record supplied no basis for a definite and firm conviction that the trial judge had erred.
Justice Stevens's dissent: The dissent emphasized Rudzewicz's Michigan residence, restaurant, employees, taxes, customers, face-to-face dealings, and operational supervision. It viewed the Michigan office as the practical center of the relationship and found the distant Miami provisions insufficient to give a small franchisee fair warning of Florida litigation. The dissent would have affirmed the Eleventh Circuit's fairness assessment.
Exam rule: For a contract dispute, identify who initiated the interstate relationship; map negotiations, expected duration, future obligations, payment destination, governing law, decisionmaking authority, and course of dealing;
connect the claim to those contacts; then apply all five fairness factors. Once purposeful contacts exist, specify the compelling hardship or policy conflict the defendant offers to defeat jurisdiction.

briefs.title: Doctrinal synthesis: specific jurisdiction

sections.Preamble:
1. Historical Line of Doctrine
Pennoyer organized adjudicatory power around territorial presence, service, consent, and property. International Shoe made the defendant's forum contacts and the fairness of adjudication the governing framework for absent defendants.
Hanson required an act by which the defendant purposefully avails itself of the forum. World-Wide Volkswagen tied foreseeability to conduct that makes forum litigation reasonably anticipatable and described products deliberately delivered into multistate markets. Burger King systematized purposeful contacts, claim connection, and fairness. Asahi divided the Court over distribution networks, and Nicastro preserved that division while deciding an isolated-sale record.
2. The Two-Stage Specific-Jurisdiction Structure
Stage one: identify forum contacts created by the defendant through purposeful affiliation, direction, or availment, then connect the claim to those contacts. Stage two: evaluate fair play and substantial justice through the defendant's burden, the forum's interest, the plaintiff's effective-relief interest, systemic efficiency, and shared substantive policies.
Burger King states the structure. Asahi shows that extreme international burdens and minimal forum interests can defeat jurisdiction. Nicastro turns on the adequacy of the forum-contact showing.
3. Contracts and Distribution Networks Use the Same Constitutional Principle
Purposeful availment asks whether the defendant created the forum affiliation that produced the litigation. In Burger
King, the defendant chose a continuing relationship centered in Florida. In distribution cases, the disputed question is what manufacturer conduct connects it to the particular State: forum targeting, knowledge of a regular sales flow, sales volume and value, distributor instructions, product adaptation, or a combination of those facts.
4. Exact Opinion Map
Asahi: eight Justices joined the fairness holding; four supported O'Connor's stream-of-commerce-plus rule; four supported Brennan's regular-flow rule; three supported Stevens's volume-value-hazard inquiry. Nicastro: four supported Kennedy's state-sovereignty and forum-targeting rationale; two concurred only in the isolated-sale result;
three supported national-market targeting as sufficient. Burger King: six joined the majority, two dissented, and one took no part.
5. The Controlling Lesson of the Fractured Cases
Asahi establishes its fairness result and leaves competing minimum-contacts methods. Nicastro establishes that one confirmed sale plus general national marketing on its record did not support jurisdiction. Justice Breyer's concurrence supplies the narrow ground: the plaintiff showed no regular forum flow and no additional forum-directed conduct. The plurality's broader demand for submission to a particular State received four votes and remains persuasive reasoning rather than a majority rule.
6. Foreseeability Stated Precisely
Jurisdictional foreseeability concerns whether the defendant's own conduct and forum connection make suit there reasonably anticipatable. Burger King locates that predictability in a deliberately created Florida relationship. Brennan's
Asahi opinion locates it in known, regular forum sales. O'Connor locates it in forum-directed additional conduct.
Breyer's Nicastro concurrence finds one isolated sale inadequate under either line.
7. International Defendants
A state court measures the foreign defendant's contacts with that State under the Fourteenth Amendment. Asahi and the
Nicastro plurality reserve whether Congress may authorize a federal court to use aggregate national contacts under the
Fifth Amendment. International fairness also gives weight to the burden of a foreign legal system, other nations' substantive and procedural interests, and the Federal Government's foreign-relations interest.
8. Fast Class and Exam Sequence
Name the forum and the sovereign exercising power. Identify the precise claim and its connection to the forum. List only contacts created by the defendant. Classify those contacts as deliberate affiliation, forum-directed conduct, regular distribution, or isolated product arrival. State each governing opinion's vote count. Apply the five fairness factors with record facts. Conclude separately on purposeful contacts, relatedness, and reasonableness.
SOURCE NOTES
Full Supreme Court opinions: Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court, 480 U.S. 102 (1987); J. McIntyre
Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro, 564 U.S. 873 (2011); Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462 (1985). The briefs use the full opinions, separate opinions, syllabi, and reported procedural citations.
State-court record for Nicastro: Nicastro v. McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd., 201 N.J. 48, 987 A.2d 575 (2010).
The state opinion supplies the two trial-court dismissals, two Appellate Division reversals, jurisdictional discovery, lower-court factual findings, and New Jersey's stream-of-commerce rule.
Reading note: Vote counts are stated at the level of each proposition. A unanimous judgment does not convert a four-Justice rationale into a holding of the Court. Each brief therefore identifies the judgment, the portions joined by a majority, and the separate tests advanced by fewer than five Justices.

briefs.title: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.
briefs.citation: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co., 339 U.S. 306 (1950). Supreme Court of the United States, argued February 8, 1950, decided April 24, 1950. Justice Jackson wrote the opinion for the Court; Justice Burton dissented, and Justice Douglas took no part. The case begins at casebook page 237 and concerns what notice due process requires before a court may enter a judgment that binds people who

sections.Parties: Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company, a New York trust company, was the trustee of a common trust fund and the petitioner in the state accounting proceeding; in the Supreme Court it was an appellee. Mullane was the appellant. The Surrogate's Court had appointed him special guardian and attorney for all persons, known or unknown and not otherwise appearing, who had or might later have an interest in the income of the fund. A special guardian is a representative the court appoints to protect people who are absent or unable to act for themselves. Vaughan, also an appellee, had been appointed to represent those interested in the principal. The beneficiaries themselves never appeared. The trust company sought a decree approving its account that would bind every beneficiary; Mullane sought to defeat the decree on the ground that the beneficiaries had not received constitutionally adequate notice.
sections.Material Facts:
New York Banking Law § 100-c allowed a trust company, with the approval of the State Banking Board, to pool the assets of an unlimited number of trusts for which it was trustee into a single fund for investment.
Each participating trust shared ratably in the fund's income, gains, losses, and expenses, but no trust or beneficiary owned any particular asset, and exclusive management rested with the trust company. Pooling gave small trusts the diversification and economy of management that only large trusts could otherwise obtain; the District of Columbia and some thirty other states had similar statutes. The trustee had to account to the court twelve to fifteen months after establishing a fund and every three years after that. A decree settling an account was binding and conclusive, as to any matter set forth in the account, on everyone with an interest in the common fund or in any participating trust. 339 U.S. at 307-09.
Central Hanover established a common fund in January 1946 and, in March 1947, petitioned the Surrogate's
Court, New York's court for estates and trusts, to settle its first account. During the accounting period 113 trusts participated, about half inter vivos (created by a living settlor) and half testamentary (created by a will), with gross capital of nearly three million dollars. The record did not show the number or residence of the beneficiaries, but they were many, and some lived outside New York. The only notice of the accounting was the notice the statute required under § 100-c(12): publication in a local newspaper for four successive weeks, stating the trust company's name and address, the name and date of establishment of the fund, and a list of the participating trusts. The notice named no beneficiary.
Earlier, when each trust first entered the fund, the trust company had mailed notice under § 100-c(9) to every beneficiary of full age and sound mind whose name and address were then known and who was entitled to share in income or, if the relevant event had already occurred, in principal. That notice enclosed the statutory provisions on notice and judicial settlement. As the Supreme Court read the New York decision, the decree would settle all questions respecting the management of the fund and would seal and terminate every claim the beneficiaries might have against the trust company for improper management during the accounting
period. The beneficiaries' interests also bore the fees and expenses of the guardians appointed to represent them. Id. at 309-11.
sections.Procedural History:
Mullane appeared specially, meaning that he appeared only to contest the court's authority without submitting to it. He objected that the statutory notice was inadequate under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth
Amendment, so the Surrogate's Court lacked jurisdiction to enter a final and binding decree. The Surrogate overruled the objections and entered a final decree accepting the accounts. The Appellate Division affirmed, and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, holding the notice constitutionally sufficient. The case reached the Supreme Court on appeal, the route then available when a state's highest court upheld a state statute against a federal constitutional challenge. Id. at 309-11.
sections.Issue:
Did New York have power to bind beneficiaries who lived outside the state and were not personally served, when the decree adjudicated personal claims against the trustee rather than title to specific property, and
Pennoyer v. Neff limited a state's power over nonresidents in actions in personam? If so, was notice by newspaper publication constitutionally adequate for each category of beneficiary: those whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence, those whose interests were conjectural or future, and known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had on its books?
sections.Holding:
The State's power to settle the account did not depend on whether the proceeding was labeled in rem, quasi in rem, or in personam. New York's interest in closing trusts that exist by the grace of its laws and are administered under the supervision of its courts established the right of its courts to determine the interests of all claimants, resident or nonresident, provided the procedure gave them full opportunity to appear and be heard.
Due process requires, before any proceeding that is to be accorded finality, notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections. The notice must reasonably convey the required information and allow a reasonable time to appear. The means chosen must be such as one desirous of actually informing the absentee might reasonably adopt. A method is valid if it is reasonably certain to inform those affected or, where conditions do not reasonably permit such notice, if it is not substantially less likely to bring home notice than other feasible and customary substitutes.
Publication was sufficient for beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence and for those whose interests were conjectural or future. It was insufficient for known present beneficiaries of known residence, who were entitled at least to notice by ordinary mail to the addresses in the trustee's records. Personal service was not required. The Court held the notice prescribed by § 100-c(12) incompatible with the Fourteenth Amendment as a basis for an adjudication depriving known persons whose whereabouts are also known of substantial property rights. Id. at 311-20.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the New York Court of Appeals and remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with its opinion. The Court expressly overruled the constitutional objections insofar as they were made on behalf of beneficiaries whose interests or addresses were unknown to the trustee; the defect lay in the notice to known present beneficiaries.
sections.Reasoning:
Mullane's first argument drew on Pennoyer. An action in personam determines a person's own rights and obligations, and under Pennoyer it required personal service within the state to bind a nonresident. An action in rem determines rights in a thing and binds everyone. Because the decree affected neither title to nor possession of any thing and adjudicated only the beneficiaries' personal rights to surcharge their trustee,
Mullane argued, it was in personam and could not bind nonresidents served only by publication. The Court declined to decide the case by classification. Proceedings to settle fiduciary accounts had been called in rem, quasi in rem, and in the nature of a proceeding in rem, and this one had features of both categories. The distinctions had originated in the property law of a very different legal system, and the rise of intangible property had blurred them. The requirements of the Fourteenth Amendment, Justice Jackson wrote, do not depend on a classification so elusive and so variable from state to state. The State's interest in closing trusts created under its law and supervised by its courts justified adjudicating the claims of all beneficiaries, wherever they lived, if the procedure gave them full opportunity to be heard. Id. at 311-13.
The question of power therefore gave way to the question of opportunity. Whatever else the Due Process
Clause requires, a deprivation of life, liberty, or property by adjudication must be preceded by notice and an opportunity for hearing appropriate to the nature of the case. The accounting could deprive beneficiaries of property in two ways: it could cut off their claims against the trustee for negligent or illegal impairment of their interests, and it could diminish their interests by allowing fees and expenses to a guardian who conducted a possibly fruitless contest in their names but without their knowledge. Against the State's vital interest in a final settlement stood the individual's interest, which Grannis v. Ordean defined as the opportunity to be heard. That right has little reality or worth unless a person is informed that the matter is pending and can choose whether to appear or default, acquiesce or contest. Id. at 313-14.
Personal service of written notice within the jurisdiction is the classic form of notice and is always adequate, but the Court had never held it indispensable in every case, and a reading of the Due Process Clause that placed impossible or impractical obstacles in the way of settling trusts could not be justified. The Court therefore stated a functional standard: notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties and afford them an opportunity to object, conveying the required information and allowing a reasonable time to respond. It added that "when notice is a person's due, process which is a mere gesture is not due process." The means employed must be those that a person who actually wanted to inform the absentee might reasonably use. Id. at 313-15.
Publication failed that test as a way of informing known people. It would be idle, the Court wrote, to pretend that publication alone is a reliable means of telling interested parties that their rights are before the courts.
Chance alone brings a small-type advertisement in the back pages of a newspaper to the attention of even a local resident, and the odds are large that it will never reach someone who lives outside the paper's circulation area. This notice did not even name the beneficiaries whose attention it was supposed to attract, so acquaintances could not call it to their attention. Measured against actual notice, the Court regarded it as no more than a feint. Id. at 315-16.
Publication has traditionally been acceptable as a supplement to action that itself is likely to warn an owner.
Libel of a ship (an admiralty proceeding against a vessel), attachment of a chattel, or entry upon real estate in the name of the law may reasonably be expected to come promptly to the owner's attention, because owners of tangible property usually arrange to learn of direct attacks on it. A state may assume that someone who leaves property within its borders has either abandoned it or left a caretaker who will warn of danger. Neither assumption held here. The beneficiaries had not abandoned their interests, and their caretaker, the trustee, became their adversary in the accounting. The trustee was released from any duty to warn them, and not even the special guardian was required or apparently expected to communicate with them. Id. at 316.
Publication remained acceptable where nothing better was reasonably possible. For beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence, an indirect and even probably futile means of notice was all the situation permitted, and in the typical case it was not much more likely to fail than any alternative a legislature could prescribe. The State could also dispense with more certain notice to beneficiaries whose interests were conjectural or future, or who could be discovered only by investigation and had not come to the trustee's knowledge in the ordinary course of business. Keeping track of changes among income beneficiaries, presumptive remaindermen (those expected to take the principal when the income interests end), and the larger number of contingent beneficiaries would impose a severe burden on the plan and would likely dissipate its advantages. Due process did not require those searches. Id. at 317-18.
Known present beneficiaries of known residence stood on a different footing. Exceptions made in the name of necessity do not sweep away the rule that, within the limits of practicability, notice must be reasonably calculated to reach interested parties; where names and addresses are at hand, the reasons for resorting to less reliable means disappear. The trustee had the income beneficiaries' names and addresses on its books and periodically sent them their income. Mailing them a copy of the statute months or years before the accounting did not satisfy the requirement. Id. at 318.
The Court did not require personal service, even on known beneficiaries. The trust presupposed a large number of small interests, and each beneficiary's interest in the integrity of the fund and the fidelity of the trustee was identical to that of the class. Objections sustained on behalf of any beneficiary would benefit all, so notice reasonably certain to reach most of those interested in objecting would safeguard the interests of everyone, and reasonable risks that notice might not reach every beneficiary were justified. The Court also observed that personal service outside the issuing state would serve the end of actual notice, whatever power of compulsion it lacked, a remark that separates the function of notice from the question of a court's power.
Id. at 318-19.
The statutory notice to known beneficiaries was inadequate because it was not reasonably calculated to reach people who could easily be informed by other means at hand; its failure to reach everyone was not the constitutional defect. The mails were an efficient and inexpensive means of communication, and the trust company's own mailing when the fund was established showed that mailed notice at the time of accounting would not seriously burden the plan. The Court asked whether publication would satisfy a prudent businessman, counting his pennies but finding it in his interest to convey information to many people whose names and addresses were in his files, and concluded that it would not. Quoting McDonald v. Mabee, it warned that great caution should be used not to let fiction deny the fair play that can be secured only by a pretty close adhesion to fact. Id. at 319-20.
sections.Separate Opinions: Justice Burton dissented. He emphasized that common trusts are available only when the instruments creating the participating trusts permit participation in a common fund, and he regarded the question whether further notice should supplement the notice and representation New York provided as one properly within the State's discretion; in his view the Federal Constitution did not require more. Justice Douglas took no part in the consideration or decision of the case. The casebook omits the dissent. Id. at 320 (Burton, J., dissenting).
sections.Notes:
Mullane separates two requirements that Pennoyer had combined: a court's power over the parties or the property, and the notice that must precede a binding judgment. The Court treated New York's power as established by the State's interest in trusts created under its law and then tested the notice independently. A court with power over a defendant can still violate due process by proceeding on inadequate notice, and personal service outside the forum can give excellent notice while conferring no power. The case also reduced the significance of the in rem and in personam labels for notice purposes; Shaffer v. Heitner, which subjected all assertions of state-court jurisdiction to the minimum-contacts standard, later made a similar move for jurisdiction.
The standard evaluates the method chosen, judged by what the sender knew or could reasonably learn, rather than whether the party actually received notice. It has two branches: a method reasonably certain to inform, or, where that is not reasonably possible, a method not substantially less likely to reach the party than feasible and customary substitutes. The analysis proceeds by sorting interested parties into categories, as the Court did: known parties with known addresses (mail at least), parties who cannot be identified or located with due diligence (publication can suffice), and parties with conjectural or remote interests (publication can suffice because investigation costs would defeat the proceeding). The Court's weighing of the individual interest against the cost of better notice anticipates the balancing the Court later formalized in Mathews v. Eldridge.
Two limits deserve attention. The Court did not require personal service, and its willingness to accept some risk that individual beneficiaries would not receive notice rested on the identity of interests within the class, reasoning that fits representative proceedings better than ordinary two-party suits. In Eisen v. Carlisle &
Jacquelin, 417 U.S. 156 (1974), the Court relied on Mullane in requiring individual notice to all members of a Rule 23(b)(3) class who can be identified through reasonable effort. The notes that follow Mullane in the casebook, summarized in the next section of this packet, apply the known-address rule to tax sales, condemnation, probate claims, eviction, and forfeiture.

briefs.title: Reasonable Notice After Mullane

sections.Sources:
Casebook pp. 245-251, Notes and Questions 1 through 11 following Mullane. The notes trace how courts applied Mullane's reasonable-calculation standard to publication, posting, mail, statutory agents, the time allowed to respond, the content of the notice, and advance waivers of notice. Citations follow the casebook.
The recurring question is what the sender knew, or could reasonably have learned, when it chose its method of notice.
Publication When Names and Addresses Are Known
McDonald v. Mabee, 243 U.S. 90 (1917), which Mullane relied on, involved a suit on a promissory note against a Texas domiciliary who had left the state to take up a domicile elsewhere while his family remained in Texas. Service was attempted by publication in a local newspaper once a week for four weeks, Mabee never appeared, and the Supreme Court held the resulting judgment void: to dispense with personal service, the substitute most likely to reach the defendant is the least that ought to be required. Mullane's own formulation is somewhat more forgiving, because it accepts a method that is not substantially less likely to reach the party than feasible substitutes; the casebook asks whether Mullane permits constructive service only when it is the method most likely to succeed.
The Court then applied the known-address rule to government proceedings against property. In Walker v.
City of Hutchinson, 352 U.S. 112 (1956), notice of a condemnation proceeding (a government taking of private property for public use) by publication in a local newspaper was inadequate for a resident owner whose name was known from official records. In Schroeder v. City of New York, 371 U.S. 208 (1962), newspaper notice in two small communities far from vacant land, together with signs posted on trees near the property, was inadequate because the owner's name and address could be found in deed records and tax rolls.
Mennonite Board of Missions v. Adams, 462 U.S. 791 (1983), extended the rule to a mortgagee whose interest would be affected by a tax sale. Because the mortgagee was identified in a publicly recorded mortgage, publication and posting had to be supplemented by mail to its last known address or by personal service; notice by mail or other means as certain to ensure actual notice is a minimum constitutional precondition to a proceeding that will adversely affect any party whose name and address are reasonably ascertainable. Justice O'Connor, joined by Justices Powell and Rehnquist, dissented on the ground that the majority had adopted a bright-line rule at odds with Mullane's balancing. Five years later Justice O'Connor wrote for the Court in Tulsa Professional Collection Services, Inc. v. Pope, 485 U.S. 478 (1988), which held that Oklahoma's probate nonclaim statute, barring creditors' claims not filed within two months after published notice, could not bar a known or reasonably ascertainable creditor (there, a hospital owed for the decedent's care) without actual notice. The Court added that actual notice may be dispensed with for creditors whose claims are merely conjectural.
Posting and Mail
Greene v. Lindsey, 456 U.S. 444 (1982), held that posting eviction notices on apartment doors in a public housing project was inadequate where process servers knew that such notices were "not infrequently" removed by children or other tenants; in those circumstances due process required notice by mail. Justice
O'Connor, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist, dissented, questioning whether mail is more reliable than posting and noting that unattended mailboxes are subject to theft. The case shows that Mullane asks about the reliability of a method in the circumstances the sender knew, not in the abstract. The casebook also asks whether the tenants' interest in avoiding public posting of their financial troubles should count in the analysis.
Actual Receipt and Follow-Up
Dusenbery v. United States, 534 U.S. 161 (2002), involved the forfeiture of about $30,000 and a car belonging to a federal prisoner. The FBI published notice and sent certified letters to the prison, to his residence at the time of arrest, and to his stepmother's address, and the prison followed logged procedures for delivering certified mail to inmates. The Court held the notice adequate: due process does not require actual receipt, and the government need not make heroic efforts to ensure delivery. Justice Ginsburg, joined by
Justices Stevens, Souter, and Breyer, dissented on the ground that the notice was substantially less likely to succeed than a feasible alternative. No Justice treated the absence of actual notice as itself unconstitutional.
Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 220 (2006), qualified that approach. When a mailed notice of a tax sale came back unclaimed, the State had to take reasonable additional steps to notify the owner if it was practicable to do so.
Chief Justice Roberts reasoned that no one who actually wanted to inform an owner would do nothing after learning that the letter had failed, and he identified reasonable steps: resending the notice by regular mail, posting it on the front door, or addressing mail to the "occupant." The State was not required to search phone books or tax rolls for a new address. Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Scalia and Kennedy, dissented, arguing that reasonableness must be judged when notice is sent and that a duty triggered by later information has no natural end point. Earlier, Covey v. Town of Somers, 351 U.S. 141 (1956), held mailed notice of a tax foreclosure inadequate when sent to a person the town knew had been adjudged insane and committed to a hospital without a guardian. Together, Covey and Jones show that knowledge that a method will fail, whether acquired before or after sending, affects what due process requires.
Statutory Agents
Wuchter v. Pizzutti, 276 U.S. 13 (1928), involved a nonresident-motorist statute like the one upheld in Hess v. Pawloski, which authorized service on the Secretary of State. The statute did not require that notice be sent to the nonresident, and a divided Court held it invalid even though the defendant in fact received notice. A statute of this kind must itself require the plaintiff or the official receiving service to communicate with the defendant. The case measures the statutory scheme rather than the result in a particular case. Szukhent later distinguished Wuchter as a limit on state statutory schemes rather than on private contractual appointments of an agent.
Time and Content of Notice
Notice must allow adequate time to respond. In Roller v. Holly, 176 U.S. 398 (1900), a defendant served in
Virginia was required to defend an action in Texas five days later, and the Court held the procedure violated due process. Federal Rule 12(a) now allows 21 days after service, or 60 days after a waiver request is sent.
Notice must also convey the information a party needs to respond. In Aguchak v. Montgomery Ward Co., 520
P.2d 1352 (Alaska 1974), a seller sued rural buyers of a snowmobile and a freezer in small-claims court and obtained a default judgment of $988.22 plus costs. The summons did not tell the buyers that they could appear by written pleading or that they could request a change of venue, and travel to court would have required an overnight stay costing $186. The Supreme Court of Alaska held that a small-claims summons must include that information and set aside the default judgment.
Advance Waiver of Notice
A cognovit note is a written instrument in which a debtor authorizes entry of judgment against it without notice or hearing if it does not pay when due; it waives prior notice, bars the assertion of defenses, and forecloses appeal from the resulting judgment. In D.H. Overmyer Co. v. Frick Co., 405 U.S. 174 (1972), the
Court held that enforcing a cognovit note does not per se violate due process and that validity depends on the circumstances, including consideration for the waiver and the parties' relative bargaining power. Fuentes v.
Shevin later distinguished Overmyer when it refused to find a waiver in a consumer's printed installment contract.
sections.Application: Start with the proceeding. Mullane applies to any proceeding that will be accorded finality and can deprive a person of property, including tax sales, probate claim bars, evictions, and forfeitures. Identify each class of interested parties and ask what the sender knew or could reasonably ascertain when it gave notice. A name and address available from the sender's own files or from public records call for mail or an equally reliable method; a party who cannot be located with due diligence may be notified by publication. Next, ask whether the method was reliable in the circumstances the sender actually knew, including known reasons it would fail, such as posted notices that disappear, an addressee known to be incompetent, or mail returned unclaimed. Finally, check the time allowed to respond, the information the notice conveyed, and whether the party validly waived notice in advance.

briefs.title: Federal Rule 4: Service of Process

sections.Sources:
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4 (text as last amended in 2016) and casebook pp. 251-272. Service refers to the act of delivering notice of a suit; process refers to the documents delivered, chiefly the summons, the court's formal notice directing the defendant to respond. Rule 4 translates Mullane's constitutional standard into specific authorized methods, so a method Rule 4 does not authorize can be defective even if it would satisfy due process. Courts often forgive technical defects when the defendant received actual notice; the casebook asks whether that tolerance extends to methods used without required court authorization, citing De
Gazelle Group, Inc. v. Tamaz Trading Establishment, 817 F.3d 747 (11th Cir. 2016). Rule 12(b)(4) and (5) supply the motions for challenging defective process and service. Rule 4.
Summons, Issuance, and Who Serves
Under Rule 3, a federal action is commenced by filing a complaint. Rule 4(a) requires the summons to name the court and the parties, be directed to the defendant, state the name and address of the plaintiff's attorney (or of an unrepresented plaintiff), state the time within which the defendant must appear and defend, warn that failure to do so will result in a default judgment, and bear the clerk's signature and the court's seal. Under
Rule 4(b), the plaintiff presents the summons to the clerk after filing the complaint, and the clerk issues a summons for each defendant. Rule 4(c) requires the summons to be served with a copy of the complaint and makes the plaintiff responsible for service within the Rule 4(m) period. Any person who is at least 18 years old and not a party may serve. The court may order service by a United States marshal on the plaintiff's request and must do so for a plaintiff proceeding in forma pauperis (permitted to litigate without paying court fees) or as a seaman under the statute that allows seamen to sue without prepaying fees.
Waiver of Service: Rule 4(d)
Rule 4(d) imposes on individuals, corporations, and associations subject to service under Rules 4(e), (f), or (h) a duty to avoid unnecessary expenses of serving the summons. The rule has a history the casebook traces.
In 1982 Congress rejected a proposed amendment that would have authorized service by registered or certified mail, amid concerns about illegible return receipts, unclaimed mail, and default judgments against people who never received the papers. In 1983 Congress adopted a system modeled on California's, under which the summons and complaint could be mailed by first-class mail with an acknowledgment form, and a defendant who failed without good cause to return it had to pay the cost of personal service. Because that system depended on the defendant's cooperation, the 1993 amendments replaced it with the current request to waive service.
The plaintiff's request must be in writing and addressed to the individual defendant or to an officer or authorized agent of an entity; name the court; include a copy of the complaint, two copies of the waiver form, and a prepaid means of returning one; inform the defendant of the consequences of waiving and not waiving;
state the date the request is sent; give the defendant a reasonable time of at least 30 days to return the waiver (60 days if the request is sent outside any judicial district of the United States); and be sent by first-class mail or other reliable means. The 1993 Advisory Committee Note to the 1993 amendment approved the use of electronic means. A defendant located in the United States who fails without good cause to sign and return a requested waiver must pay the expenses later incurred in making service and the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, of any motion required to collect them.
The incentive to waive is time. A defendant who timely returns a waiver need not answer until 60 days after the request was sent (90 days if sent outside the United States), compared with 21 days after formal service
under Rule 12(a). When the plaintiff files the waiver, no proof of service is required, and the rules apply as if the summons and complaint had been served when the waiver was filed. Waiving service does not waive objections to personal jurisdiction or venue. Because service is treated as occurring only when the waiver is filed, a plaintiff facing a statute of limitations that runs until service may be safer serving formally than waiting for a waiver; the casebook poses that question in its notes.
Individuals in the United States: Rule 4(e)
Rule 4(e)(1) permits service by any method allowed by the law of the state where the district court sits or where service is made. Rule 4(e)(2) adds three federal methods: (A) delivering a copy of the summons and complaint to the individual personally; (B) leaving a copy at the individual's dwelling or usual place of abode with someone of suitable age and discretion who resides there; and (C) delivering a copy to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service.
Personal delivery rarely raises doctrinal questions, but evasive defendants test what delivery requires. The casebook's excerpt from McKelway's 1935 New Yorker profile of process server Harry Grossman illustrates the legal phrase "place and leave with": courts held that throwing papers at James Gordon Bennett and striking him in the chest was not proper service, but that laying papers on the shoulder of a defendant hiding under his wife's petticoats was sufficient. Courts generally treat a server who is in the defendant's presence, makes clear what the papers are, and leaves them near a defendant who refuses to take them as having accomplished personal delivery.
Abode service turns on facts. In National Development Co. v. Triad Holding Corp., 930 F.2d 253 (2d Cir.
1991), a Saudi citizen maintained twelve homes around the world. Papers were left with his housekeeper at his New York apartment, valued at $20 to $25 million, on a day he was actually living there. The Second
Circuit held that a person can have more than one dwelling house or usual place of abode and that service at the one where the defendant was living that day was, if not the most likely method, reasonably calculated to give actual notice. The casebook asks whether the result should change if he had been at another residence that day.
Service on an agent authorized by appointment normally requires an actual appointment for the specific purpose of receiving process. A person's acceptance of process, or claim of authority, does not bind the defendant without evidence that the defendant intended to confer that authority. National Equipment Rental,
Ltd. v. Szukhent, briefed separately, upheld an appointment made in a printed lease.
Corporations and Associations: Rule 4(h)
Rule 4(h)(1) permits service on a corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association in the United States either under state law, through Rule 4(e)(1), or by delivering the summons and complaint to an officer, a managing or general agent, or any other agent authorized by appointment or by law, with an additional mailing to the defendant if a statute appointing the agent so requires. Rule 4(h)(2) governs service abroad by reference to Rule 4(f), excluding personal delivery.
Courts read the categories functionally. In Insurance Co. of North America v. S/S "Hellenic Challenger", 88
F.R.D. 545 (S.D.N.Y. 1980), a marshal left papers in an admiralty cargo suit with a claims adjuster while the claims manager, one of the few employees expressly authorized to accept service, was out sick. The adjuster misplaced the papers, and the defendant learned of the suit only when its bank account was attached after a default judgment. The court upheld service because the adjuster was so integrated into the organization that he would know what to do with the papers: he had accepted service at least twice before and worked next to
the claims manager, separated from him only by the manager's glass-walled office. His loss of the papers was a mistake in the ordinary course of the defendant's business and did not justify relief. By contrast, the casebook cites American Institute of Certified Public Accountants v. Affinity Card, Inc., 8 F. Supp. 2d 372 (S.D.N.Y. 1998), which held service on the vice president of a different corporation sharing the defendant's office insufficient even though both corporations were owned by the same individual, who had received actual notice.
In Fashion Page, Ltd. v. Zurich Insurance Co., 50 N.Y.2d 265 (1980), a receptionist sent a process server to a vice president's executive secretary, who said "I can take it." Rather than decide whether she was a managing agent, the New York Court of Appeals held her an agent authorized by appointment, because she had regularly accepted summonses for at least five years. A corporation may assign the task of accepting process, but it cannot escape the consequences of the procedures it establishes, and a process server may rely on corporate employees to identify the proper person.
Service Abroad: Rule 4(f)
Rule 4(f) governs service on an individual in a foreign country, and Rule 4(h)(2) applies most of it to entities.
Rule 4(f)(1) authorizes any internationally agreed means reasonably calculated to give notice, principally the
Hague Service Convention, which requires each contracting state to designate a Central Authority to receive and execute requests for service from other contracting states; the casebook counted 79 contracting states as of June 2021. Where no agreement applies or the agreement allows other means, Rule 4(f)(2) permits methods reasonably calculated to give notice: the foreign country's own methods, a letter rogatory (a formal request from one court to a foreign court for assistance), or, unless foreign law prohibits it, personal delivery or mail requiring a signed receipt sent by the clerk. Rule 4(f)(3) permits other means not prohibited by international agreement, as the court orders.
Several decisions define the Convention's reach. Water Splash, Inc. v. Menon, 137 S. Ct. 1504 (2017), held that the Convention permits service by mail if the receiving state has not objected and mail service is authorized under otherwise-applicable law. Volkswagenwerk Aktiengesellschaft v. Schlunk, 486 U.S. 694 (1988), held that the Convention applies only when documents must be transmitted abroad, so service on a
German corporation's domestic subsidiary as its involuntary agent under state law did not implicate it. The
Convention does not govern service in noncontracting states, and a voluntary waiver of service may not implicate it at all. In Rio Properties, Inc. v. Rio International Interlink, 284 F.3d 1007 (9th Cir. 2002), the court upheld court-ordered email service on a foreign internet business under Rule 4(f)(3), describing that provision as one means among several rather than an extraordinary last resort; later courts have divided over email and social-media service depending on the evidence that the account is likely to reach the defendant.
For foreign states, Republic of Sudan v. Harrison, 139 S. Ct. 1048 (2019), held that the Foreign Sovereign
Immunities Act's mail provision requires the packet to be addressed and dispatched to the foreign minister at the ministry in the foreign state, not to its embassy in the United States.
Territorial Reach: Rule 4(k)
Serving a summons or filing a waiver establishes personal jurisdiction over a defendant who is subject to the jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction in the state where the district court sits; over a party joined under
Rule 14 or 19 and served within a judicial district of the United States not more than 100 miles from where the summons issued; and when a federal statute authorizes it. Rule 4(k)(2) adds jurisdiction over a defendant on a claim arising under federal law if the defendant is not subject to jurisdiction in any state's courts of general jurisdiction and exercising jurisdiction is consistent with the Constitution and laws of the United
States. Rule 4(k) ties the service rules to the personal-jurisdiction analysis studied earlier: proper service is necessary, but a federal court ordinarily reaches only as far as the forum state's courts could.
Proof of Service and Sewer Service: Rule 4(l)
Unless service is waived, the server must file proof of service, by affidavit unless the server is a marshal or deputy marshal; failure to prove service does not affect the validity of service. This filing is traditionally called the return. In Miedreich v. Lauenstein, 232 U.S. 236 (1914), the Court upheld a mortgage-foreclosure judgment against a state resident who alleged that the sheriff had falsely returned service, treating the return as conclusive because state law allowed recovery against the sheriff on his bond. Today most jurisdictions treat the return as strong evidence of service rather than conclusive proof; a defendant's own denial generally will not overcome a private process server's affidavit, and the required standard of proof varies.
Sewer service is the practice of discarding the papers and filing a false affidavit of service, so that the defendant never learns of the suit and a default judgment follows. In United States v. Brand Jewelers, Inc.,
318 F. Supp. 1293 (S.D.N.Y. 1970), the court held that the United States had standing to enjoin a seller of consumer goods on easy credit from systematically obtaining default judgments through sewer service; the
1972 consent decree vacated defaults obtained from 1969 to 1971 and made the seller's attorney responsible for fair service. New York responded with a series of reforms: its 1970 amendment to CPLR 308(2), which allowed service by leaving papers with a person of suitable age and discretion at the defendant's workplace or home and mailing a second copy, without first showing diligent efforts at personal delivery, a requirement viewed as the main cause of sewer service; requirements in 1973 for detailed statements about how process was served; amendments after a 1986 investigation found that about 48,000 of 140,000 annual default judgments in New York City were tainted; the 2009 Pfau v. Forster & Garbus proceeding against debt-collection firms; and a New York City requirement that licensed process servers keep GPS records of service attempts.
Time Limit and Statutes of Limitations: Rule 4(m)
If a defendant is not served within 90 days after the complaint is filed, the court, on motion or on its own after notice to the plaintiff, must dismiss the action without prejudice as to that defendant or order service within a specified time. If the plaintiff shows good cause for the failure, the court must extend the time for an appropriate period. The Supreme Court has observed that the rule permits an extension even without good cause, Henderson v. United States, 517 U.S. 654 (1996), a point that matters most when the limitations period has run and a dismissal without prejudice would operate as a dismissal with prejudice. The 90-day limit does not apply to service in a foreign country under Rule 4(f), 4(h)(2), or 4(j)(1); the casebook notes that circuits divide over what time limit, if any, then applies.
Timing of service interacts with statutes of limitations. For a claim based on federal law, the action is commenced for limitations purposes when the complaint is filed under Rule 3, West v. Conrail, 481 U.S. 35 (1987). For a state-law claim in federal court, state law usually determines when the action is commenced,
Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., 446 U.S. 740 (1980), and in states that require service to commence an action, a defect in service can be fatal because the limitations period may expire before it is corrected. A challenge to untimely service is generally raised under Rule 12(b)(5).
sections.Application:
Confirm that the summons meets Rule 4(a) and was issued by the clerk. Decide whether to request a waiver, weighing the cost savings against the risk that the limitations period will run before the waiver is filed.
Identify the defendant's category (individual in the United States, individual abroad, entity, government) and the methods available for that category, including methods borrowed from state law. Check who served, where, and on whom: for abode service, whether the place was the defendant's dwelling on that day and the recipient resided there; for agents, whether an actual appointment exists; for entities, whether the recipient's role supports service. Confirm service within 90 days, file proof of service, and consider whether Rule 4(k) and the Constitution support personal jurisdiction. A defendant raises defects in the summons under Rule
12(b)(4), defects in delivery under Rule 12(b)(5), and must do so in its first Rule 12 motion or responsive pleading.

briefs.title: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent
briefs.citation: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent, 375 U.S. 311 (1964). Supreme Court of the United States, argued November 20, 1963, decided January 6, 1964. Justice Stewart wrote for a five-Justice majority. Justice Black dissented, and Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, dissented separately. The case appears at casebook page 257 and concerns whether a person named i

sections.Parties:
National Equipment Rental, Ltd., a corporation with its principal place of business in New York, leased farm equipment to the respondents. It was the plaintiff in the district court and the petitioner in the Supreme Court.
The Szukhents, Michigan farmers who had leased the equipment, were the defendants and respondents.
Florence Weinberg, the person the lease designated to receive process for them in New York, was not a party.
The lessor sought to sue the Szukhents in New York for unpaid rent; the Szukhents sought to quash service on the ground that Weinberg was not their agent.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1961 the Szukhents leased farm equipment from the petitioner on a printed form less than a page and a half long, containing eighteen numbered paragraphs. The last paragraph, printed just above the respondents' signatures in the same type as the rest of the form, provided that the agreement would be deemed made in
Nassau County, New York, and governed by New York law, and that the lessee designated Florence
Weinberg, of 47-21 Forty-first Street, Long Island City, New York, as agent for the purpose of accepting service of any process within New York. The Szukhents did not know Weinberg. The dissent later noted that she was chosen by the company, had never met the Szukhents, received nothing from them, undertook no obligation to them, and was revealed after the suit began to be the wife of one of the company's officers. 375
U.S. at 312-14; id. at 319 (Black, J., dissenting).
In 1962 the petitioner sued in federal district court in New York, alleging that the Szukhents had failed to make the periodic payments the lease required. A United States marshal delivered two copies of the summons and complaint to Weinberg. The same day she mailed them to the Szukhents with a letter stating that the documents had been served on her as their agent under the lease. The petitioner also notified the
Szukhents by certified mail that process had been served on Weinberg. Id. at 313-14.
sections.Procedural History: On the Szukhents' motion, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York quashed service. It reasoned that although Weinberg had promptly notified the Szukhents and sent them the papers, the lease did not explicitly require her to do so, so there was a "failure of the agency arrangement to achieve intrinsic and continuing reality." The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, 311 F.2d 79 (2d Cir.), and the Supreme Court granted certiorari. Id. at 314.
sections.Issue: Was a person designated in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees, who was a stranger to them and whose appointment did not expressly require her to forward process, "an agent authorized by appointment" to receive service within Federal Rule 4(d)(1) (now Rule 4(e)(2)(C)), where she in fact promptly transmitted the summons and complaint to them?
sections.Holding: Parties to a contract may agree in advance to submit to the jurisdiction of a given court, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or even to waive notice altogether. Under general principles of agency law, an appointed agent's prompt acceptance of process and transmittal of it to the principal validates the agency even without an explicit promise to transmit. Weinberg was therefore an agent authorized by appointment within the Rule, and service on her was valid. The Rule is a uniform federal standard, and even if state law were relevant, neither Michigan nor New York law requires an appointed agent to promise expressly to forward process. The Court limited its holding to a case in which prompt notice was actually given: a different case would be presented if Weinberg had not promptly notified the Szukhents. Id. at 315-18.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded, leaving the Szukhents subject to suit in the Eastern District of New York.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court first set aside Wuchter v. Pizzutti, on which the Szukhents relied. Wuchter concerned the limits the
Fourteenth Amendment places on a state statute that subjects nonresidents to its courts' jurisdiction by designating a public official to receive process. The question here was whether a party to a private contract may appoint an agent to receive service within the meaning of the Federal Rule, where the agent is not personally known to the party and has not expressly undertaken to transmit notice. Id. at 315.
The purpose of the clause was clear: the petitioner inserted it, and the Szukhents agreed to it, to ensure that any litigation under the lease would take place in New York. It was settled, as the lower courts had recognized, that contracting parties may agree in advance to submit to a court's jurisdiction, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or to waive notice altogether. The Court framed the only question before it as whether Weinberg was an agent authorized by appointment; no question of subject-matter jurisdiction or venue was presented. Id. at 312, 315-16.
On that question the Court applied general principles of agency law. Weinberg's prompt acceptance of the papers and her transmittal of them to the Szukhents, under the authority the lease conferred, was itself sufficient to validate the agency, even though she had not promised in advance to forward process. The Court emphasized that it was applying a Federal Rule governing federal courts in all fifty states. Even assuming that a uniform federal standard should give way to contrary state policy, no relevant state rule would invalidate the agency: Michigan's statute validating service under similar circumstances did not require an express undertaking to notify the principal, and New York law, which the lease selected, did not require one either. Id. at 316-17.
