The Court rejected the argument that the agency was invalid because Weinberg had a conflict of interest, based on the facts that she did not know the Szukhents and might be related to an officer of the company. The argument ignored the narrow nature of the agency. Weinberg was appointed for the single purpose of receiving service, and both the lessor and the lessees had an equal interest in ensuring that, if litigation arose, the lessees received the adequate and timely notice that is a prerequisite to a valid judgment. A footnote added that there was no allegation that Weinberg had any pecuniary interest in the litigation. Id. at 317-18 & n.9.
The Court confined its holding. It held only that, prompt notice having been given, Weinberg was an agent authorized by appointment. If she had not promptly notified the Szukhents, a claim might well be made that
her failure had invalidated the agency, and the Court expressly did not reach a case in which the defendant received no personal notice. Id. at 315, 318.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Justice Black dissented. He stressed that the Szukhents had never dealt with, met, or heard of Weinberg, that she was handpicked by the company, and that only after suit was it revealed that she was the wife of one of its officers. He would have held that New York law governed and that, as the lower courts found, the appointment was invalid under it; alternatively, a federal definition of agency should exclude her; and upholding service raised serious due process questions. He predicted that such clauses would spread into the boilerplate of equipment leases and conditional sales contracts, giving large companies a green light to force individuals to defend in distant commercial centers or suffer default, and he called the notion that the
Szukhents knowingly consented to suit in New York "a fiction—not even an amiable one." Id. at 318-33 (Black, J., dissenting).
Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, dissented on the ground that federal standards should define an agent authorized by appointment and that those standards should impose three requirements. The Rule should deny validity to the appointment of an agent whose interests conflict with those of the supposed principal. The appointment should include an explicit condition that the agent transmit process to the principal forthwith, drawing on Wuchter's reasoning. And because the corporate plaintiff prepared the printed form, an individual purchaser should not be bound by the appointment without proof, beyond a signature, that he understandingly consented to be sued in a state other than his residence. Id. at
333-34 (Brennan, J., dissenting).
sections.Notes:
The majority resolved the case under the Federal Rule and general agency law, and it did not decide any due process question. The casebook asks why the Court looked to agency principles rather than the Due Process
Clause and whether the Constitution has any role when a party contractually waives service. The limit stated in the opinion is central to the holding: service was upheld because prompt notice was actually given, which gives the Szukhents the same practical notice Mullane requires. The opinion leaves open whether a contractual appointment of an agent who never forwards the papers would support a judgment.
Justice Black's objection concerns consent more than notice. Weinberg's prompt mailing gave the Szukhents actual notice; the burden he identified was the cost of defending far from home under a clause buried in a printed form. The same question returns in the enforcement of forum-selection clauses in consumer form contracts and, as the casebook's second note asks, in "shrinkwrap," "clickwrap," and "browsewrap" agreements assented to with a click or a tap. The Contracts materials on rolling contracts in Hill v. Gateway
2000 address the parallel question of when a consumer is bound by terms that appear only in a standard form.

briefs.title: Wyman v. Newhouse
briefs.citation: Wyman v. Newhouse, 93 F.2d 313 (2d Cir. 1937), cert. denied, 303 U.S. 664 (1938). United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, decided December 6, 1937. Judge Manton wrote the opinion for a panel that included Judges Learned Hand and Swan. The case appears at casebook page 276 under the heading "Etiquette of Service" and concerns whether a judgment based on service obtained by luring the

sections.Parties: Wyman, the appellant, had obtained a default judgment against Newhouse in a Florida state court and sued in federal court in New York to enforce it. Newhouse, the appellee, was a New York resident who had never lived in Florida. Wyman sought enforcement of the Florida judgment; Newhouse contended that the Florida court never acquired jurisdiction over him because he was tricked into entering Florida to be served.
sections.Material Facts:
Wyman and Newhouse were both married during their relationship, and Wyman's husband died before the suit. The two had known each other for some years and had engaged in what the court called meretricious relations, meaning a sexual relationship outside marriage. Newhouse's affidavits established the following facts, and Wyman did not deny making the representations they described. On October 25, 1935, while
Newhouse was in Salt Lake City, Utah, he received a telegram from Wyman: "Account illness home planning leaving. Please come on way back. Must see you." When he returned to New York, he received a letter stating that her mother was dying in Ireland, that she was leaving the United States for good to go to her mother, and that she could not go without seeing him once more and discussing her affairs. They then spoke by telephone, and she repeated the substance of the letter in a hysterical and distressed voice. He promised to come to Florida in a week or ten days. Before he left, she wrote him a letter expressing love and affection and her delight at his coming, and they exchanged telegrams arranging accommodations in Miami, one reaching him in Washington, D.C., en route. 93 F.2d at 314.
Newhouse arrived at the Miami airport at six in the morning. He saw Wyman standing with her sister about
75 feet away, and a deputy sheriff, after identifying him, served him with process in a suit for $500,000 for money loaned, money advanced, and seduction under promise of marriage. A photographer tried to take his picture. A stranger then offered to take him to the home of a lawyer who knew Wyman's attorney; the lawyer invited him to his office, where Newhouse found one of Wyman's lawyers waiting. Newhouse did not retain the Florida lawyer. He flew back to New York that evening, and his New York counsel advised him to ignore the Florida summons. He did so, and a default judgment was entered after a jury assessed damages. Id.
sections.Procedural History: Wyman sued Newhouse on the Florida judgment in federal district court in New York. Newhouse moved to dismiss the complaint before trial under Rule 113 of the New York Rules of Civil Practice, and the motion was decided on affidavits. The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure had not yet taken effect, and federal courts in actions at law followed state procedure under the Conformity Act. The district court granted the motion and dismissed the complaint. Wyman appealed, and after the Second Circuit affirmed, the Supreme Court denied certiorari. Id. at 313-14.
sections.Issue: Must a New York court give effect to a Florida default judgment when the Florida court obtained personal jurisdiction by serving a defendant whom the plaintiff fraudulently induced to enter Florida? May the defendant raise the fraud as a defense to enforcement in New York without having challenged service or defended on the merits in Florida?
sections.Holding: Fraud that induces a defendant to come within a court's territorial jurisdiction so that he may be served defeats the court's jurisdiction over his person. A fraud affecting jurisdiction is equivalent to a lack of jurisdiction, so a judgment procured in that way is void and is not binding when the plaintiff tries to enforce it in another state. The defendant need not attack the judgment in the rendering state or defend on the merits there; he may raise the fraud as an equitable defense when sued on the judgment, and the enforcing court may consider the jurisdictional question collaterally. Id. at 315.
sections.Judgment: The Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the complaint, so the Florida judgment could not be enforced against Newhouse in New York.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first found the facts established. The affidavits and the reasonable inferences from them convincingly showed that Newhouse was induced to enter Florida by fraud: Wyman falsely represented her mother's illness, her intention to leave the United States, and her love and affection for him, when her sole purpose was to bring him within Florida's jurisdiction so that he could be served in an action for damages.
The timing of the service, the presence of a deputy sheriff and a photographer at the airport, and the waiting lawyers supported that conclusion, and Wyman did not deny making the representations. Id. at 314.
Service of process on a person physically present in a state ordinarily confers personal jurisdiction, the rule of
Pennoyer v. Neff. The court treated fraud as an exception to that rule. Newhouse's presence in Florida was the product of Wyman's deception, and a fraud affecting jurisdiction is the equivalent of a lack of jurisdiction. A judgment procured by that kind of fraud lacks jurisdiction and is null and void. Id. at 315.
Full faith and credit did not require a different result. The Constitution's Full Faith and Credit Clause, Article
IV, § 1, and its implementing statute (then 28 U.S.C. § 687, now § 1738) require each state to give sister-state judgments the effect they have where rendered, but a judgment rendered without jurisdiction over the defendant is not entitled to that effect. A judgment recovered in a sister state through the fraud of the party procuring the appearance of another is not binding on the latter when enforcement is sought in another state.
Id.
Newhouse was not required to go back to Florida. He had no obligation to proceed against the judgment there, and his equitable defense in answer to the suit on the judgment was sufficient. Nor did he have to make out a defense on the merits in Florida, because an error in entering judgment against a party over whom the court had no jurisdiction permits the jurisdictional question to be raised collaterally, that is, in a later proceeding brought to enforce the judgment. The complaint was therefore properly dismissed. Id.
sections.Separate Opinions: The panel was unanimous. The reported decision contains no concurrence or dissent.
sections.Notes:
The casebook pairs Wyman with Tickle v. Barton, 95 S.E.2d 427 (W. Va. 1956). There the plaintiff's attorney, concealing his identity and purpose, telephoned a Virginia defendant and invited him to a high school football banquet in West Virginia, where a deputy sheriff served him. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia held that service procured by fraud, trickery, or artifice does not give a court jurisdiction over the person served, and it held sufficient the defendant's plea in abatement raising that defense. The cases differ in posture. Barton challenged service directly in the forum. Newhouse defaulted and waited to attack the judgment when Wyman tried to enforce it, a strategy that preserved his objection but would have left him with no defense on the merits if the New York court had rejected his fraud claim. The deception in Wyman also exploited a personal relationship and a fabricated family emergency, and its facts were effectively uncontested.
The casebook asks whether the result would change if Newhouse had been in Florida and the trickery had been used only to flush him out of hiding. Courts generally distinguish trickery that brings a defendant into the jurisdiction, which manufactures the basis for jurisdiction, from trickery that induces a defendant already present to come forward to be served, which only overcomes evasion; the second is usually tolerated.
Long-arm statutes and service outside the forum now make luring defendants less necessary. Burnham v.
Superior Court upheld jurisdiction based on in-state service on a defendant voluntarily present in the forum;
the Wyman and Tickle rule addresses presence that the plaintiff obtained by deception. The section of the casebook containing Wyman also includes related limits on service within the forum, such as immunity for nonresidents attending court proceedings and the United Nations Headquarters Agreement immunity considered in Kadic v. Karadzic, 70 F.3d 232 (2d Cir. 1995), where the court held that Karadzic was not immune when served in New York outside the Headquarters District.

briefs.title: Federal Rule 12: Defenses, Objections, and Timing

sections.Sources:
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12 (as amended effective December 1, 2024), read with Rules 4(d) and 7(a).
Rule 12 sets the time to respond to a complaint, lists the defenses a defendant may raise by motion, and determines which defenses are lost if not raised promptly. The syllabus pairs it with Rule 4 because Rule
12(b)(4) and (5) are the vehicles for challenging defective process and service, and because the casebook's note on Roller v. Holly asks how much time a defendant has to respond. Rule 12.
Time to Respond: Rule 12(a)
A defendant must serve an answer within 21 days after being served with the summons and complaint. If the defendant timely waived service under Rule 4(d), the answer is due 60 days after the request for waiver was sent, or 90 days if it was sent to the defendant outside any judicial district of the United States. A party must answer a counterclaim or crossclaim within 21 days after service, and a reply ordered by the court within 21 days after service of the order unless the order specifies otherwise. The United States, its agencies, and its officers and employees sued in their official capacities have 60 days after service on the United States attorney; officers and employees sued individually for acts connected with federal duties have 60 days after service on the officer or the United States attorney, whichever is later. The 2024 amendment made clear that a different time set by a federal statute controls.
Serving a Rule 12 motion alters these periods. If the court denies the motion or postpones deciding it until trial, the responsive pleading is due 14 days after notice of the court's action; if the court grants a motion for a more definite statement, it is due 14 days after that statement is served. A defendant who files a Rule 12 motion therefore does not also have to answer until the motion is resolved.
The Seven Defenses: Rule 12(b)
Every defense must be asserted in the responsive pleading if one is required, but a party may raise seven defenses by motion: (1) lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, meaning the court's authority over the type of case; (2) lack of personal jurisdiction, meaning the court's power over the defendant; (3) improper venue, meaning the wrong district; (4) insufficient process, a defect in the summons itself, such as a missing seal or signature, the wrong defendant's name, or a wrong response time; (5) insufficient service of process, a defect in how or when the summons was delivered, such as leaving papers with someone who does not reside at the defendant's abode or serving after the Rule 4(m) period; (6) failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted; and (7) failure to join a party required under Rule 19. A motion asserting any of these defenses must be made before pleading if a responsive pleading is allowed.
No defense or objection is waived by joining it with other defenses or objections in a responsive pleading or motion. That sentence abolished the special appearance in federal court. Under older practice, reflected in
Mullane's special appearance before the Surrogate, a defendant who wanted to contest jurisdiction had to appear solely for that purpose, and raising any other matter could be treated as a general appearance that consented to jurisdiction. Under Rule 12, a defendant may combine jurisdictional objections with defenses on the merits in the same filing.
Other Rule 12 Motions
After the pleadings are closed, but early enough not to delay trial, a party may move for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c). If, on a Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion, the court considers matters outside the pleadings, Rule 12(d) requires it to treat the motion as one for summary judgment under Rule 56 and give all parties a reasonable opportunity to present pertinent material. Rule 12(e) permits a motion for a more definite statement when a pleading is so vague or ambiguous that the party cannot reasonably prepare a response; the motion must be made before responding and must point out the defects. Rule 12(f) permits the court to strike an insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter. Under Rule 12(i), on a party's motion, any Rule 12(b) defense and any Rule 12(c) motion must be heard and decided before trial unless the court defers it.
Consolidation and Waiver: Rules 12(g) and 12(h)
A Rule 12 motion may be joined with any other motion allowed by the rule. Once a party makes a Rule 12 motion, it may not make another motion under the rule raising a defense or objection that was available but omitted, except as Rule 12(h)(2) and (3) allow.
The defenses listed in Rule 12(b)(2) through (5), covering personal jurisdiction, venue, process, and service, are waived if omitted from a Rule 12 motion when they were available, or if they are neither made by motion nor included in the responsive pleading or an amendment allowed as a matter of course under Rule 15(a)(1).
A defendant who moves only under Rule 12(b)(6) therefore forfeits objections to personal jurisdiction, venue, process, and service. The defenses of failure to state a claim, failure to join a required party, and failure to state a legal defense to a claim are preserved longer: they may be raised in any pleading allowed under Rule 7(a), by a Rule 12(c) motion, or at trial. Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction is never waived; if the court determines at any time that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, it must dismiss the action.
Appearing, Defaulting, and Collateral Attack
A defendant who believes the court lacks personal jurisdiction or that service was defective has two broad options. It may appear and raise the objection under Rule 12, in which case the court's ruling on jurisdiction binds it and cannot be relitigated when the judgment is later enforced, Baldwin v. Iowa State Traveling Men's
Ass'n, 283 U.S. 522 (1931). Or it may stay away, suffer a default judgment, and challenge jurisdiction when the plaintiff seeks to enforce the judgment, as Newhouse did in Wyman. The second course preserves the jurisdictional objection but forfeits any defense on the merits if the jurisdictional challenge fails. Separately, waiving service under Rule 4(d) does not waive objections to personal jurisdiction or venue, which remain subject to Rule 12(h)(1).
sections.Application: Calculate the response deadline from the date of service or, if service was waived, from the date the waiver request was sent. Before filing anything, list every available Rule 12(b) defense. Personal jurisdiction, venue, process, and service objections must appear in the first Rule 12 motion, or in the answer if no motion is made, or they are lost. Distinguish a defect in the summons (Rule 12(b)(4)) from a defect in delivery or timing (Rule 12(b)(5)). Consider whether matters outside the pleadings will convert a Rule 12(b)(6) motion into a summary-judgment motion. Remember that subject-matter jurisdiction can be raised at any time, and that failure to state a claim can be raised through trial.

briefs.title: Opportunity to Be Heard
briefs.citation: Opportunity to Be Heard: Casebook pp. 278-296

sections.Sources:
Casebook Chapter 3, Part D, pp. 278-296, assigned to be read with care although it will not be covered by case presentation. The section applies Mullane's statement that due process requires notice and an opportunity for hearing appropriate to the nature of the case. The Court's decisions since the 1960s fall into two groups: challenges to private creditors' use of provisional remedies (Sniadach, Fuentes, Mitchell, North
Georgia Finishing, and Doehr), and claims to a hearing before the government withdraws a benefit (Goldberg and Mathews). Sniadach, Fuentes, and Doehr are briefed separately.
Provisional Remedies
A provisional remedy is a court order, obtained at the start of a suit or while it is pending, that seizes or encumbers the defendant's property for the plaintiff's benefit before any judgment. Attachment seizes or places a lien on the defendant's property to secure satisfaction of a possible judgment. Garnishment is attachment of property that a third party, called the garnishee, holds for the defendant, such as wages owed by an employer or funds in a bank. Replevin is an action to recover possession of specific personal property, and a prejudgment writ of replevin lets the plaintiff take the property before trial. Sequestration, as used in
Louisiana, is a court order holding property in the court's custody during the suit. These remedies derive from common-law writs and are now statutory; they were traditionally treated as exceptions to the requirement of prior notice and hearing.
The Prejudgment Remedy Cases
Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. (1969) struck down Wisconsin's prejudgment wage garnishment, which froze wages on a summons issued at the creditor's lawyer's request with no opportunity for a hearing before trial. Justice Harlan's concurrence framed the requirement as notice and a hearing aimed at establishing the validity, or at least the probable validity, of the claim before the deprivation. The decision left open whether its rationale reached property other than wages and what extraordinary situations could justify seizure without a prior hearing.
Fuentes v. Shevin (1972) answered broadly. By a vote of four to three, it invalidated Florida and
Pennsylvania statutes that allowed a creditor to obtain a writ of replevin for household goods on a conclusory application and a bond, with no prior hearing. Temporary deprivations count, a buyer's possessory interest in goods bought on installment is property, the goods need not be necessities, and seizure without a hearing is permissible only in truly unusual situations involving an important public interest, a special need for prompt action, and a government official's decision under a narrowly drawn statute.
Mitchell v. W.T. Grant Co., 416 U.S. 600 (1974), upheld a Louisiana sequestration statute allowing ex parte seizure (seizure on one party's application without notice to the other) where the applicant claimed a possessory interest and the defendant could conceal, waste, remove, or dispose of the property. The suit concerned an overdue installment balance, and the Court emphasized the vendor's interest in preventing waste of the property, the court's involvement in authorizing the writ, the suitability of the dispute for documentary proof, and the immediate availability of a post-seizure hearing. North Georgia Finishing, Inc. v.
Di-Chem, Inc., 419 U.S. 601 (1975), then invalidated a Georgia garnishment statute because the writ issued on conclusory allegations without an early hearing or other safeguard against mistaken repossession.
Connecticut v. Doehr (1991) invalidated, as applied, a statute allowing prejudgment attachment of a home on a tort plaintiff's affidavit, without prior notice or hearing, extraordinary circumstances, or a bond. It adapted
the Mathews factors to disputes between private parties, giving principal weight to the interest of the party seeking the remedy.
Factors the Cases Used
The casebook observes that the cases never stated an overall test and identifies the factors they used. The first factor is who decides: a judge or a clerk. The second is what interest the applicant has: whether it has a pre-existing interest in the property. The third is when the hearing occurs: before the seizure or immediately afterward. The fourth is why the seizure is sought: to establish jurisdiction or to provide security, and, if for security, whether exceptional circumstances such as a risk of destruction of the asset exist. The fifth is how the applicant must proceed: whether it must show probable cause or meet a lesser standard, whether its allegations must be sworn and based on personal knowledge, and whether the dispute can be resolved by uncontested documents. The casebook also asks whether the Sniadach line should apply when attachment is used to obtain jurisdiction, as in Shaffer.
Government Benefits and the Mathews Test
Until the mid-twentieth century, government benefits such as welfare payments, civil service jobs, and licenses were not treated as property protected by due process. Their inclusion, associated with Charles
Reich's article The New Property, was a major constitutional development. In Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S.
254 (1970), the Court held that a welfare recipient is entitled to an evidentiary hearing before benefits are terminated, because termination pending resolution of a dispute may deprive an eligible recipient of the very means by which to live while waiting; the hearing need not be a full trial but must be tailored to the capacities and circumstances of those to be heard.
In Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976), the Court held that a pretermination hearing was not required before Social Security disability benefits were cut off, and it stated a three-factor balancing test: first, the private interest affected by the official action; second, the risk of an erroneous deprivation through the procedures used and the probable value of additional or substitute safeguards; and third, the government's interest, including the function involved and the fiscal and administrative burdens that additional procedures would entail. The casebook asks whether applying Mathews would have changed the outcome in Fuentes and how the Sniadach factors fit the Mathews framework; Doehr supplies the Court's own answer for prejudgment remedies.
Limits and Later Applications
Due process hearing rights attach to adjudicative action, not legislation. In Jones v. Governor of Florida, 975
F.3d 1016 (11th Cir. 2020) (en banc), the court reversed an injunction against Florida's requirement that people with felony convictions pay outstanding fines, fees, and restitution before voting. Relying on
Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization, the majority held that the deprivation occurred through legislative action, meaning a general law applying prospectively to more than a few people, so the affected persons were entitled to no process beyond the legislative process and Mathews did not apply. A dissent argued, through an example about unpaid traffic citations, that denying people the information needed to comply with a general law could not be constitutionally permissible.
Other notes show the factors at work. Shaumyan v. O'Neill, 987 F.2d 122 (2d Cir. 1993), upheld the same
Connecticut attachment statute as applied to a contractor seeking payment for repairs, because the dispute turned largely on written documentation and the contractor had a substantial pre-existing interest in the home once its labor and materials were incorporated. Diaz v. Paterson, 547 F.3d 88 (2d Cir. 2008), upheld New
York's lis pendens statute, which lets a plaintiff claiming an interest in real property record a notice of the pending suit, applying the Mathews factors as construed in Doehr. Bennis v. Michigan, 516 U.S. 442 (1996), rejected a wife's due process challenge to forfeiture of a jointly owned car used by her husband in a crime, relying on a long line of cases permitting forfeiture of an innocent owner's interest. Nelson v. Colorado, 137
S. Ct. 1249 (2017), held under Mathews that Colorado could not require defendants whose convictions were invalidated to prove innocence by clear and convincing evidence to recover fees, costs, and restitution they had paid.
The final note addresses counsel. In Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981), the Court recognized a presumption that an indigent litigant has a right to appointed counsel only when loss of physical liberty is at stake and held that due process did not require counsel before termination of a mother's parental rights on the facts presented. In Turner v. Rogers, 564 U.S. 431 (2011), the Court held that due process does not automatically require counsel for an indigent parent facing civil contempt incarceration for nonpayment of child support, where the opposing parent is unrepresented and the State provides alternative safeguards, but it found those safeguards missing and held that the incarceration violated due process.
sections.Application:
First decide whether there is a deprivation of property or liberty by state action through an adjudicative process; Jones shows that legislative action falls outside the hearing requirement. For a prejudgment remedy between private parties, apply Doehr's version of Mathews: weigh the defendant's property interest, including partial and temporary impairments; the risk of error given who decides, what showing is required, and whether the dispute is documentary or fact-intensive; the value of safeguards such as a prior hearing, an immediate post-deprivation hearing, or a bond; and the plaintiff's interest, especially any pre-existing interest in the property or evidence that the defendant will dissipate it. For a government benefit, apply the three
Mathews factors directly. In either setting, extraordinary circumstances may justify postponing the hearing, but a hearing must follow promptly.

briefs.title: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. of Bay View
briefs.citation: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp. of Bay View, 395 U.S. 337 (1969). Supreme Court of the United States, argued April 21, 1969, decided June 9, 1969. Justice Douglas wrote for the Court, Justice Harlan concurred, and Justice Black dissented. The casebook presents the case in Note 1 at page 279; the brief draws on the full opinion. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
Christine Sniadach, a wage earner, was the defendant in the garnishment action and the petitioner in the
Supreme Court. Family Finance Corporation of Bay View, the creditor, was the plaintiff and a respondent.
Her employer, Miller Harris Instrument Co., was named as garnishee, the third party holding money owed to the debtor. The creditor sought to freeze part of Sniadach's wages pending trial of its claim; Sniadach sought dismissal of the garnishment as a violation of due process.
sections.Material Facts:
Family Finance began a garnishment action naming Sniadach as defendant and Miller Harris as garnishee.
The complaint alleged a claim of $420 on a promissory note. The employer answered that it held $63.18 in wages earned by Sniadach and not yet paid, and that it would pay half to her as a subsistence allowance and hold the other half, $31.59, subject to the court's order. 395 U.S. at 338.
Under Wisconsin's procedure, the clerk of court issued the garnishment summons at the request of the creditor's lawyer. Service on the garnishee froze the wages, and the creditor then had ten days to serve the summons and complaint on the debtor. The wages remained frozen until the main suit was tried, and the debtor could unfreeze them only by winning on the merits. The debtor had no opportunity to be heard before the wages were frozen. Id. at 338-39.
sections.Procedural History:
Sniadach moved to dismiss the garnishment proceedings on the ground that the procedure violated the Due
Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it provided no notice or hearing before the wages were taken. The Wisconsin courts rejected the challenge, and the Wisconsin Supreme Court sustained the procedure, 37 Wis. 2d 163, 154 N.W.2d 259 (1967). The Supreme Court granted certiorari. Id. at 338.
sections.Issue: Does a state procedure that permits a creditor to freeze a debtor's wages through garnishment before trial, without notice to the debtor or an opportunity to be heard, violate the Due Process Clause?
sections.Holding: Yes. Wages are a specialized type of property presenting distinct problems in the economic system, and prejudgment garnishment of the Wisconsin type is a taking that may impose tremendous hardship on wage earners with families to support. Summary procedures may satisfy due process in extraordinary situations, but Wisconsin's statute was not narrowly drawn to meet any such situation, and none was present. Absent notice and a prior hearing, the procedure violated the fundamental principles of due process. Id. at 339-42.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court acknowledged that Sniadach would eventually receive a hearing on the merits of the creditor's claim. In the meantime, however, she lost the use of wages she had already earned without any opportunity to be heard or to present any defense. Summary seizure had been upheld in extraordinary situations, such as the protection of the public from bank failures and misbranded drugs, and in cases involving attachment of a nonresident's property, but no situation requiring special protection of a state or creditor interest appeared here. Sniadach lived in the Wisconsin community, so personal jurisdiction over her was readily obtainable.
Id. at 339.
The Court then explained why wages deserve particular protection. Relying on congressional testimony gathered for the Consumer Credit Protection Act of 1968, it noted that until that recent act of Congress, which forbids discharging employees because their wages have been garnished for one debt, garnishment often cost the debtor a job, and it always drained family income. The creditor's leverage was enormous: the creditor could demand not only the original debt but also the collection fees its attorneys incurred in the garnishment. The Court also quoted congressional testimony that in a vast number of cases the debt was fraudulent, saddled on a poor and ignorant person trapped in an easy-credit nightmare. Prejudgment garnishment of this kind could, as a practical matter, drive a wage-earning family to the wall. Where the taking of property is so obvious, the Court concluded, little argument is needed to show that the procedure violates due process absent notice and a prior hearing. Id. at 340-42.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Justice Harlan concurred. He responded to the argument that a temporary freeze does not deprive anyone of property: the property taken was the use of the garnished wages during the period between garnishment and the end of the main suit, and that deprivation was not de minimis. Apart from special situations, he wrote, due process is afforded only by the kinds of notice and hearing aimed at establishing the validity, or at least the probable validity, of the underlying claim before the debtor can be deprived of his property or its unrestricted use. Id. at 342-44 (Harlan, J., concurring).
Justice Black dissented. He accused the majority of invalidating a state law because it found the law unwise and of using a vague fundamental-fairness standard derived from natural law rather than the Constitution's text. In his view Wisconsin's procedure, which ultimately gave the debtor notice and a hearing, was consistent with the Court's earlier decisions upholding prejudgment attachment, such as McKay v. McInnes and Ownbey v. Morgan, and the policy choice belonged to the legislature. Id. at 344-51 (Black, J., dissenting).
sections.Notes:
The opinion's emphasis on wages and family hardship left two questions open, as the casebook notes:
whether the rationale reached prejudgment seizures of other property when the hardship was less severe, and what extraordinary situations justify seizure without a prior hearing. Fuentes answered the first question broadly for household goods, and Doehr extended protection to real estate the owner continued to occupy.
Sniadach addressed prejudgment garnishment only. Garnishment after judgment, once the creditor's claim has been adjudicated, remains available, subject to the federal limits Title III of the Consumer Credit
Protection Act places on the portion of disposable earnings that may be garnished. The opinion's reference to readily available personal jurisdiction also connects to the casebook's question whether the Sniadach line should apply when attachment is used to obtain jurisdiction over a nonresident.

briefs.title: Fuentes v. Shevin
briefs.citation: Fuentes v. Shevin, 407 U.S. 67 (1972), reh'g denied, 409 U.S. 902 (1972). Supreme Court of the United States, argued November 9, 1971, decided June 12, 1972, together with Parham v. Cortese. Justice Stewart wrote for a four-Justice majority joined by Justices Douglas, Brennan, and Marshall. Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun. Justices Powell and Rehnquist,

sections.Parties:
Margarita Fuentes, a Florida consumer whose household goods were seized, was the appellant; Robert
Shevin, Florida's Attorney General, defended the Florida statute, and Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, the seller, was also an appellee. In the companion Pennsylvania case, consumers whose goods had been seized under Pennsylvania's replevin statute challenged it against state officials and the creditors. The consumers sought declarations that the statutes were unconstitutional and injunctions against their enforcement.
sections.Material Facts:
Fuentes bought a gas stove and a service policy from Firestone under a conditional sales contract, and later a stereophonic phonograph on the same terms. The total cost was about $500 plus a financing charge of more than $100. Firestone retained title, but Fuentes was entitled to possession unless she defaulted. She made installment payments for more than a year. With about $200 remaining, a dispute arose over the servicing of the stove. Firestone sued in small-claims court for repossession of the stove and stereo, claiming she had refused to make her remaining payments. At the same time, and before Fuentes had received the summons,
Firestone obtained a writ of replevin, and a deputy sheriff and a Firestone agent seized the goods from her home. 407 U.S. at 70-71.
Florida's statute allowed a writ to issue on the applicant's complaint and bond alone. The applicant had to allege, in conclusory fashion, that it was lawfully entitled to possession and post a bond for double the value of the property. The clerk issued the writ, which commanded the officer to seize the goods and to summon the defendant to answer; if the goods were in a dwelling and not surrendered, the officer could break the building open. The officer held the goods for three days, during which the defendant could reclaim them by posting its own bond for double their value; otherwise they went to the applicant pending final judgment.
Pennsylvania's statute was more summary: the applicant needed only to file an affidavit of the value of the property and a bond, did not have to file any suit, and the person whose goods were seized had to sue to obtain a hearing. Id. at 73-78.
The Pennsylvania appellants included buyers of household goods under installment contracts whose sellers obtained writs by claiming default, and Rosa Washington, whose former husband, a local deputy sheriff, obtained a writ to seize their son's clothes, furniture, and toys during a custody dispute. Id. at 71-72.
sections.Procedural History:
Fuentes sued in federal district court, challenging Florida's prejudgment replevin procedures under the Due
Process Clause. The Pennsylvania appellants brought a similar suit. In each case a three-judge district court, a special panel then required for suits seeking to enjoin state statutes on constitutional grounds, upheld the statute: Fuentes v. Faircloth, 317 F. Supp. 954 (S.D. Fla. 1970), and Epps v. Cortese, 326 F. Supp. 127 (E.D.
Pa. 1971). The consumers appealed directly to the Supreme Court. Id. at 71-72.
sections.Issue: Do statutes that allow a private party to obtain a writ of replevin and have state officers seize goods from another person's possession, on an ex parte application and a bond, without notice or an opportunity for a hearing before the seizure, violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Florida and Pennsylvania statutes are unconstitutional insofar as they deny the right to an opportunity to be heard before chattels are taken from their possessor. To serve its purpose, the hearing must come at a time when the deprivation can still be prevented. A temporary, nonfinal deprivation is a deprivation; a buyer's possessory interest in goods purchased under a conditional sales contract is property even though the seller retains title; and due process protects property generally, not only necessities. Seizure without a prior hearing is permitted only in extraordinary situations, which were absent where only private gain was at stake. The printed contract clauses permitting the seller to retake the goods did not waive the right to a prior hearing. Id. at 80-96.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court vacated the judgments of both three-judge district courts and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court first described the procedure's practical effect. At the moment the defendant receives the complaint seeking repossession, the property has already been seized, without prior notice or any chance to challenge the writ. The defendant will eventually have a hearing as defendant in the repossession action and can recover the goods in the meantime only by posting a bond for double their value. The process also lacked judicial supervision: private parties, serving their own advantage, could unilaterally invoke state power to take goods from another, with no state official deciding whether to issue the writ, reviewing the basis of the claim, or evaluating the need for immediate seizure. The State, the Court wrote, acted largely in the dark. Id.
at 73-75, 93.
The purpose of the right to be heard is to protect a person's use and possession of property from arbitrary encroachment and to minimize substantively unfair or mistaken deprivations, a danger that is especially great when the State seizes goods simply on a private party's application. That purpose is served only if the hearing comes when the deprivation can still be prevented. A later hearing can return the goods and may award damages, but it cannot undo the fact that an arbitrary taking has occurred. The Florida and Pennsylvania safeguards, a bond, a conclusory allegation, and exposure to damages, tested no more than the strength of the applicant's own belief in its rights, and a bond's minimal deterrent effect was no substitute for an informed evaluation by a neutral official. Id. at 80-84.
The Court rejected three arguments for limiting the right. First, the opportunity to post a counterbond within three days did not make the seizure a non-deprivation, because a temporary, nonfinal deprivation of property is a deprivation under the Fourteenth Amendment. Second, although the sellers retained title, the buyers had a possessory interest in the goods, dearly bought through installment payments and protected by contract, and that interest was property. Third, the Court refused to confine due process to necessities such as wages; the
Fourteenth Amendment speaks of property generally, and courts should not decide which consumer goods are important enough to protect. Id. at 84-90.
Extraordinary situations can justify seizure without a prior hearing, but they must be truly unusual. In the cases allowing it, the seizure was directly necessary to secure an important governmental or general public interest; there was a special need for very prompt action; and the State kept strict control over its monopoly of legitimate force, with a government official deciding under a narrowly drawn statute that the seizure was necessary in the particular case. Examples included tax collection, war needs, bank failures, and misbranded drugs and contaminated food. No such interest justified seizing household goods when no more than private gain was directly at stake. Id. at 90-93.
Finally, the consumers had not waived their rights. The contracts provided that on default the seller "may take back," "may retake," or "may repossess" the goods, but they said nothing about waiving a prior hearing or about the process, whether final judgment, self-help, or prejudgment replevin with or without a hearing, by which repossession would occur. A waiver of constitutional rights must, at the least, be clear. The Court contrasted D.H. Overmyer Co. v. Frick Co., which upheld a cognovit note negotiated between corporations with the advice of counsel; here there was no bargaining over terms, and the parties were far from equal in bargaining power. Id. at 94-96.
The Court stressed the limits of its holding. It did not decide the form of the required hearing, which may vary and is a subject for legislation, and it did not question the power of a state to seize goods before final judgment; it held only that the seizure must follow a hearing that tests at least the probable validity of the underlying claim. Id. at 96-97.
sections.Separate Opinions: Justice White, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun, dissented. He emphasized that the creditor also has a property interest in goods bought on installment, including a security interest that can be impaired if the goods are hidden, damaged, or depreciate while the debtor, who has stopped paying, keeps them. Sellers have strong economic reasons not to repossess without a real default, and in most cases the default is undisputed, so a prior hearing would add cost and delay with little benefit. He would have deferred to the legislative judgments reflected in state law and in the Uniform Commercial Code's rules on secured transactions. He also predicted that creditors could avoid the decision by stating in their credit instruments that they may retake possession without a hearing, so that the result would have little impact and represented "no more than ideological tinkering with state law." Id. at 97-103 (White, J., dissenting).
sections.Notes:
Fuentes was the high point of the prior-hearing requirement, and the four-to-three vote with two Justices absent made it vulnerable. Two years later, after Justices Powell and Rehnquist had joined the Court,
Mitchell v. W.T. Grant Co. upheld Louisiana's sequestration procedure, stressing judicial supervision, sworn and specific allegations, the creditor's vendor's lien, a bond, and an immediate post-seizure hearing. Justice
Stewart's dissent in Mitchell argued that the decision effectively overruled Fuentes. Doehr reconciled the line through a Mathews-style balance in which a prior hearing is the default and the plaintiff's pre-existing interest, exigency, and procedural safeguards can justify postponing it.
Two further limits matter. Fuentes concerns seizures carried out by state officers under state procedures;
private self-help repossession under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code, when conducted without a state actor, generally falls outside the Due Process Clause, compare Flagg Bros., Inc. v. Brooks, 436 U.S. 149 (1978). The waiver analysis also connects to Szukhent and Overmyer: a printed form can appoint an agent for service, but it waives a constitutional hearing right only if the waiver is clear, and bargaining power bears on enforcement.

briefs.title: Connecticut v. Doehr
briefs.citation: Connecticut v. Doehr, 501 U.S. 1 (1991). Supreme Court of the United States, argued January 7, 1991, decided June 6, 1991. Justice White delivered the opinion of the Court as to Parts I, II, and III, which Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Marshall, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter joined in full and Justice Scalia joined as to Parts I and III. Part IV, on the need for a bond, w

sections.Parties: John F. DiGiovanni, who planned to sue Brian K. Doehr for assault and battery, obtained a prejudgment attachment on Doehr's home. The State of Connecticut intervened in the Court of Appeals, at that court's invitation under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b), which allows a state to intervene to defend the constitutionality of its statute; Connecticut and DiGiovanni were the petitioners. Doehr, the homeowner, was the respondent. Doehr sought a declaration that the attachment statute violated due process; Connecticut and DiGiovanni defended it. 501 U.S. at 4-8.
sections.Material Facts:
On March 15, 1988, DiGiovanni applied to the Connecticut Superior Court for an attachment of $75,000 on
Doehr's home in Meriden, Connecticut, in connection with a civil action for assault and battery he was bringing against Doehr in the same court. The suit did not involve Doehr's real estate, and DiGiovanni had no pre-existing interest in the home or any of Doehr's other property. Connecticut law allowed a court or judge to authorize prejudgment attachment of real property without a hearing on verification by oath of the plaintiff or another competent affiant that there was probable cause to sustain the validity of the plaintiff's claim. The statute did not require the plaintiff to post a bond to cover the defendant's damages if the attachment proved wrongful. Id. at 5-6.
DiGiovanni's affidavit, in five one-sentence paragraphs, stated that the facts in his complaint were true, that
Doehr had willfully, wantonly, and maliciously assaulted him, that the assault broke his left wrist and bruised his right eye among other injuries, that he had incurred medical expenses, and that in his opinion these facts showed probable cause that judgment would be rendered for him. On the strength of these submissions, a
Superior Court judge found probable cause and ordered the attachment to the value of $75,000. The sheriff attached the property four days later. Only then did Doehr receive notice, and he had not yet been served with the complaint. The notice told him he could seek a hearing to argue that there was no probable cause, to ask that the attachment be vacated or modified or a bond substituted, or to claim an exemption. Id. at 6-7.
sections.Procedural History:
Instead of seeking the post-attachment hearing, Doehr sued DiGiovanni in federal district court, claiming that the statute violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court upheld the statute and granted summary judgment to DiGiovanni. A divided panel of the Second Circuit reversed in an opinion by Judge Pratt, reported as Pinsky v. Duncan, 898 F.2d 852 (2d Cir. 1990). The court held that
Sniadach and its progeny permit a prior hearing to be postponed only where exceptional circumstances justify the delay and sufficient additional safeguards are present. It emphasized that, unlike the documentary issues in Mitchell, an assault claim turned on disputed facts about a fight that a judge could not reliably assess on the plaintiff's version alone, and Judge Pratt concluded, in his own view, that the lack of a bond was an independent defect. Connecticut had intervened in the Court of Appeals after oral argument there, at that court's invitation, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari. Id. at 7-8.
sections.Issue:
Does a state statute that authorizes prejudgment attachment of real estate without prior notice or hearing, without a showing of extraordinary circumstances, and without requiring the plaintiff to post a bond satisfy the Due Process Clause when invoked by a tort plaintiff who has no pre-existing interest in the property?
Must due process also require a bond?
sections.Holding:
When a state statute lets a private party enlist state power to deprive another of property through prejudgment attachment, the adequacy of the procedure is judged by a modified version of the Mathews v. Eldridge test.
The court considers, first, the private interest affected by the prejudgment measure; second, the risk of erroneous deprivation through the procedures used and the probable value of additional or alternative safeguards; and third, with principal attention, the interest of the party seeking the prejudgment remedy, with due regard for any ancillary interest the government may have in providing the procedure or avoiding the burden of greater protections.
Applying that test, the Connecticut statute violated due process as applied: the homeowner's interest was significant, the risk of error was substantial, and the plaintiff's interest in an ex parte attachment was minimal because he had no pre-existing interest in the property and did not allege that Doehr was about to transfer or encumber it. Id. at 9-18.
A four-Justice plurality would further have held that due process requires the plaintiff to post a bond or other security in addition to a hearing or a showing of exigency, and that a bond does not excuse the need for a hearing. Id. at 18-24 (plurality opinion).
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court began by placing the case in the line from Sniadach through Fuentes, Mitchell, and North Georgia
Finishing, whose results varied with the type of remedy. Mathews had drawn on those cases to decide what process is due when the government itself deprives a person of property. Prejudgment remedies ordinarily arise in disputes between private parties, so the Court adjusted the third Mathews factor to focus principally on the interest of the party seeking the remedy rather than on the government's. Id. at 9-11.
The private interest was significant. For a homeowner, attachment ordinarily clouds title, impairs the ability to sell or otherwise transfer the property, taints the owner's credit rating, reduces the chance of obtaining a home equity loan or additional mortgage, and can even place an existing mortgage in technical default where the mortgage has an insecurity clause. Connecticut correctly argued that these effects do not amount to a complete, physical, or permanent deprivation and are less severe than the temporary total loss of household goods or wages. But the Court had never limited due process protection to such extreme deprivations;
temporary or partial impairments of property rights caused by attachments, liens, and similar encumbrances are enough. Id. at 11-12.
The risk of erroneous deprivation was substantial. Attachment deprives the defendant of property on the basis of a contingency, a future damages award, that may never occur. Connecticut required a finding of probable cause to sustain the validity of the claim, but the meaning of that standard was obscure: the State first said it required a showing of the suit's objective likelihood of success; Doehr read it as requiring only the plaintiff's subjective good-faith belief; and at oral argument the State said it required something like a claim sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss. Under any of these readings the risk of error was too great. A standard satisfied by a facially valid complaint or the plaintiff's belief would allow attachment on claims a jury would reject or that the defendant would dispute, and in the good-faith case even on claims that failed to state a cause of action. Even under the strictest reading, the judge received only a skeletal, one-sided affidavit and could make no realistic assessment of the likelihood of success. An assault case does not involve the ordinarily uncomplicated matters that lend themselves to documentary proof, as a debt or delinquent payments do. Id. at 12-14.
The safeguards Connecticut provided did not adequately reduce that risk. The statute offered an expeditious post-attachment hearing, notice of that hearing, judicial review of an adverse decision, and a double-damages action if the suit was begun without probable cause. Similar protections existed in Mitchell, but there the plaintiff had a vendor's lien to protect, the dispute involved documentary matters, and the plaintiff had to post a bond. None of those features was present here. A later hearing might show that probable cause was lacking, but it could not cure the temporary deprivation an earlier hearing could have prevented. Id. at 14-15.
The interests favoring an ex parte attachment were too slight to justify the procedure. DiGiovanni had no existing interest in Doehr's real estate; his only interest was ensuring that assets would be available to satisfy a judgment if he won. He did not allege that Doehr was about to transfer or encumber the property or take any other step that would make it unavailable. The Court acknowledged that such an allegation, properly supported, would be an exigent circumstance permitting the hearing to be postponed until after attachment.
The State's interest could not exceed the plaintiff's, and Connecticut could not plead administrative burdens because it already provided an immediate post-deprivation hearing. Id. at 16.
History and current practice supported the result. Traditional attachment statutes were limited to situations in which the defendant had taken or threatened action that would render a judgment uncollectible, were confined to creditors' claims, and required a bond. A survey of modern statutes showed that nearly every state requires a pre-attachment hearing, a showing of exigent circumstances, or both before an attachment may issue. Id. at 16-18.
In Part IV, the plurality addressed the bond. Without a bond, the risk of wrongful deprivation remains unacceptably high even with a hearing or exigency requirement, because until the post-attachment hearing the defendant has no protection against damages where no exigency in fact existed or the claim was worthless, and even a full hearing yields only an educated prediction of who will win. The double-damages remedy did not substitute for a bond, because recovering under it would require proof of something like
fraud, malice, or failure to state a claim. At the same time, a bond does not excuse a hearing: the harms from an erroneous attachment, such as a lost sale, a lost loan for a child's education, or a mortgage placed in technical default, cannot be fully undone by payment at the end of the case. Id. at 18-23 (plurality opinion).
sections.Separate Opinions:
Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justice Blackmun, concurred in Parts I, II, and III and in the judgment. He observed that all the earlier cases involved personal property, such as bank deposits and chattels, and the physical seizure of the property, so the defendant lost its use and possession; Connecticut's attachment created only an incipient lien and left Doehr in possession. The Court's holding therefore broke new ground, but he agreed that the deprivation was significant. He declined to join Part IV, calling it unwise and unnecessary to decide hypothetical questions about bonds and exigent circumstances before concrete cases presented them. Id. at 26-30 (Rehnquist, C.J., concurring).
Justice Scalia joined Parts I and III and concurred in the judgment. Because the kind of attachment at issue was not a procedure recognized at common law, he agreed that its validity should be tested under Mathews v.
Eldridge and that it failed that test. The casebook omits his opinion. Id. at 30 (Scalia, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).
sections.Notes:
Doehr supplies the current framework for prejudgment remedies and answers the question the casebook asks after Fuentes: the Court now evaluates such remedies with a Mathews-type balance in which the plaintiff's interest replaces the government's as the principal third factor. The case also extends Sniadach and Fuentes to real estate and to deprivations that leave the owner in possession, which is the point Chief Justice Rehnquist identified as new. The holding is as applied: a plaintiff with a pre-existing interest, a documentary claim, or a supported allegation that the defendant is about to dissipate the property could justify a different result.
Shaumyan v. O'Neill shows that effect: the Second Circuit upheld the same statute as applied to a contractor who attached a homeowner's property in a payment dispute, because the evidence was largely documentary and the contractor had a substantial pre-existing interest once its labor and materials were incorporated into the home. The bond requirement in Part IV commanded only four votes and is not a holding of the Court.
After Doehr, commentators questioned lis pendens statutes, under which a plaintiff claiming an interest in real property records a notice of the pending suit without a hearing; the Second Circuit upheld New York's statute in Diaz v. Paterson, applying the Mathews factors as construed in Doehr.

briefs.title: Gray v. American Radiator & Standard Sanitary Corp.
briefs.citation: 22 Ill. 2d 432, 176 N.E.2d 761 (Ill. 1961). Supreme Court of Illinois. Klingbiel, J. No. 35872. Opinion filed June 14, 1961; rehearing denied September 20, 1961. Direct appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County.

sections.Parties:
Appellant and plaintiff: Phyllis Gray, an Illinois resident who sought damages for injuries caused by an exploding water heater.
Nonresident defendant and appellee: Titan Valve Manufacturing Company, an Ohio corporation that manufactured the heater's safety valve and challenged Illinois personal jurisdiction. Defendant, cross-claimant, and additional appellant: American Radiator
& Standard Sanitary Corporation, which incorporated Titan's valve into its water heater and sought contractual indemnification from
Titan if Gray recovered against it. Other defendants named in the underlying products-liability action were outside the jurisdictional issue decided on appeal.
sections.Procedural History:
Cook County filing and statutory basis: Gray filed a damages action in the Circuit Court of Cook County against Titan, American
Radiator, and others. Her complaint alleged that Titan negligently manufactured the safety valve and that the defect proximately caused the explosion and her Illinois injuries. Illinois Civil Practice Act section 17(1)(b), Ill. Rev. Stat. 1959, chapter 110, paragraph
17, treated a nonresident's commission of a tortious act within Illinois as submission to Illinois jurisdiction. Section 16, paragraph 16, authorized personal delivery of summons outside the State to a nonresident who had so submitted.
Out-of-state service: Summons issued and was personally served on Titan's registered agent in Cleveland, Ohio. The service therefore depended on two distinct propositions: section 17 had to create adjudicatory authority over Titan, and section 16 had to supply a valid method for notifying Titan outside Illinois. Titan conceded the adequacy and statutory regularity of the section 16 notice for purposes of the appeal; it contested Illinois's authority to bind it.
Special appearance and motion to quash: Titan appeared specially, preserving its objection to personal jurisdiction while asking the court to quash service. Its affidavit stated that Titan conducted no business in Illinois, maintained no agent physically present there, and sold its completed valves to American Radiator outside Illinois. Titan argued that manufacturing conduct in Ohio supplied no tortious act within Illinois under section 17(1)(b), and that treating the Illinois injury as a sufficient contact would exceed the
Fourteenth Amendment.
Cross-claim and trial-court ruling: American Radiator answered Gray's complaint and cross-claimed against Titan. The cross-claim alleged that Titan made warranties to American Radiator and owed indemnification if American Radiator became liable to Gray. The circuit court granted Titan's motion, quashed the out-of-state service, and dismissed both Gray's complaint and American Radiator's cross-claim against Titan. The court thereby ended Titan's participation before any adjudication of negligence, warranty, indemnity, causation, or damages.
Direct appeal and final disposition: Gray appealed directly to the Supreme Court of Illinois because Titan's due-process challenge placed a constitutional question in issue. American Radiator also supported reversal of the order that eliminated its cross-claim. The
Illinois Supreme Court reversed and remanded with directions to deny Titan's motion to quash. The merits returned to the Cook
County circuit court with Titan subject to personal jurisdiction. The court denied rehearing on September 20, 1961.
sections.Material Facts:
Titan manufactured the safety valve in Ohio and sold the completed valve to American Radiator outside Illinois. American Radiator incorporated the valve into a hot-water heater in Pennsylvania. The heater then moved through ordinary commercial distribution to an
Illinois consumer. It exploded in Illinois and injured Gray there. Gray alleged that negligent valve construction proximately caused the injury. The appellate record identified no direct Illinois sales, employees, office, or agent of Titan and supplied no quantified volume for Titan products reaching Illinois.
Titan did not characterize this heater's Illinois use as an isolated instance. The court inferred from the ordinary commercial distribution of appliances that Titan's transactions produced substantial use of its valves in Illinois and that the valves were manufactured for incorporation into products expected to reach ultimate consumers in multiple States. Illinois was also the place of injury, Gray's residence, the likely location of injury and damages witnesses, and the jurisdiction whose substantive law would govern the occurrence.
sections.Issue: Two questions: (1) Does Illinois Civil Practice Act section 17(1)(b) classify a tort as committed in Illinois when the defendant's negligent manufacturing occurred elsewhere and the final injury necessary for tort liability occurred in Illinois? (2) If the statute reaches that conduct, does the Fourteenth Amendment permit Illinois to exercise in-personam jurisdiction over the component manufacturer through personal service on its Ohio registered agent?
sections.Holding:
Statutory authorization: Yes. A tortious act under section 17(1)(b) includes the injury that completes the alleged tort. Illinois was the place of the wrong because the final event necessary to liability occurred there. Constitutional authority: Yes. Titan's placement of valves into the ordinary commercial chain, with ultimate use in Illinois contemplated and with the present claim arising from an
Illinois injury caused by the product, supplied a substantial forum connection. The forum's interests, local evidence, modern distribution practices, and manageable litigation burden made the exercise reasonable. Notice: Service on Titan's Ohio registered agent under section 16 furnished the accepted method of notification. Disposition: Reversed and remanded with directions to deny the motion to quash.
sections.Reasoning:
Analytical order and competing positions: The court proceeded through three separate civil-procedure questions. First, it interpreted the Illinois long-arm statute. Second, it tested the authorized jurisdiction against the Fourteenth Amendment. Third, it confirmed that the chosen service method supplied reasonable notification. Gray and American Radiator treated the Illinois injury and ordinary distribution of Titan's product as the forum connection. Titan located the relevant act at its Ohio factory and emphasized the absence of
Illinois personnel, direct sales, and a documented Illinois business volume.
Meaning of 'tortious act': The statutory phrase incorporated the complete tort. Negligent conduct becomes legally tortious through resulting injury; the injury therefore forms an inseparable part of the statutory event. Using the then-prevailing place-of-wrong rule from Restatement of Conflict of Laws section 377, the court located the tort where the last event required for liability occurred. Gray's injury completed the alleged tort in Illinois. This construction allowed section 17(1)(b) to reach Titan even though its employee performed the manufacturing conduct in Ohio. 22 Ill. 2d at 435-36.
Statutory reach and constitutional limit: Illinois precedent construed section 17 as reaching nonresidents to the boundary permitted by due process. That construction did not collapse the two inquiries. The legislature supplied the asserted authority through sections 16 and 17; the Fourteenth Amendment independently determined whether Illinois could enter a binding personal judgment. Titan's special appearance properly presented both issues before the merits.
Notice and adjudicatory power: The court expressly separated minimum contacts from notification. Section 16's personal service on
Titan's registered agent gave Titan a realistic opportunity to appear and defend. The constitutional power question asked whether
Titan's own commercial relationship to Illinois made the resulting judgment legitimate. Titan's concession on notice left the second question as the live constitutional dispute. 22 Ill. 2d at 436-37.
Development from Pennoyer through International Shoe: The court described personal jurisdiction as moving from Pennoyer's territorial service model toward International Shoe's evaluation of contacts, fair play, and substantial justice. International Shoe showed that a systematic claim-producing course of forum business supports jurisdiction; Perkins showed that sufficiently substantial forum activity can support claims arising elsewhere; Hanson required a connection created through the defendant's invocation of forum benefits. Gray used those authorities to ask whether this particular transaction and injury formed a substantial Illinois connection. 22 Ill. 2d at 437-41.
Single transaction and claim relationship: McGee established that one deliberate, continuing transaction can support specific jurisdiction when the claim arises from that transaction. Gray extended the same claim-centered logic to products: quantified continuous business supplied one route to minimum contacts, while a product transaction substantially connected to the forum and producing the lawsuit supplied another. The cause of action arose directly from the valve's Illinois use and injury. 22 Ill. 2d at 438-40.
Commercial distribution and indirect benefits: Modern component manufacturers commonly reach consumers through assemblers and independent middlemen. Titan elected to manufacture valves for incorporation into heaters sold in interstate commerce. The court inferred that this commercial design led to substantial Illinois use and allowed Titan to benefit from Illinois law protecting the marketing and consumption of products containing its valves. The distributor's physical delivery, rather than Titan's own shipment, preserved the commercial relationship between Titan's conduct and Illinois. 22 Ill. 2d at 441-43.
Forum and litigant interests: Illinois possessed a direct regulatory and remedial interest because an Illinois resident suffered injury in
Illinois from a product used there. Illinois substantive law governed the occurrence, and witnesses concerning injury, damages, and the explosion were likely located there. Modern transport and communication reduced Titan's defense burden. Those circumstances made
Illinois a convenient and reasonable forum for resolving the product-related dispute. 22 Ill. 2d at 443-44.
Connection to World-Wide Volkswagen: Gray later appears on both levels of World-Wide Volkswagen. The Oklahoma Supreme
Court declined to use Gray's place-of-injury construction for Oklahoma subsection 1701.03(a)(3) because Oklahoma's adjacent subsection (a)(4) expressly governed out-of-state acts producing in-state injuries. The U.S. Supreme Court cited Gray when describing jurisdiction over a manufacturer or distributor that delivers products into commercial distribution with an expectation that consumers will purchase them in the forum. The comparison makes defendant-directed market distribution the important factual bridge.
1L explanation: Start with the Illinois statute. Injury in Illinois completed the alleged tort and activated section 17(1)(b); section 16 then supplied out-of-state personal service. Due process asked whether Titan's commercial placement of the valve, its contemplated ultimate use in Illinois, and the claim-producing Illinois injury formed a fair forum relationship. The court answered yes and restored both Gray's claim and American Radiator's cross-claim against Titan.

briefs.title: World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson
briefs.citation: 444 U.S. 286 (1980). U.S. Supreme Court. White, J. Argued October 3, 1979; decided January 21, 1980. No. 78-1078. Certiorari to World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 1978 OK 131, 585 P.2d 351 (Okla. 1978).

sections.Parties:
Petitioners and jurisdictional objectors: World-Wide Volkswagen Corporation, a New York corporation serving as the regional distributor for Volkswagen products sold to dealers in New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut; and Seaway Volkswagen, Inc., the
New York retail dealer in Massena that sold the Robinsons' Audi. Underlying plaintiffs and respondents: Kay Robinson, suing for her own injuries; Harry Robinson, individually and as father and next friend for the injured children; and the children, including Eva
May Robinson and George Samuel Robinson. Named judicial respondent: Charles S. Woodson, District Judge of Creek County, whose continued exercise of in-personam jurisdiction the petitioners sought to prohibit.
Other underlying defendants: Audi NSU Auto Union Aktiengesellschaft, the manufacturer, and Volkswagen of America, Inc., the
U.S. importer. Volkswagen also entered a special appearance in the trial court, then declined to seek Oklahoma Supreme Court review.
Audi and Volkswagen therefore remained defendants in the Oklahoma action and were outside the jurisdictional judgment reviewed by the U.S. Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History:
Products-liability filing: After the Oklahoma accident, the Robinsons filed a manufacturers' products-liability action in the District
Court for Creek County, Oklahoma. They alleged defective design and placement of the Audi's gasoline tank and fuel system and joined the manufacturer, importer, regional distributor, and retail dealer. Oklahoma's Uniform Interstate and International Procedure
Act, 12 Okla. Stat. 1971 sections 1701.01 et seq., supplied the asserted long-arm authority over the out-of-state companies.
Special appearances and trial-court rulings: World-Wide and Seaway entered special appearances to contest personal jurisdiction under the Fourteenth Amendment. Their papers also used the phrases 'venue of the subject matter' and 'venue over the subject matter.'
The Creek County court treated the appearances as special, rejected their constitutional objection, and denied reconsideration. Those rulings were unreported. The merits action remained pending.
Preservation and waiver issue: The Robinsons later argued that petitioners had waived their objection by combining personal-jurisdiction language with a challenge concerning subject matter and by taking merits depositions in Oklahoma. The trial court retained the special-appearance characterization, and the Oklahoma Supreme Court decided the jurisdictional questions. The
U.S. Supreme Court accordingly treated the objection as preserved and reached the merits. 444 U.S. at 295 n.10.
Original proceeding for prohibition: World-Wide and Seaway invoked the Oklahoma Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and petitioned for a writ of prohibition directing Judge Woodson to stop exercising personal jurisdiction. Prohibition served as the pretrial vehicle for obtaining appellate review of adjudicatory authority before the petitioners litigated the products-liability merits. The
Oklahoma Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction and denied the writ. 1978 OK 131, paragraphs 0-3, 17.
Oklahoma statutory analysis: Section 1701.03(a)(3) covered tortious injury in Oklahoma caused by an act or omission in Oklahoma.
The state court held that the alleged design and distribution acts occurred outside Oklahoma. It declined to classify the place of injury as the place of the act under Gray, because subsection (a)(4) separately governed an Oklahoma injury caused by an out-of-state act.
Subsection (a)(4) authorized jurisdiction when the defendant regularly did or solicited Oklahoma business, engaged in another persistent Oklahoma course of conduct, or derived substantial revenue from goods used or consumed or services rendered in
Oklahoma. 585 P.2d at 353-54.
Oklahoma ruling under subsection (a)(4): The state court reasoned that an automobile's designed mobility made Oklahoma use foreseeable and inferred from the vehicle's value and evidence of petitioners' goods being used in Oklahoma that the petitioners derived substantial revenue from goods used there. Five justices joined the opinion, two concurred in the result, and one concurred in part and dissented in part without opinion. The court therefore found statutory authority, assumed original jurisdiction, and denied prohibition. 585 P.2d at 354-55.
U.S. Supreme Court review and disposition: The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 440 U.S. 907 (1979), to resolve a conflict between Oklahoma and the highest courts of at least four other States concerning jurisdiction over out-of-state automobile sellers. The
Court reviewed the Fourteenth Amendment question while accepting Oklahoma's authoritative construction of its own long-arm statute. By a six-to-three judgment, it reversed the Oklahoma Supreme Court. Oklahoma consequently lacked power to bind
World-Wide and Seaway in this action; the claims against Audi and Volkswagen remained pending in Creek County. 444 U.S. at
290-91, 299 & nn.6, 9.
sections.Material Facts:
Harry and Kay Robinson, then New York residents, purchased a new Audi from Seaway in Massena, New York, in 1976. In 1977 the family left New York to establish a new home in Arizona. While they drove through Oklahoma, another vehicle struck the Audi from behind. The gasoline tank ruptured, fire entered the passenger compartment, and Kay Robinson and the children suffered severe burns.
The other driver played no role in the jurisdictional litigation.
World-Wide's New York office administered a contractual regional distribution territory limited to New York, New Jersey, and
Connecticut. Seaway was a New York corporation operating its dealership in Massena. The record treated World-Wide, Seaway,
Volkswagen, and Audi as independent corporations connected by contracts. World-Wide and Seaway conducted no Oklahoma activity, closed no Oklahoma sales, performed no Oklahoma services, maintained no Oklahoma agent, shipped no products to
Oklahoma, and purchased no advertising calculated to reach Oklahoma.
The evidentiary record contained one vehicle sold by these petitioners that had entered Oklahoma: the Robinson Audi, carried there by its purchasers during their interstate move. The petitioners received no direct revenue from Volkswagen service centers in Oklahoma.
