Litronic's 90-day term in place. Only the knockout rule removed both terms and let the Code's reasonable-time standard rescue Northrop. A brief that says the court simply preferred the majority rule misstates the reasoning: Posner thought the California approach most sensible and applied the majority rule because he predicted that Illinois would.
Two further points connect the case to the rest of the assignment. First, the additional-versus-different distinction must be drawn before § 2-207(2) is applied in a majority-rule jurisdiction; in Bayway the Tax
Clause was analyzed as an additional term, so the knockout rule never arose. Second, Official Comment 6 states that where clauses on confirming forms conflict, each party is assumed to object to the other's clause and the conflicting terms do not become part of the contract; courts adopting the knockout rule frequently cite that comment, although Posner's opinion rested on the case law and the Code's uniformity policy rather than on Comment 6.

briefs.title: Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc.
briefs.citation: Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc., 105 F.3d 1147 (7th Cir. 1997), cert. denied, 522 U.S. 808 (1997). United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, No. 96-3294, argued December 10, 1996, decided January 6, 1997; rehearing and rehearing en banc denied February 3, 1997. Judge Easterbrook wrote the opinion for a panel that included Judges Cummings and Wood. The case concerns whether terms shipped i

sections.Parties:
Rich and Enza Hill, who bought a Gateway computer by telephone, were the plaintiffs and appellees. They sued on behalf of a class of similarly situated purchasers and wanted their claims heard in court. Gateway
2000, Inc., a direct seller of personal computers by telephone and mail order, and David Prais, an individual defendant whose role the opinion does not describe, were the defendants and appellants. Gateway sought to enforce the arbitration clause included in the terms shipped with the computer.
sections.Material Facts:
The Hills ordered a Gateway computer by telephone and gave a credit card number. A box arrived containing the computer, software, and a four-page statement of terms that, by its own words, governed unless the customer returned the computer within 30 days. One of the terms was an arbitration clause. Gateway's advertisements stated that its products came with limited warranties and lifetime support. The Hills kept the computer more than 30 days before complaining about its components and performance. They conceded noticing the statement of terms but denied reading it closely enough to discover the agreement to arbitrate.
The box did not display a notice that additional terms were inside. 105 F.3d at 1148, 1150.
sections.Procedural History: The Hills sued Gateway in federal district court in Illinois. They alleged that the product's shortcomings made Gateway a racketeer, with mail and wire fraud as the predicate offenses, and sought treble damages under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) for themselves and a class of all other purchasers. Gateway moved to enforce the arbitration clause under the Federal Arbitration Act. The district court refused, finding that the record was insufficient to support a valid arbitration agreement between the parties or to show that the plaintiffs had been given adequate notice of the arbitration clause. Gateway took an interlocutory appeal, an appeal before final judgment, under 9 U.S.C. § 16(a)(1)(A), which permits immediate review of an order refusing to compel arbitration. Id. at 1148.
sections.Issue:
Did the Hills accept Gateway's terms, including the arbitration clause, by keeping the computer beyond the
30-day return period, so that the Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcement of the clause? Does the approach of ProCD, Inc. v. Zeidenberg, 86 F.3d 1447 (7th Cir. 1996), extend beyond software and beyond contracts that remain to be performed on both sides? Does UCC § 2-207 govern a transaction in which only one party's form exists? Does the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act, or any requirement that an arbitration clause be conspicuous or disclosed before the sale, defeat the clause?
sections.Holding:
A vendor, as master of the offer, may invite acceptance by conduct and may propose limitations on the kind of conduct that constitutes acceptance. A buyer who receives goods together with terms, has the opportunity to read the terms and return the goods, and instead keeps them past the stated period accepts the terms;
competent adults are bound by such documents whether or not they read them. That rule concerns contract formation generally, not software, and it applies to a transaction in which the buyer pays before seeing the full terms. Section 2-207 has no application when there is only one form. The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act does not require a seller to recite its terms before the sale, and the Federal Arbitration Act forbids any special requirement that an arbitration clause be prominent. By keeping the computer beyond 30 days, the Hills accepted Gateway's offer, including the arbitration clause. Id. at 1148-51.
sections.Judgment: The Seventh Circuit vacated the district court's decision and remanded with instructions to compel the Hills to submit their dispute to arbitration.
sections.Reasoning:
The Federal Arbitration Act requires courts to enforce an agreement to arbitrate "save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract," and the Hills' argument that the arbitration clause did not stand out was not such a ground. Whether a contract including the clause was formed depended on ordinary contract law, which the court took to be the same in Illinois and South Dakota, the two states whose law might govern. Id. at 1148.
The court treated ProCD as controlling. ProCD held that a vendor may propose that a contract be formed only after the customer has had a chance to inspect both the product and the terms, with retention as acceptance and return as rejection; the software buyer there was bound by a license inside the box because he used the product after reading the terms. Gateway shipped computers with the same accept-or-return offer that ProCD made. A contract need not be read to be effective. Payment before the disclosure of full terms is common for air travel, insurance, and many other transactions, and Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute, 499
U.S. 585 (1991), enforced a forum-selection clause printed among three pages of terms attached to a cruise ticket. Practical considerations pointed the same way: if a telephone sales representative had to read a four-page statement of terms before taking a credit card number, "the droning voice would anesthetize rather than enlighten many potential buyers," and customers would simply hang up. Id. at 1148-49.
The Hills offered several distinctions, each of which the court rejected. To the argument that ProCD was limited to software, the court answered that "ProCD is about the law of contract, not the law of software," and that Gateway's box was in any event crammed with software. To the argument that ProCD applied only to executory contracts, those with performance still owed on both sides, the court answered that the objection was legally wrong because the question was formation rather than performance, and factually wrong because both contracts were incompletely performed: Gateway's warranty and lifetime-support promises bound it to future performance that consumers value. To the argument that a merchant must give notice of terms before the sale, the court observed that Gateway's advertisements told buyers the products came with limited warranties and lifetime support, and that how limited the warranty was, and what support was offered, could be learned only from the terms. It identified three ways shoppers learn the terms of direct-sale goods. They can ask the vendor to send the terms before deciding whether to buy; the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act requires firms to distribute their warranty terms on request, and the Hills did not contend that Gateway would have refused to enclose its remaining terms as well. They can consult public sources such as computer
magazines and vendors' Web sites. Or they can inspect the documents after delivery and return the product if the terms are unacceptable. The Hills took the third route and were bound by its outcome. Id. at 1149-50.
The court held that the Hills' reliance on § 2-207 was misplaced: the battle-of-the-forms provision addresses conflicting forms exchanged by two parties, and when there is only one form, § 2-207 is irrelevant, as ProCD had already concluded. It also rejected the argument that the arbitration clause had to be prominent. Under
Doctor's Associates, Inc. v. Casarotto, 517 U.S. 681 (1996), the Federal Arbitration Act is inconsistent with any requirement that an arbitration clause be singled out for special notice; the terms inside Gateway's box stand or fall together. The Hills' final distinction, raised at oral argument, was that ProCD's box announced that terms were inside while Gateway's did not. The court found that difference functional rather than legal: a notice on the box serves shoppers browsing store shelves, while a telephone buyer has already ordered before seeing the box and receives the terms with the product, together with the return period in which to evaluate them. Id. at 1150.
As to the fraud allegations, Prima Paint Corp. v. Flood & Conklin Manufacturing Co., 388 U.S. 395 (1967), sends a claim that the contract as a whole was induced by fraud to the arbitrator; only a claim that the arbitration clause itself is unenforceable as part of a scheme to defraud is for the court, and the Hills made no such claim. RICO claims are no less arbitrable than claims in contract or tort. Whatever may be said for or against the cost and efficacy of arbitration was, in the court's view, for Congress and the contracting parties to weigh. Id. at 1151.
sections.Separate Opinions: The panel was unanimous. The reported decision contains no concurrence or dissent.
sections.Notes:
Hill extends ProCD from a software license read before use to a consumer goods transaction in which the buyer pays by telephone and first sees the terms on delivery. The literature calls this structure a rolling contract or a "money now, terms later" transaction; those are commentators' labels, and the opinion itself speaks of an accept-or-return offer. The holding rests entirely on formation. Easterbrook treated the vendor as the offeror, retention past the return period as acceptance, and § 2-207 as inapplicable; the substance of the arbitration clause, including its cost and forum, was not examined, and no unconscionability argument was presented.
The case has been contested on each of those steps. Klocek v. Gateway, Inc., 104 F. Supp. 2d 1332 (D. Kan.
2000), rejected the premise that the vendor is the offeror and held that § 2-207 applies to a single form, reading Official Comment 1 to cover a written confirmation that follows an earlier agreement. Brower v.
Gateway 2000, Inc., 246 A.D.2d 246 (N.Y. App. Div. 1998), followed Hill on formation but held the same clause's arbitration-cost provisions unconscionable. Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts § 2(b) accepts post-assent terms only if the business gave notice of them before the consumer assented and the consumer could terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value, or personal burden; on the Hills' facts the reasonableness of Gateway's pre-sale notice and of a 30-day return window would be contested questions rather than settled ones.

briefs.title: Klocek v. Gateway, Inc.
briefs.citation: Klocek v. Gateway, Inc., 104 F. Supp. 2d 1332 (D. Kan. 2000). United States District Court for the District of Kansas, No. 99-2499-KHV, memorandum and order of June 15, 2000, by Judge Kathryn H. Vratil. The action was later dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction in a motion the plaintiff joined, Klocek v. Gateway, Inc., 2000 WL 1372886 (D. Kan.), so the ruling was never reviewed on appe

sections.Parties:
William S. Klocek, an individual consumer who represented himself (pro se), was the plaintiff. Gateway,
Inc., which sold him a computer, and Hewlett-Packard, Inc., which made a scanner he bought to use with it, were the defendants. Gateway sought dismissal and an order compelling arbitration under paragraph 10 of its
Standard Terms and Conditions Agreement. Hewlett-Packard moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Klocek sought damages, individually and for a class, for products that did not work as promised and for false promises of technical support.
sections.Material Facts:
Klocek's complaint stated that he lived in Missouri. Gateway's affidavit said only that it shipped a computer to him on or about August 31, 1997. Klocek responded that he bought the computer in person at Gateway's store in Overland Park, Kansas, on August 27, 1997, and took it with him. The box contained the computer, a battery, power cables, instruction manuals, and Gateway's Standard Terms and Conditions Agreement, a four-page document with sixteen numbered paragraphs. At the top of the first page, in emphasized type inside a printed box, a notice stated: "This document contains Gateway 2000's Standard Terms and
Conditions. By keeping your Gateway 2000 computer system beyond five (5) days after the date of delivery, you accept these Terms and Conditions." Paragraph 10, headed Dispute Resolution, provided that any dispute or controversy arising out of or relating to the agreement or its interpretation would be settled exclusively and finally by arbitration under the Rules of Conciliation and Arbitration of the International Chamber of
Commerce, conducted in Chicago, Illinois, before a sole arbitrator, with any award final and binding.
Gateway offered no evidence that at the time of the sale it told Klocek about the Standard Terms, the five-day review period, or the arbitration clause; its evidence showed only that it enclosed the document in the box for him to read afterwards. Klocek alleged that Gateway induced him and other consumers to buy computers and support packages through false promises of technical support, and individually claimed breach of contract and breach of warranty on the ground that the computer was not compatible with standard peripherals and
Internet services as warranted. Against Hewlett-Packard he alleged a breach of the duty to warn that its scanner was incompatible with Gateway computers. 104 F. Supp. 2d at 1334-35, 1337.
sections.Procedural History:
Klocek filed in the District of Kansas under diversity jurisdiction. Gateway moved on November 22, 1999, to dismiss and to compel arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 3-4. Hewlett-Packard moved separately to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the damages alleged against it did not satisfy the $75,000 amount-in-controversy requirement. Klocek filed motions of his own, including for class certification and sanctions. The court applied a standard similar to summary judgment: Gateway bore an initial burden to show an enforceable agreement to arbitrate, and only if it met that burden would the burden shift to Klocek to show a genuine issue of fact for trial. The court could not tell from the record whether
Kansas, Missouri, or some other state's law governed formation, but found no material difference between
Kansas and Missouri law because both states had adopted the relevant provisions of UCC Article 2. Id. at
1335-37.
sections.Issue: Did Klocek agree to the arbitration clause in the Standard Terms? Answering that question required the court to decide whether the Seventh Circuit's approach in Hill and ProCD should be followed; whether § 2-207 applies to a transaction in which only one party's form exists; which party was the offeror; whether Gateway's acceptance was expressly conditional on assent to the Standard Terms; and whether a buyer who is not a merchant expressly assents to additional terms by keeping the goods beyond a stated period.
sections.Holding:
Whether the parties agreed to arbitrate is governed by ordinary state contract law, and the party seeking arbitration must prove the agreement. In a typical consumer transaction the purchaser is the offeror and the vendor accepts by completing the sale or shipping the goods. Terms shipped with the goods are additional terms in an expression of acceptance or a written confirmation, and § 2-207 applies even though only one form exists. An acceptance is expressly conditional under § 2-207(1) only if it clearly tells the offeror that the offeree is unwilling to proceed unless the additional terms are included. Where the buyer is not a merchant, additional terms are proposals that become part of the contract only if the buyer expressly agrees to them, and express assent cannot be presumed from silence or a failure to object.
Gateway offered no evidence that it, rather than Klocek, made the offer; no evidence that it conditioned the sale on acceptance of the Standard Terms; and no evidence that Klocek expressly agreed to them. Keeping the computer beyond five days did not demonstrate express agreement on this record. Gateway therefore failed to carry its burden of proving an agreement to arbitrate. Id. at 1337-41.
sections.Judgment:
The court overruled Gateway's motion to dismiss and compel arbitration. It sustained Hewlett-Packard's motion and dismissed the claims against it for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, and it overruled Klocek's own motions. Gateway was given until June 30, 2000, to file a supplemental motion if it contended that some law other than that of Kansas or Missouri governed formation, with a response due July 24 and a reply due
August 7, 2000, and the court reserved the possibility of a jury trial on whether an arbitration agreement existed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court started from the Federal Arbitration Act's framework. Federal policy favors arbitration and resolves doubts about the scope of arbitrable issues in its favor, but whether an agreement to arbitrate exists is decided under ordinary state-law principles of contract formation, and the party seeking arbitration bears a summary-judgment-like burden of proving that agreement. Gateway rested its motion on Hill and ProCD. Id.
at 1336-38.
Judge Vratil examined those cases and declined to follow them. In each, the Seventh Circuit had concluded without support that § 2-207 was irrelevant because only one written form was involved, and it had provided no explanation for its conclusion that the vendor is the master of the offer. Neither conclusion, the court found, is supported by the statute or by Kansas or Missouri law. By its terms § 2-207 applies to "an acceptance or written confirmation" and says nothing that requires a second form; Official Comment 1 states that the section applies where an agreement has been reached orally and is followed by one or both parties sending formal memoranda that add terms. Other courts had treated terms shipped with goods the same way:
Step-Saver Data Systems, Inc. v. Wyse Technology, 939 F.2d 91 (3d Cir. 1991), held that box-top license terms were proposals under § 2-207 that required the buyer's express assent because the contract had already been formed by the parties' conduct; Arizona Retail Systems, Inc. v. Software Link, Inc., 831 F. Supp. 759 (D.
Ariz. 1993), treated a license shipped with software as a proposed modification requiring express assent; and
U.S. Surgical Corp. v. Orris, Inc., 5 F. Supp. 2d 1201 (D. Kan. 1998), held that a single-use restriction on packaging that arrived after the sales contract was formed was a proposed modification needing the buyer's agreement. Id. at 1338-40.
The court then identified the offeror. In typical consumer transactions the purchaser is the offeror and the vendor the offeree, as in Brown Machine, Division of John Brown, Inc. v. Hercules, Inc., 770 S.W.2d 416 (Mo. Ct. App. 1989), and Rich Products Corp. v. Kemutec, Inc., 66 F. Supp. 2d 937 (E.D. Wis. 1999). A vendor can be the offeror in a particular transaction, but Gateway offered no factual evidence supporting that characterization here. The court therefore assumed that Klocek offered to buy the computer, in person or by order, and that Gateway accepted by completing the sale or shipping the goods. Under § 2-207(1) the
Standard Terms were either an expression of acceptance or a written confirmation containing additional terms. Gateway's acceptance was not expressly conditional on assent to those terms: a conditional acceptance must clearly express the offeree's unwillingness to proceed unless the additional terms are included, and shipping the goods with the terms attached did not communicate any unwillingness to proceed without
Klocek's agreement. Gateway also offered no evidence that at the time of the sale it told Klocek the transaction was conditioned on acceptance of the Standard Terms. Id. at 1340-41.
Because Klocek was not a merchant, § 2-207(2) treated the additional terms, including arbitration, as proposals that became part of the contract only if he expressly agreed to them. Gateway argued that the five-day notice made retention of the computer an acceptance of the terms. The court disagreed on this record. Express assent cannot be presumed from silence or a mere failure to object; Gateway's evidence showed only that it enclosed the Standard Terms for Klocek to read after the purchase, with no evidence that the parties discussed additional terms or that Klocek was told the five-day review period was a condition of the sale. Keeping the computer past five days was therefore insufficient to show that Klocek expressly agreed to the Standard Terms, and Gateway had not shown an enforceable agreement to arbitrate. Because Gateway had not addressed choice of law, the court allowed it to renew the motion if it contended that another state's law would produce a different result. Id. at 1341.
Hewlett-Packard's motion succeeded on a separate ground: the damages alleged against it fell short of the
$75,000 required for diversity jurisdiction, and the complaint did not support a punitive award large enough to close the gap. Id. at 1342.
sections.Separate Opinions: A single district judge decided the motions. The reported decision contains no separate opinion.
sections.Notes:
Klocek and Hill involve the same seller, materially similar documents, and opposite results, and the divergence turns on two framing choices. First, who made the offer: Hill treats the vendor as master of the offer, while Klocek applies the default that the purchaser offers and the vendor accepts by shipping. Second, what body of law governs the terms that arrive with the goods: Hill excludes § 2-207 because there is one form, while Klocek applies it as written and reads Comment 1 to cover confirmations that follow an earlier agreement. Once Klocek's framing is accepted, the consumer's status as a non-merchant makes the box terms proposals requiring express assent, and retention alone does not supply it.
The holding is narrower than it is sometimes described. The court decided that Gateway failed to prove its case on this record; a vendor that shows it disclosed the terms and the review period at the point of sale, or that it was the offeror, could reach a different outcome under the same framework. The Restatement of the
Law, Consumer Contracts § 2(b) adopts a rule between the two cases: it permits terms delivered after assent to be adopted, as Hill does, but only if the business proves that it gave the consumer notice of those terms before assent and a reasonable opportunity to review and terminate afterward, a burden that resembles the one Gateway failed to carry in Klocek.

briefs.title: Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts § 2(b) and (c)

sections.Sources:
Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts § 2 (Am. L. Inst. 2024). The American Law Institute's membership approved the Restatement at its May 2022 Annual Meeting, subject to minor revisions, and the
Institute published it in 2024. The abbreviation RLCC (sometimes RCC) is a citation convention rather than an official title. Like other Restatements, it describes common-law rules and is persuasive authority unless a court adopts it. Section 2 governs when standard contract terms are adopted as part of a consumer contract:
subsection (a) covers terms made available before the consumer assents, subsection (b) covers terms first made available afterward, and subsection (c) states the consequence when some terms are not adopted. The text summarized below is the published black-letter as reproduced in secondary sources; the assigned casebook excerpt governs for class. ALI publication notice; ALI Adviser summary of § 2.
sections.Text:
Section 1 supplies the vocabulary. In substance, a consumer contract is a contract between a business and a consumer, a consumer is an individual who transacts primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and a standard contract term is a term drafted in advance for use in multiple transactions rather than negotiated with the particular consumer. Reasonableness under the Restatement is judged on the totality of the circumstances. These definitions mark the boundary of the section: the merchant-to-merchant exchanges in Bayway, Northrop, Dorton, and C. Itoh fall outside it, while the consumer purchases in Hill and Klocek fall within it.
Subsection (a) states the baseline. A standard term is adopted if the business demonstrates that the consumer manifested assent to the transaction after receiving reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it in the contract, together with a reasonable opportunity to review it. Two features carry through the rest of the section. The business bears the burden of proof, and adoption of a term is analyzed separately from assent to the transaction as a whole.
Subsection (b): Terms Made Available After Assent
Subsection (b) addresses the transaction in Hill and Klocek: the consumer pays or otherwise assents first and sees the standard terms only later. A term that is available for review only after the consumer manifests assent is adopted if the business demonstrates three things. First, before manifesting assent, the consumer received reasonable notice that a standard term would be provided later and would be part of the contract, informing the consumer of the opportunity to review it and to terminate the contract, and explaining that a failure to terminate would result in adoption of the term. Second, after manifesting assent, the consumer received a reasonable opportunity to review the term. Third, after the term was made available, the consumer received a reasonable opportunity to terminate the transaction without unreasonable cost, loss of value, or personal burden, and did not exercise that power.
Each element responds to a criticism of Hill. The first element requires pre-assent notice of the existence of later terms and of the consequence of keeping the goods; Hill required no such notice and treated advertisements mentioning a limited warranty and the availability of terms on request as sufficient. The third element makes the exit route substantive: a return window that is too short, or that imposes restocking fees, return shipping, or loss of value, does not satisfy it. Under this test Gateway would have failed on the Klocek record, because it offered no evidence of any notice at the point of sale, and would have faced contested questions on the Hill record about the adequacy of its pre-sale notice and the cost of returning a computer within 30 days.
The subsection also departs from Klocek. That decision required a non-merchant buyer's express assent to terms arriving with the goods and refused to infer assent from retention. Subsection (b) permits adoption through retention, provided the business proves the notice and termination conditions. The Restatement thus accepts the accept-or-return structure in principle and regulates its conditions, rather than rejecting it as
Klocek did or accepting it without conditions as Hill did.
Subsection (c): Contract Without the Unadopted Terms
Subsection (c) answers the question that § 2-207(3) answers for merchants: what happens when a contract exists but some proposed terms did not make it in. If the consumer manifests assent to the transaction, the contract is not rendered unenforceable because some standard terms were not adopted under subsections (a) and (b). The contract's terms are those adopted under (a) and (b); any unadopted standard terms that the consumer elects to invoke; any terms, standard or not, to which both parties actually agreed; and terms supplied or incorporated by law.
Three consequences follow. The business cannot escape the bargain by arguing that its own terms failed; the failure of a standard term never voids the transaction. The consumer's election is one-directional: a consumer may choose to rely on an unadopted term that is favorable, such as a warranty or service promise, while the business cannot invoke an unadopted term against the consumer. And the gap left by an unadopted term is filled by law, so an arbitration clause that fails under (b) leaves the parties in court, and a failed warranty disclaimer leaves the implied warranties of Article 2 in place.
sections.Application:
Begin by confirming that the contract is a consumer contract and that the disputed term is a standard term.
Then locate the moment of assent and ask whether the term was available before it. If it was, apply subsection (a): reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review. If it was not, apply subsection (b) element by element, keeping the burden on the business: pre-assent notice of later terms and of the review-and-terminate mechanism; a post-assent opportunity to review; and an opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value, or personal burden that the consumer did not use. If any element fails, subsection (c) governs: the contract survives, the term drops out unless the consumer elects it, and the law supplies whatever the term would have covered.
Suppose a consumer orders a laptop by telephone, is told nothing about terms, and finds a five-day return notice and an arbitration clause in the box. Under subsection (b) the business cannot show pre-assent notice, so the arbitration clause is not adopted, and under subsection (c) the sale stands with disputes resolved in court. Suppose instead that the order confirmation states that terms will be enclosed, that the consumer may return the laptop within 30 days at the business's expense for a full refund, and that keeping it adopts the terms. The first element is met, and the case turns on whether the review and termination opportunities were reasonable in the circumstances, including any cost or burden of the return.

briefs.title: UCC § 2-207: Additional and Different Terms

sections.Sources:
UCC § 2-207 and its Official Comments 1 through 7, with §§ 2-104, 2-206, and 2-309 as supporting provisions. The earlier note on §§ 2-204 through 2-207 in this packet introduces the section; this note works through the four questions the assigned cases raise: who must prove material alteration and what surprise and hardship mean (Bayway); how different terms are treated (Northrop); whether the section applies when only one form exists (Hill and Klocek); and how the merchant rule changes the analysis for consumers (Klocek).
The text reproduced by Cornell is the model Code; the enacted version of the governing state controls an actual dispute, and the cases applied New York (Bayway), Illinois (Northrop), Illinois or South Dakota (Hill), and Kansas or Missouri (Klocek) law. § 2-207; § 2-206; § 2-104; § 2-309.
sections.Text:
Subsection (1): a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance, or a written confirmation sent within a reasonable time, operates as an acceptance even though it states terms additional to or different from those offered or agreed upon, unless acceptance is expressly made conditional on assent to the additional or different terms. Subsection (2): the additional terms are construed as proposals for addition to the contract;
between merchants they become part of the contract unless (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to the terms of the offer, (b) they materially alter it, or (c) notification of objection has already been given or is given within a reasonable time after notice of them is received. Subsection (3): conduct by both parties recognizing the existence of a contract establishes one even though the writings do not, and the terms then consist of those on which the writings agree together with supplementary terms incorporated under the Code.
Official Comment 1 identifies two situations the section covers: an agreement reached orally or by informal correspondence and followed by one or both parties sending formal memoranda that add terms, and an exchange of forms in which the offeree's response adds or changes terms. Comment 3 sends the question whether additional or different terms become part of the agreement to subsection (2). Comments 4 and 5 give examples of terms that do and do not materially alter a contract. Comment 6 addresses conflicting clauses in confirming forms. Comment 7 explains subsection (3).
The Merchant Rule and Consumers
Subsection (2)'s first sentence applies to everyone: additional terms are proposals. The second sentence, which makes proposals part of the contract by default, applies only between merchants, a term § 2-104 defines to include a person who deals in goods of the kind or who by occupation holds itself out as having relevant knowledge or skill. When either party is not a merchant, a proposal becomes part of the contract only if the other party assents to it. Klocek applied that rule to a consumer buyer and required express assent, holding that silence, failure to object, and retention of the goods beyond a stated period did not supply it on the record before the court. The merchant rule is therefore the hinge between the commercial cases and the consumer cases: Bayway's presumption of inclusion has no counterpart when the buyer is a consumer.
Material Alteration: Burden, Surprise, and Hardship
Comment 4 defines a material alteration as a term that would result in surprise or hardship if incorporated without the other party's express awareness, and lists examples such as a disclaimer of the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness, a clause reserving the seller's power to cancel on the buyer's failure to meet any invoice when due, and a clause requiring complaints in a time materially shorter than customary or reasonable. Comment 5 lists terms that ordinarily do not materially alter a contract, such as a clause setting a reasonable time for complaints, a clause fixing interest on overdue invoices at customary rates, and a clause limiting remedies in a reasonable manner. The examples are illustrations; Dorton treated materiality as a question of fact for the trial court.
Bayway settled two operational questions for the Second Circuit. The party opposing inclusion of the term bears the burden of proving material alteration, because subsection (2) makes inclusion the default and the exceptions must be established by the party invoking them. Surprise has a subjective component, what the party actually knew, and an objective component, what a reasonable merchant should have known; the objective component is proved through trade usage, course of dealing, and the parties' own forms. Hardship in Bayway was treated as at least doubtful as an independent ground, on Judge Posner's view that hardship is a consequence of a material alteration rather than a criterion, and a party's inability to afford a term it could have avoided did not qualify.
Different Terms
Subsection (1) refers to additional or different terms, and subsection (2) refers only to additional terms.
Northrop catalogues the three responses. Some courts treat different terms as additional terms and apply the materiality analysis of subsection (2); a materially different term in the acceptance then fails and the offeror's term stands. Others hold that different terms in the acceptance are simply ignored, so the offeror's terms control. The majority, applying what is commonly called the knockout rule, hold that conflicting terms cancel each other and the Code's gap-fillers supply the missing term; Comment 6, which states that where clauses on confirming forms conflict each party is assumed to object to the other's clause and the conflicting terms do not become part of the contract, is frequently cited for this approach. Northrop predicted that Illinois would follow the majority, so the seller's 90-day warranty and the buyer's unlimited warranty both dropped out and
§ 2-309's reasonable-time standard governed. A brief should identify the jurisdiction's approach before classifying a term, because the classification decides the outcome only in a knockout jurisdiction.
One Form, Confirmations, and Contracts by Conduct
Hill holds that § 2-207 is irrelevant when there is only one form, treating the section as confined to a battle between two forms. Klocek holds the opposite, relying on the statutory reference to "a written confirmation" and on Comment 1's first situation, in which one party's memorandum follows an oral agreement. Bayway illustrates the confirmation setting between merchants: the parties agreed by telephone, each sent a confirmation, and the seller's confirmation added a term that became part of the contract under subsection (2) because the buyer could not prove material alteration. The Hill and Klocek split also reflects a disagreement about who the offeror is. If the vendor is master of the offer and retention is acceptance, no acceptance with additional terms ever occurs; if the purchaser's order is the offer and shipment is acceptance, the terms in the box are additional terms under subsection (2) and, for a consumer, require express assent.
Subsection (3) supplies the fallback when the writings do not form a contract, as in C. Itoh, or when a court prefers to rest on conduct. Both parties' performance establishes the contract, and its terms are those on which the writings agree plus the Code's supplementary provisions; a term found in only one writing is excluded.
Northrop observed that analyzing the exchange under subsection (3) would have produced the same result as the knockout rule under subsection (2), because both routes replace the conflicting warranties with the Code's default.
sections.Application:
Work in order. Identify the offer and the acceptance, or the prior agreement and the confirmation, and decide which document is being measured against which; in a consumer purchase, decide who the offeror is and be prepared to defend the choice, since Hill and Klocek diverge at that step. Ask whether the response is a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance or a timely confirmation, and whether it is expressly conditional in the strict sense Dorton and C. Itoh require. If a contract forms under subsection (1), classify each disputed term as additional or different and identify the jurisdiction's approach to different terms.
Determine merchant status; for a non-merchant, additional terms require assent. Between merchants, apply subsection (2)(a) through (c), placing the burden of proving material alteration on the party opposing the term and proving surprise objectively through usage and dealing. If the writings do not form a contract but the parties performed, apply subsection (3) and exclude any term found in only one writing. For a consumer transaction with terms delivered after payment, note that the Restatement of the Law, Consumer Contracts §
2(b) replaces this analysis with a notice-and-exit test that the business must satisfy.

briefs.title: Mattei v. Hopper
briefs.citation: 51 Cal. 2d 119, 330 P.2d 625 (1958). Supreme Court of California, in bank. Spence, J. S.F. No. 19806; decided October 24, 1958. Appeal from a judgment entered after a bench trial.

sections.Parties:
Plaintiff / appellant: Peter O. Mattei, a real-estate developer assembling land for a shopping center. He signed the buyer's side of the deposit receipt, paid the deposit, pursued leases, and sought damages after the conveyance failed.
Defendant / respondent: Amelia F. Hopper, owner of the adjacent parcel. She offered to sell the property, later repudiated through counsel, and obtained judgment at trial. Relevant third party: Coldwell Banker & Company, the real-estate intermediary charged with obtaining leases satisfactory to Mattei.
sections.Procedural History:
Mattei filed an action for damages alleging that Hopper breached the parties' written land-sale agreement by failing to convey the parcel. The case was tried to the court without a jury. The trial court treated Mattei's satisfaction clause as leaving performance within his unrestricted choice, characterized the agreement as illusory and lacking mutuality, and entered judgment for Hopper.
Mattei appealed. The California Supreme Court reviewed the written instrument's legal effect and the consideration question. It held that the deposit receipt created a contract, that good faith governed Mattei's judgment about the leases, and that this enforceable obligation supplied consideration. The court reversed the judgment. Chief Justice Gibson and
Justices Shenk, Carter, Traynor, and Schauer joined Justice Spence. Justice McComb dissented without an opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Mattei planned a shopping center on a tract beside Hopper's land. A real-estate agent negotiated with Hopper for several months. Hopper rejected several proposals because the offered price was inadequate. She then submitted an offer, and Mattei accepted it the same day. Their writing used the agent's deposit-receipt form.
The stated purchase price was $57,500. Mattei had to deposit $1,000 with the agent. The agreement gave him 120 days to examine title and consummate the transaction. At the end of that period, the balance became payable when Hopper tendered a good and sufficient deed. The concluding provision stated that the transaction was subject to Coldwell
Banker obtaining leases satisfactory to the purchaser.
The lease provision served the shopping-center project. Mattei wanted time to secure tenant commitments before paying the balance and taking title. The commercial value of the assembled site depended on lease features that included term length, renewal rights, covenants, restrictions, rent, tenant creditworthiness, and the nature of each tenant's business.
Mattei paid the $1,000 deposit and worked to obtain leases. Before the 120-day period expired, Hopper's attorney informed him that Hopper would decline to sell on the deposit receipt's terms. Hopper later received notice that satisfactory leases had been obtained and that Mattei offered the unpaid purchase price. Hopper withheld the deed required by the writing.
sections.Issue: Two connected questions: (1) Did the signed deposit receipt create an immediate contract whose performance was conditioned on Mattei's obtaining satisfactory leases? (2) Did the satisfaction provision impose a legally enforceable standard on Mattei's judgment and thereby preserve consideration for Hopper's conveyance promise?
sections.Holding:
Contract formation: The deposit receipt created a binding contract when the parties signed it. The lease clause made
Mattei's duty to complete the purchase conditional on obtaining leases satisfactory to him and gave him a contractual power to terminate if that condition failed. Consideration: Mattei had to evaluate the leases through honest, good-faith judgment. That legal duty restricted his discretion and made his promise sufficient consideration. Disposition:
Judgment for Hopper reversed.
sections.Reasoning:
Interpretation of 'subject to': The court read the entire deposit receipt as one transaction. The writing stated the property, price, deposit, performance period, deed tender, and lease condition. This structure formed a present agreement and located the satisfaction event within performance. The clause therefore allocated leasing risk to Mattei during the 120-day period.
Consideration and mutuality: In a bilateral contract, each exchanged promise must impose a legal obligation. A promise becomes illusory when its maker retains unrestricted freedom to perform or withdraw. The terms 'illusory promise' and 'lack of mutuality' identify the same formation inquiry: whether the exchange contains consideration.
Modern doctrine states the point through Restatement (Second) Section 79: once consideration exists, mutuality supplies no additional requirement.
Two satisfaction standards: A satisfaction condition concerning commercial value, quality, operative fitness, or mechanical utility ordinarily uses an objective reasonable-person standard. A condition concerning taste, fancy, or judgment uses the promisor's actual judgment, governed by honesty and good faith. The selected standard comes from the subject matter the parties assigned to the promisor.
Classification of the leases: Shopping-center leases required evaluation of many interacting factors: duration, renewal options, covenants, restrictions, rent, financial responsibility, and business mix. Those considerations called for business judgment. Mattei therefore possessed subjective evaluative authority coupled with a duty to exercise that authority honestly and in good faith. Genuine dissatisfaction with the proposed leases could excuse his purchase performance; a strategic or fabricated claim of dissatisfaction would breach the agreement.
Why the good-faith duty supplies consideration: Mattei promised to accept leases that satisfied his honest judgment and to complete the purchase when that condition occurred. Hopper could challenge a refusal by proving that Mattei's stated dissatisfaction lacked genuineness. That exposure to judicial review created a real legal detriment and supported the reciprocal conveyance promise.
Third-party performance: The leases came from prospective shopping-center tenants; Hopper's promised performance was conveyance of the land. The court applied the same good-faith standard because the contract made those leases the condition by which Mattei's performance would be measured. Mattei's evaluative duty retained the same content when applied to third-party leases.
Doctrinal history: Earlier mutuality formulations often asked whether a court could compel each side at formation.
Satisfaction cases developed enforceable standards for apparently broad discretion. The First Restatement Section 265 and the Williston and Corbin treatises treated a satisfaction promise as an undertaking to exercise honest judgment.
Mattei used that established approach to connect interpretation, implied good faith, and consideration.
Prior California dicta: Lawrence Block Co. v. Palston described buyer-approval clauses as unrestricted because judgment lacked a reasonable-person measure. Its actual result rested on an unaccepted counteroffer. Pruitt v. Fontana repeated that language, while its result concerned a later oral agreement and estoppel against a statute-of-frauds defense. Mattei disapproved the dicta to the extent they treated objective reasonableness as the only enforceable standard. Honest good faith supplies the standard for judgment-based satisfaction.
Rule and application sequence: Identify the promised performance; decide whether the disputed language creates a formation condition or a performance condition; classify the subject of satisfaction; select objective reasonableness or subjective good faith; then ask whether that standard meaningfully restricts discretion. Here, the signed receipt formed the contract, lease acceptability involved judgment, and good faith bound Mattei.

briefs.title: Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. v. Zoltek Corp.
briefs.citation: 543 F.3d 987 (8th Cir. 2008). U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. Colloton, J., joined by Shepherd, J., and Erickson, D.J., sitting by designation. Nos. 07-2057 and 07-2171; submitted January 14, 2008; filed October 8, 2008.

sections.Parties:
Plaintiffs / appellees / cross-appellants: Structural Polymer Group, Ltd. and Structural Polymer Systems, Ltd., British corporations referred to together as SP. They manufactured prepreg, bought carbon fiber, obtained a jury verdict for lost profits, and sought restoration of the vacated alternative award. Defendant / appellant / cross-appellee: Zoltek
Corporation, a Missouri corporation that manufactured carbon fiber. It supplied SP under the 2000 agreement, left the
2005 and 2006 orders unfilled, and challenged liability and damages after trial.
sections.Procedural History:
On February 22, 2005, SP sued Zoltek in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri for breach of the
2000 Supply Agreement. SP sought lost profits through December 31, 2006, future lost profits through the contract's
December 31, 2010 end date, and specific performance. The dispute included whether the agreement covered Panex 35 after Zoltek discontinued Panex 33. SP pleaded alternative counts tied to Panex 35 and Panex 33.
During trial, Zoltek sought to present lack of mutuality as a basis for treating the Supply Agreement as unenforceable.
District Judge Carol E. Jackson classified the contention as an affirmative defense omitted from Zoltek's answer, denied a late amendment, and independently held that the writing contained consideration as a matter of law. The court also found insufficient evidence for Zoltek's requested abandonment instruction.
On November 29, 2006, the jury found for SP and awarded $21,138,518 on the Panex 35 calculation and $14,906,377 on the alternative Panex 33 calculation, a combined $36,044,895 in past lost profits. It declined future lost profits.
Because SP's counts sought alternative recovery for the same maximum quantity of large-tow fiber, the district court granted relief under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 59(e), vacated the $14,906,377 component as duplicative, and entered a $21,138,518 judgment.
Zoltek moved under Rule 50(b) for judgment as a matter of law and under Rule 59(a) for a new trial on liability and damages. The district court denied both motions. Zoltek appealed. SP cross-appealed the Rule 59(e) reduction and initially challenged the denial of specific performance. SP terminated the Supply Agreement effective February 29,
2008 and withdrew the specific-performance portion of its cross-appeal.
The Eighth Circuit reviewed the Rule 50(b) ruling de novo, viewing the record in the verdict winner's favor and asking whether a reasonable jury could reach the verdict. It reviewed denial of a new trial, evidentiary rulings, jury instructions, and the Rule 59(e) alteration under abuse-of-discretion standards. The court affirmed the judgment in full.
sections.Material Facts:
Carbon fiber consists of filament bundles. The parties used 'large-tow' or Large Filament Count fiber for bundles containing at least 48,000 filaments. 'Small-tow' fiber commonly contained 24,000 or fewer filaments, cost more to make, and offered superior quality. SP wove carbon fiber into textile-like sheets and impregnated them with resin to produce prepreg, a strong, light material that builders could mold into products such as wind-turbine blades.
In November 2000, Zoltek and SP entered a Supply Agreement running from November 6, 2000 through December 31,
2010. Zoltek promised to manufacture and sell all of SP's requirements for Large Filament Count Carbon Fibers meeting the Panex 33 specifications at the then-current market price. SP promised to obtain from Zoltek its total requirements for carbon fiber of suitable quality in SP's reasonable opinion. Annual volume could reach the quantity SP actually purchased in the preceding contract year plus one million pounds.
The agreement also contained price protection. When another supplier offered large-tow fiber at a lower market price,
Zoltek had a right of first refusal. A matching offer by Zoltek required SP to purchase from Zoltek; a decision by Zoltek to leave the price unmatched permitted SP to purchase from the competing source. The mechanism preserved Zoltek's supply position whenever it met the market offer.
The parties formed the agreement to develop large-tow carbon fiber as a lower-cost alternative in the wind-energy market, where manufacturers then used mostly small-tow fiber. Zoltek produced Panex 33 before April 2002. SP bought 28,219.17 pounds in 2000 and 20,943.91 pounds in 2001. SP ordered 1,763.70 pounds in 2002 and returned it for asserted quality defects.
In April 2002, Zoltek ended Panex 33 production and introduced Panex 35, another large-tow product. SP's 2003 requirements produced zero orders for either product. It ordered and received 548,935 pounds of Panex 35 in 2004. The litigation concerned a 1,480,138-pound Panex 35 order in 2005 and SP's claimed entitlement to 2,480,138 pounds in
2006. Both disputed orders remained unfilled.
SP also bought small-tow fiber from other sellers. Trial evidence described small-tow and large-tow as distinct products with different quality and applications. Zoltek argued that their functional interchangeability let SP manipulate its large-tow requirements. The jury found that SP performed its contractual obligations.
sections.Issue: Primary consideration question: Did SP's promise to buy its total good-faith requirements of suitable large-tow carbon fiber from Zoltek, subject to an annual quantity cap and Zoltek's price-matching right, supply consideration even though SP began with zero large-tow requirements and retained judgment about quality? Additional appellate questions concerned abandonment, evidentiary rulings, proof and instruction of lost profits, the Gamesa shipment, and duplication of the alternative verdicts.
sections.Holding:
Consideration: The Supply Agreement contained mutuality and consideration as a matter of Missouri law. UCC
Section 2-306 imposed good faith on SP's requirements, the quality phrase used SP's reasonable opinion, the annual cap constrained expansion, and Zoltek's right to match a competing price preserved the purchase obligation. Other rulings:
The trial judge properly withheld an abandonment instruction; the court's curative directions resolved the evidentiary concern; sufficient evidence and a proper Missouri instruction supported the past lost-profit award; the Gamesa transaction fell outside the offset calculation; and the second alternative award duplicated the first. Disposition:
Affirmed on Zoltek's appeal and SP's cross-appeal.
sections.Reasoning:
Mutuality is a consideration inquiry: Zoltek's mutuality argument asserted that SP's side of the exchange imposed no legal detriment. The Eighth Circuit invoked Restatement (Second) Section 79 and Missouri decisions: satisfaction of the consideration requirement completes the formation inquiry, and mutuality supplies no separate element. Missouri ordinarily treats the sufficiency of consideration in a written agreement as a question of law for the court.
Zero requirements at formation: Missouri's enactment of UCC Section 2-306(1), Mo. Rev. Stat. Section
400.2-306(1), measures quantity by the buyer's actual requirements occurring in good faith. SP therefore promised to order its genuine large-tow needs from Zoltek. A zero level could result from a good-faith operation of SP's business. A zero level chosen to divert covered demand or escape the bargain could support a breach claim. The enforceable good-faith standard supplied consideration from the outset.
Formation and performance: The writing's enforceability depended on the legal constraint governing SP's quantity decisions. SP's actual order pattern concerned performance under that constraint. A claimed manipulation of requirements therefore presented a breach theory for the jury while the good-faith promise continued to supply consideration at formation.
Price protection: The right of first refusal created a defined sequence. SP could present a lower third-party offer;
Zoltek could match it; a match bound SP to buy from Zoltek; and an unmatched price opened third-party purchasing.
Because Zoltek controlled whether it would meet the market price and a match activated SP's purchase duty, the clause preserved a real obligation.
Product substitution: Large-tow fiber was the contract's requirements category. SP's acquisition of small-tow fiber from other suppliers could constitute breach if SP used an interchangeable product in bad faith to divert a covered large-tow requirement. The jury found SP's performance compliant. Distinct product evidence also supported treating the purchases as outside the large-tow category.
Abandonment: Zoltek relied at trial on SP's absence of orders from February 2002 into early 2004. Under Missouri law, unilateral abandonment based on specified acts can be resolved by the court; mutual abandonment requires positive and unequivocal conduct supporting a shared intent to end the contract. UCC Section 2-306 permits a buyer's requirements to reach zero through good-faith business operation. The two-year order gap therefore remained compatible with continued performance and fell short of the abandonment standard.
After the verdict, Zoltek invoked the parties' April 2004 Panex 35 Supply/Purchase Agreement as proof of mutual abandonment of the 2000 agreement. At trial, Zoltek had used that document to argue that Panex 35 fell outside the
2000 agreement. The later mutual-abandonment theory arrived after the relevant instruction stage and was unpreserved.
The district court properly withheld the requested instruction on the theory actually presented.
Evidentiary rulings: At a preliminary-injunction hearing, Zoltek's attorney Alan Kohn stated that Zoltek was ready, willing, and able to perform the older Panex 33 contract while disputing Panex 35 coverage. SP used the statement at trial. The appellate court held that its admission supported the existing trial result. When SP purchasing manager Paul
Lyon referred to a supposed prior judgment requiring Panex 33 supply, the district judge sustained Zoltek's objection, struck the statement, immediately directed the jury to disregard it, and later confined the jury's consideration to admitted evidence. Those directions cured the risk of prejudice.
Lost-profit proof: Missouri allows lost profits naturally and proximately caused by breach, within the parties' contemplation, and established with reasonable certainty. SP expert Donna Smith used ordinary-course budgets, a managing director's lost-sales summary concerning Vestas and Gamesa, management discussions, depositions, Zoltek public reports, market-shortage evidence, SP's processing capacity, and an actual 35 percent profit margin from the preceding eighteen months. She deducted avoided variable costs and calculated $21,138,518 on 3,960,276 pounds of unfilled Panex 35 demand. Cross-examination supplied the means to test her assumptions, and the evidence allowed the jury to find the past loss with reasonable certainty.
Gamesa transaction: A separate Zoltek-Gamesa contract allowed Gamesa to select a prepreg processor, and Gamesa selected SP. Gamesa and Zoltek negotiated the agreement and controlled its price and quantity; SP processed the fiber and transferred it to Gamesa. Testimony supported treating the shipment as performance of Gamesa's contractual right.
The jury therefore properly kept the $13,353,696 shipment outside the 2000 Supply Agreement offset. SP disclosed the underlying data well before trial, giving Zoltek adequate time to meet the revised alternative calculation submitted twenty-two days before trial.
Instruction and duplicated verdict: The district court used Missouri Approved Instruction 4.01, directing fair compensation for loss directly caused by breach and reasonable certainty for future loss. Read in context, the instruction conveyed Missouri's certainty requirement for lost profits. SP pleaded Panex 35 recovery and Panex 33 recovery in the alternative. The annual formula allowed a maximum of 3,960,276 pounds of covered large-tow fiber, satisfied through Panex 35 or Panex 33. Adding both awards compensated 6,960,276 pounds and exceeded that ceiling.
Rule 59(e) permitted the district court to remove the duplicate $14,906,377 component.
Doctrinal significance: The case shows three distinct controls on discretion: an implied good-faith quantity standard under Section 2-306, an express reasonable-opinion quality standard, and an express annual cap. It also separates an enforceable requirements promise at formation from a later allegation that the buyer exercised its discretion in bad faith.

briefs.title: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon
briefs.citation: 222 N.Y. 88, 118 N.E. 214 (1917). New York Court of Appeals. Cardozo, J. Argued November 14, 1917; decided December 4, 1917.

sections.Preamble: Review of 177 A.D. 624, 164 N.Y.S. 576 (App. Div. 1st Dep't 1917).
sections.Parties: Plaintiff / appellant in the Court of Appeals: Otis F. Wood, a marketer with a business organization suited to placing commercial endorsements. The agreement gave him exclusive marketing and licensing authority, and he sued for the share of revenues lost through independent endorsements. Defendant / respondent: Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon, a prominent fashion creator whose personal approval increased the market value of designs and products. She granted the exclusive rights, retained approval authority, later made endorsements independently, and attacked the agreement's consideration on the pleadings.
sections.Procedural History:
Wood filed a contract action alleging that Lady Duff-Gordon violated his exclusive rights by endorsing articles outside his agency and withholding the resulting profits. The complaint set out the signed written agreement in full. Lady
Duff-Gordon used the New York code-pleading procedure described in the reports as a demurrer and as a motion for judgment on the pleadings. The motion accepted the complaint's well-pleaded facts for purposes of testing whether they stated a legal cause of action.
Special Term denied Lady Duff-Gordon's motion, allowing Wood's claim to proceed. The Appellate Division, First
Department, unanimously reversed on April 20, 1917. Justice Davis read the writing as requiring Wood to collect and divide revenues only when he elected to arrange an endorsement, sale, or license. Because the text stated no express undertaking to generate such transactions, the intermediate court held that Wood's promises supplied neither mutuality nor consideration and granted judgment on the pleadings for Lady Duff-Gordon. 177 A.D. 624, 164 N.Y.S. 576.
Wood appealed to New York's highest court. The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed
Special Term, with costs in both appellate courts. Judge Cardozo wrote for a four-judge majority joined by Judges
Cuddeback, McLaughlin, and Andrews. Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Chase and Crane dissented without separate opinions. The ruling resolved only the legal sufficiency of Wood's contract claim; the merits of performance, breach, and damages remained for later adjudication.
sections.Material Facts:
Lady Duff-Gordon's approval and name carried commercial value in fashion markets. Manufacturers paid for her endorsement, and her own fabrics, garments, parasols, and related designs gained value when marketed under her name. She retained Wood to convert that commercial influence into licensing and sales revenue.
The signed agreement gave Wood, subject to Lady Duff-Gordon's approval, the exclusive right to place her endorsement on other creators' designs. It also gave him the exclusive right to sell her own designs or license others to manufacture and market them. The arrangement began April 1, 1915, ran for at least one year, and continued from year to year unless terminated by ninety days' notice.
Lady Duff-Gordon's compensation consisted of one-half of all profits and revenues generated by contracts Wood made under the exclusive agency. Wood promised to collect the revenues, remit her share, account monthly for all money received, and obtain patents, copyrights, and trademarks when his judgment found them useful to protect affected names, ideas, and articles. The writing recited that Wood possessed a business organization adapted to placing the endorsements she approved.
Wood alleged full performance on his side. He further alleged that Lady Duff-Gordon independently endorsed fabrics, dresses, and millinery for valuable consideration, excluded him from the transactions, and retained the revenues. Those acts directly implicated the exclusivity grant and the agreed revenue division.
sections.Issue: Does a signed exclusive marketing agreement supported by a revenue-sharing structure, monthly accounting duties, intellectual-property duties, and recitals identifying the marketer's specialized organization imply a promise that the marketer will use reasonable efforts, thereby supplying consideration for the fashion creator's exclusive grant?
sections.Holding:
Yes. Reading the complete writing in its commercial setting, Wood assumed a duty to use reasonable efforts to place
Lady Duff-Gordon's endorsements and market her designs. That implied promise supplied consideration and made her exclusivity promise enforceable. The complaint therefore stated a contract claim. The Court of Appeals reversed the
Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term's denial of judgment on the pleadings.
sections.Reasoning:
Whole-agreement interpretation: Cardozo drew the obligation from the agreement's recitals, grants, compensation formula, duration, and express administrative duties. Contractual meaning arose from how those provisions operated together in the parties' planned business. The court used implication to articulate the performance commitment carried by the transaction's structure.
Exclusivity: For at least one year, Lady Duff-Gordon placed her endorsement and designs within Wood's sole commercial channel. Wood's acceptance of that exclusive agency carried the duty to operate the channel. Exclusivity concentrated marketing authority in him and made his performance essential to the exchange.
Recital and institutional capacity: The agreement identified Wood's business organization as adapted to placing approved endorsements. That recital supplied a concrete intended use for his organization. It linked the grant to Wood's existing capacity and supported an undertaking to deploy that capacity for the agreed purpose.
Compensation design: Lady Duff-Gordon received half of the revenue produced through Wood's contracts. Her contractual return therefore depended directly on his efforts. A reasonable-efforts duty gave the revenue-sharing formula the business efficacy the parties assigned to it and protected the value she transferred through exclusivity.
Express downstream promises: Wood had to collect and divide money, provide monthly accounts, and secure or protect intellectual-property rights when his judgment called for it. Those duties presupposed commercial activity producing contracts, revenue, and protectable interests. They reinforced the implication that he would make reasonable efforts to bring those predicates into existence.
Content of the implied term: 'Reasonable efforts' creates an objective performance obligation informed by the market, the enterprise, the parties' purpose, available opportunities, and Wood's represented business capacity. It requires diligent pursuit of the exclusive undertaking while preserving business judgment about particular proposed transactions, each of which remained subject to Lady Duff-Gordon's approval.
Consideration: Lady Duff-Gordon exchanged exclusive commercial rights for Wood's promised efforts, revenue administration, profit sharing, accounting, and protective work. The implied efforts term exposed Wood to breach liability for an unreasonable failure to develop the business. That legal commitment supplied the bargained-for obligation supporting her promise.
Historical setting: The Appellate Division used a formal mutuality inquiry focused on an express sentence compelling
Wood to procure deals. Cardozo's approach reflected a broader early-twentieth-century movement toward reading agreements in their commercial context. He relied on The Moorcock's business-efficacy reasoning and New York exclusive-agency authorities. The result treats implication as interpretation of the parties' manifested transaction.
Connection to UCC Section 2-306(2): Article 2 later stated a parallel rule for goods: a lawful exclusive-dealing agreement ordinarily imposes best efforts on the seller to supply and on the buyer to promote. Wood supplies the common-law model for deriving an efforts obligation from exclusivity and commercial purpose.
Pleading significance: The Court of Appeals accepted Wood's allegations at this stage and determined that the writing could support enforcement. Wood would still bear the burden of proving his own performance, Lady Duff-Gordon's breach, causation, and damages. Lady Duff-Gordon could litigate whether her challenged transactions fell within the grant and whether Wood satisfied his implied duty.
Rule and application sequence: Read every express term and recital; identify the transaction's evident purpose;
determine whether exclusivity or compensation makes performance by one side essential; formulate the minimum term that gives the exchange its intended operation; then test whether that implied term supplies a legal obligation. Here, reasonable efforts fit the writing and completed the consideration analysis.

briefs.title: Contract in Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon (SEL)

sections.Preamble: Agreement effective April 1, 1915. Assigned SEL document; provisions are organized with the descriptions in the pleaded writing reported at 177 A.D. 624 and the Court of Appeals' construction at 222 N.Y. 88.
sections.Parties:
Grantor and fashion creator: Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon, whose name, personal approval, original designs, and fashion reputation formed the licensed commercial assets. Exclusive marketer and license arranger: Otis F. Wood, whose organization and judgment formed the distribution and contracting mechanism. The agreement coordinates Lady
Duff-Gordon's approval power with Wood's market-development role.
sections.Procedural History:
Wood attached or reproduced the writing in his complaint. Its terms therefore supplied the object of Lady
Duff-Gordon's motion for judgment on the pleadings. The Appellate Division isolated Wood's express conditional duties and found consideration absent. The Court of Appeals read the complete instrument and implied reasonable efforts. The SEL contract should be read at both levels: first as drafted terms allocating authority and revenue; then as the text interpreted in the reported opinions.
sections.Material Facts:
Recitals: The writing identifies Lady Duff-Gordon's unique and high position as a creator of fashion in America,
England, and France. It states that her personal approval and endorsement over her name carry distinct monetary value for manufacturers of fashion articles, fabrics, and accessories. It also identifies Wood's business organization as adapted to placing endorsements she approves.
Endorsement grant: Wood receives the exclusive authority to place Lady Duff-Gordon's endorsement on the designs and articles of others. Lady Duff-Gordon retains approval over the use of her name and endorsements. Within that approval structure, Wood uses his judgment to identify placements advantageous to her and to arrange the resulting contracts.
Original-design grant: Wood also receives the exclusive authority to sell Lady Duff-Gordon's own creations or license others to manufacture and sell them. The two grants cover separate revenue streams: endorsement of third-party products and commercialization of products she created.
Collection and revenue division: Wood collects the profits and revenues generated by endorsements, sales, and licenses. Lady Duff-Gordon receives one-half of the resulting profits and revenues. Wood receives the balance and bears the costs associated with securing the revenues as described in the reported writing. He must account to her monthly for money received.
Intellectual-property protection: Wood must obtain the patents, copyrights, or trademarks that his judgment finds necessary to protect names, ideas, rights, and articles affected by the agreement. He also controls protective proceedings through his judgment. The parties share the expenses of obtaining and protecting those rights equally.
Duration and termination: The exclusive arrangement begins April 1, 1915 and lasts for at least one year. It then continues in annual periods. A party may end a renewal through ninety days' notice. This guaranteed initial period gives
Wood time to develop opportunities and gives Lady Duff-Gordon a defined interval in which her commercial rights move through his agency.
Approval and judgment: Lady Duff-Gordon controls approval of proposed uses of her name and fashion authority.
Wood controls market selection and the business judgment involved in placement, licensing, intellectual-property registration, and protective proceedings. These paired powers divide creative-brand control from commercial execution. Each judgment must be exercised consistently with the agreement's purpose and the general duty of good faith.
sections.Issue: What enforceable exchange and performance standard emerge from the contract's recitals, two exclusive grants, approval allocation, revenue sharing, monthly accounting, intellectual-property duties, cost sharing, and fixed initial term?
sections.Holding: The express terms create an exclusive commercialization arrangement. Lady Duff-Gordon supplies her name, approval, designs, and exclusive access; Wood supplies the exclusive agency, commercial judgment, collection and accounting services, intellectual-property work, and reasonable efforts to generate endorsements, sales, and licenses. The reasonable-efforts duty arises from the complete structure and supplies the consideration supporting the grant.
sections.Reasoning:
The contract's architecture: The recitals identify the commercial asset and Wood's capacity. The grants transfer control over defined revenue channels. The approval clauses protect the brand. The accounting and intellectual-property clauses administer transactions. The duration gives the enterprise time to operate. The compensation clause makes successful development the source of both parties' return. Together, those provisions describe an operating relationship.
Express and implied obligations: The writing states collection, division, accounting, registration, protection, cost sharing, approval, and exclusivity expressly. Reasonable efforts supplies the level of market-development activity that connects those clauses. This implied term follows from the parties' manifested design and defines conduct a court can evaluate.
Why exclusivity matters: Lady Duff-Gordon places the covered commercialization channels in Wood's hands during the term. His control over the only authorized channel creates responsibility to cultivate it. Her reciprocal exclusivity duty requires her to route covered endorsements, sales, and licenses through the agreed relationship and share resulting revenues.
Why compensation matters: Wood's efforts produce the fund the parties divide. A one-half share gives each party an incentive to approve and pursue valuable transactions. The implied duty addresses agency inactivity; Lady
Duff-Gordon's approval right addresses uses that could harm her name or conflict with her creative judgment.
Standards of performance: Reasonable efforts evaluates Wood's overall pursuit of opportunities. Good faith governs each party's discretionary powers. Monthly accounting measures revenue administration. The IP clause uses Wood's judgment within the protective purpose. Lady Duff-Gordon's approval power operates within the exclusive relationship and the covenant of good faith.
Cold-call distinction: The Appellate Division asked whether the document contained an express command requiring
Wood to produce endorsements, sales, or licenses. The Court of Appeals asked what commitment the document as a whole conveyed. The latter method uses exclusivity, purpose, and payment design as evidence of an implied promise and preserves each express allocation of judgment.
Connection to the assigned doctrine: The document illustrates interpretation performing work within consideration doctrine. Once reasonable efforts is part of Wood's promise, he incurs legal detriment and Lady Duff-Gordon receives a bargained-for performance commitment. UCC Section 2-306(2) later supplies a comparable best-efforts term by statute for exclusive dealing in goods.

briefs.title: UCC Section 2-306 - Output, Requirements, and Exclusive Dealings

sections.Preamble:
Uniform Commercial Code Article 2. Quantity and efforts rule for sales of goods. The brief paraphrases the enacted text and organizes
Official Comments 1-5; Missouri applies the provision through Mo. Rev. Stat. Section 400.2-306.
sections.Parties: Output contract: a seller commits the quantity its business actually produces, and the buyer commits to take that defined output under the agreement. Requirements contract: a buyer commits the quantity its business actually needs, and the seller commits to supply that defined demand. Exclusive dealing: a seller or buyer grants the other an exclusive channel for the kind of goods concerned. Article 2 applies because each arrangement concerns a sale of goods.
sections.Procedural History: Section 2-306 is a statutory contract-construction rule adopted through state commercial codes. It supplies quantity and performance content when parties use output, requirements, or exclusive-dealing terms. Official Comment 1 explains that the section reads commercial background, intent, and good faith into the agreement. The rule covers manufacturers and nonproducing enterprises such as dealers and distributors.
sections.Material Facts:
Subsection (1): A quantity measured by seller output or buyer requirements means the party's actual quantity occurring in good faith. A tender or demand also must remain within a proportion reasonably related to a stated estimate. When the agreement contains no estimate, normal or otherwise comparable prior output or requirements supplies the reference point.
Subsection (2): A lawful exclusive-dealing agreement carries reciprocal efforts duties unless the parties agree to a different allocation. The seller must use best efforts to supply the goods. The buyer must use best efforts to promote their sale. The duties arise through the Code as terms of the agreement.
sections.Issue: How does Article 2 give definite, enforceable content to sales agreements whose quantity depends on one party's future business activity or whose performance depends on an exclusive distributor's future efforts?
sections.Holding: Section 2-306 validates these agreements by measuring quantity through actual good-faith output or requirements, constraining substantial variation through estimates or comparable history, and attaching best-efforts obligations to lawful exclusive dealing. These standards create enforceable promises while preserving the quantity flexibility the parties selected.
sections.Reasoning:
