Commercial purpose: Fixed quantities fit transactions with predictable volume. Output and requirements terms serve businesses whose production or demand changes with ordinary operations. Section 2-306 enforces that chosen flexibility through commercial standards and uses the enterprise's actual good-faith activity as the quantity measure.
Good faith as the quantity measure: The party controlling the variable quantity must operate the relevant plant or business honestly and according to commercial standards of fair dealing in the trade. The resulting actual output or demand defines the quantity. A decision designed to recapture a contract price advantage, divert covered business, or manufacture demand for opportunistic gain violates that standard.
Elasticity and cessation: Ordinary good-faith variation can move materially from earlier volume and can reach discontinuance. Official Comment 2 gives a requirements buyer's shutdown for lack of customer orders as a permissible example. A shutdown chosen solely to curtail losses under the particular contract supports a finding of bad faith. The factual inquiry asks why the business quantity changed and whether the reason fits fair commercial operation.
Expansion: Normal expansion undertaken in good faith falls within the agreement. A sudden enlargement that changes the enterprise used to measure output or requirements can exceed the contract's scope. A sharp market-price increase under a fixed-price requirements deal is relevant because it can reveal an effort to enlarge volume in order to exploit the contract price.
Estimates, prior dealings, and express limits: A stated estimate is the center around which the parties contemplated variation. Comparable prior output or requirements serves that role when the agreement gives no estimate. An express minimum or maximum marks a clear boundary on elasticity. The unreasonably-disproportionate limitation evaluates magnitude against those reference points, while good faith evaluates the commercial reason for the quantity decision.
Zero quantity: A buyer can have zero actual requirements when a good-faith business development eliminates demand. A seller can have zero output when a good-faith business development ends production. The promise remains enforceable because the party must determine quantity through the protected business activity and the statutory good-faith standard. Structural Polymer applies this principle to SP's period without large-tow orders.
Best efforts in exclusive dealing: Official Comment 5 describes reasonable diligence and good faith in supplying goods and expanding or promoting the market. The exclusive agent must make reasonable effort to develop the product's sales; the principal must support the exclusive channel and honor the agreed territorial or product exclusivity.
'Best efforts' is contextual and receives content from the product, market, duration, party capabilities, course of performance, and commercial practice.
Good faith and best efforts perform different functions: Subsection (1) polices the honesty and commercial legitimacy of the quantity generated by an output or requirements enterprise. Subsection (2) imposes affirmative diligence in supplying or promoting goods under exclusivity. An exclusive requirements arrangement can activate both standards.
Enterprise transfer: Official Comment 4 places the effect of selling the business under other law. When the contract continues after a transfer, the new owner's quantity remains measured by actual good-faith operation in relation to the enterprise's normal pre-sale operation. That normal operation also sets the boundary against a sudden strategic expansion or contraction.
Consideration: A requirements buyer gives up the contractual freedom to place genuine covered demand elsewhere;
an output seller gives up the freedom to sell genuine covered production elsewhere. Good faith makes the quantity-setting discretion legally reviewable. Best efforts makes an exclusive distributor's or supplier's future activity legally reviewable. Each constraint supplies the commitment needed for consideration.
Statute of Frauds function: Output and requirements language identifies a quantity through the agreed measuring mechanism. In a signed Article 2 writing, that mechanism can satisfy the quantity-term function because Section 2-306 gives it definite legal content. Express estimates, minimums, maximums, product definitions, and market-price provisions further define the enforceable scope.
Connection to Wood: Wood implied reasonable efforts from the exclusive grant, the revenue share, the recital describing Wood's organization, and the parties' commercial purpose. Section 2-306(2) states a comparable default rule for exclusive dealing in goods. The common-law case demonstrates the interpretive reasoning; the Code supplies the term directly within its statutory field.
Connection to Mattei: The land sale falls outside Article 2. Its satisfaction clause and Section 2-306 share a method:
discretion receives an enforceable standard through interpretation and background law. Mattei's honest judgment governs lease satisfaction; Section 2-306's good faith governs business-generated quantity.
Connection to Structural Polymer: SP promised its total requirements of suitable large-tow fiber, defined quality through its reasonable opinion, accepted an annual cap, and gave Zoltek a price-matching right. Missouri Section
400.2-306 supplied good faith. The combined express and implied constraints created consideration and directed later breach analysis.
Integrated exam sequence: (1) Classify the transaction as goods, services, land, or mixed. (2) Identify the variable term: satisfaction, requirements, output, or exclusivity. (3) Locate express controls such as estimates, caps, approval rights, price matching, duration, and accounting. (4) add the applicable background standard: reasonable person, honest good faith, reasonable efforts, or best efforts. (5) Decide consideration at formation by asking whether discretion is legally constrained. (6) Decide breach by applying that constraint to the later conduct. (7) Measure relief within the same quantity and causation limits.
Core synthesis: Each assigned authority treats interpretation as part of the consideration analysis. Mattei attaches honest judgment to a satisfaction condition. Wood derives reasonable efforts from an exclusive agency's structure.
Section 2-306 attaches good faith to variable quantity and best efforts to exclusive dealing. Structural Polymer applies the Code rule and the parties' express safeguards to a long-term requirements contract. The enforceable standard turns future discretion into a promise a court can administer.

briefs.title: Definiteness and Preliminary Agreements: Supplement Provisions

sections.Sources:
Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 27, 33, 34, 204, and 362, and UCC §§ 2-204(3) and 2-305. The syllabus assigns the supplement without naming sections; these are the provisions the assigned cases apply or that govern the same questions. The Restatement describes common-law rules and is persuasive authority unless a court adopts it; the UCC provisions govern sales of goods as enacted in each state, and courts sometimes apply them by analogy to other contracts, as the Ohio Supreme Court did in Oglebay Norton. §
2-204; § 2-305.
The Definiteness Requirement
Restatement § 33(1) provides that even a manifestation intended as an offer cannot be accepted so as to form a contract unless the terms of the contract are reasonably certain. Under § 33(2), terms are reasonably certain if they provide a basis for determining whether a breach has occurred and for giving an appropriate remedy.
Section 33(3) adds that leaving one or more terms open or uncertain may show that the parties did not intend their communications as an offer or an acceptance. Definiteness therefore does two jobs: it tests whether a court can enforce the bargain, and it serves as evidence of whether the parties meant to be bound at all. The comments recognize that the more terms the parties leave open, the less likely it is that they intended a binding agreement, and that a court may supply a reasonable price when the parties manifested an intention to conclude a contract but left price unsettled.
Several provisions reduce the demand for completeness. Section 34 treats terms as reasonably certain even when they let a party choose terms during performance, allows part performance to remove uncertainty and show that a bargain was formed, and permits action in reliance to make a contractual remedy appropriate even when uncertainty remains. Section 204 directs a court, when the parties have not agreed on a term essential to determining their rights and duties, to supply a term that is reasonable in the circumstances.
Section 362 sets the corresponding limit on equitable relief: specific performance or an injunction will not be granted unless the terms are certain enough to provide a basis for an appropriate order.
Open Terms in Sales of Goods: UCC §§ 2-204(3) and 2-305
Section 2-204(3) provides that a contract for sale does not fail for indefiniteness even though one or more terms are left open, if the parties intended to make a contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for giving an appropriate remedy. Section 2-305 applies that principle to price. Under § 2-305(1), the parties can conclude a contract even though the price is not settled, and the price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery if nothing is said about price, if the price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, or if the price is to be fixed by an agreed market or other standard set or recorded by a third person and it is not so set or recorded. A price to be fixed by one party must be fixed in good faith, and if a price fails to be fixed through one party's fault, the other may treat the contract as cancelled or fix a reasonable price. Under §
2-305(4), however, if the parties intended not to be bound unless the price was fixed or agreed, and it was not, there is no contract.
The Code thus reverses the common-law presumption applied in Sun Printing: when price is left to future agreement, the question under § 2-305 is whether the parties intended to be bound, and if they did, the court supplies a reasonable price. Section 2-305(1)(c) also addresses the failure of an external pricing index, the problem in Oglebay Norton, where the published rate the parties relied on ceased to exist.
Preliminary Agreements and Written Memorials
Restatement § 27 provides that manifestations of assent that are sufficient to conclude a contract are not prevented from doing so because the parties also intend to prepare and adopt a written memorial of their agreement, although the circumstances may show that the agreements are only preliminary negotiations. The comments identify circumstances that bear on that question, including the extent of agreement, whether the contract is of a type usually put in writing, whether it needs a formal writing for its full expression, whether it has few or many details, the amount involved, and whether it is common or unusual. Teachers Insurance &
Annuity Ass'n v. Tribune builds on the same inquiry and adds a middle category: a preliminary commitment that binds the parties to negotiate open terms in good faith without binding them to the final transaction.
Reliance Without a Contract
When the parties never form a contract because terms remain open or because they did not intend to be bound, a party that relied on the other's assurances may still recover under Restatement § 90 if a promise foreseeably induced its action and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement; the remedy may be limited as justice requires. Cyberchron and Dixon apply that doctrine to assurances made during negotiations and limit recovery to reliance expenditures. Restitution for benefits conferred, sometimes pleaded as quantum meruit (recovery of the reasonable value of services or goods provided), is a separate route that depends on a benefit to the defendant rather than on a promise.
sections.Application: Begin by asking whether the parties intended to be bound, using their language, the context of negotiations, the number and importance of open terms, any partial performance, and the customs of the relevant market. If they intended a final contract, ask whether the terms are reasonably certain enough for a court to identify a breach and fashion a remedy, and whether a missing term can be supplied by § 204, § 2-305, or an agreed standard. If they intended only to commit to negotiate, analyze a duty of good-faith negotiation as in Tribune and Channel Home Centers. If neither a contract nor a negotiation commitment exists, consider promissory estoppel and restitution. The remedy follows the theory: expectation damages or specific performance for a complete contract, damages for breach of a duty to negotiate, and reliance damages under § 90.

briefs.title: Teachers Insurance & Annuity Association v. Tribune Co.
briefs.citation: Teachers Insurance & Annuity Ass'n of America v. Tribune Co., 670 F. Supp. 491 (S.D.N.Y. 1987). United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, No. 83 Civ. 0047, decided May 27, 1987, as amended June 26, 1987. Judge Pierre N. Leval wrote the opinion after a bench trial. The case concerns whether a signed loan commitment letter that left terms open bound the borrower, and it sta

sections.Parties:
Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association of America (TIAA), a large institutional lender, was the plaintiff. It had issued a commitment to lend $76 million to the Tribune Company. Tribune, the newspaper publisher, was the defendant. TIAA sought damages for Tribune's refusal to go forward with the loan;
Tribune maintained that the commitment letter was not binding and that its obligation was conditioned on favorable accounting treatment that it never obtained.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1982 Tribune sought to sell the Daily News Building at 220 East 42nd Street in Manhattan. The buyer,
LaSalle Partners, would pay largely through a long-term purchase-money mortgage, meaning a loan from the seller secured by the property sold. To obtain cash immediately without showing the transaction as new debt,
Tribune planned to borrow a matching amount from a lender and to use "offset" accounting, under which the mortgage owed to it and the loan it owed would cancel each other on its balance sheet. Tribune circulated an offering to lenders in August 1982 and sought a firm commitment by mid-September. 670 F. Supp. at
492-93.
On September 22, 1982, TIAA issued a commitment letter for a $76 million loan with a fourteen-year term at a 15.25 percent yield, accompanied by a two-page term sheet covering the principal economic terms. The letter stated that upon TIAA's receipt of an accepted counterpart, the parties' agreement "shall become a binding agreement between us," and it contemplated the preparation and execution of documents satisfactory to TIAA. Nothing in the letter or term sheet made the loan contingent on Tribune's ability to use offset accounting. Tribune's lawyers had warned against signing a letter with binding-agreement language, but
Tribune, fearing loss of the commitment, accepted on October 6, adding that its acceptance was subject to approval by its board of directors and to preparation of documentation satisfactory to Tribune. The board met on October 28 and authorized the borrowing, leaving final terms to its finance committee. TIAA allocated the
$76 million within its lending budget. Id. at 493-95, 502-03.
Meanwhile the Financial Accounting Standards Board had issued a proposal in mid-October questioning offsetting of this kind, and Tribune's accountants grew concerned. Interest rates also fell sharply, making the
15.25 percent loan much less attractive. On December 2, Tribune proposed to proceed only if the loan were conditioned on assurance that offset accounting would be available, and TIAA refused. Tribune closed the sale of the building on December 6 and did not proceed with the loan. Id. at 495-96.
sections.Procedural History:
TIAA sued Tribune in the Southern District of New York for breach of the commitment. After a bench trial,
Judge Leval issued findings of fact and conclusions of law. Liability was decided in this opinion, and the measure of damages was reserved for later determination. New York law governed.
sections.Issue: Did the commitment letter, which stated that it would become binding on acceptance but left terms open and contemplated final documentation, create an enforceable obligation? If it did not bind Tribune to the loan itself, did it bind Tribune to negotiate the open terms in good faith, and did Tribune breach that obligation by insisting that the loan be conditioned on offset accounting?
sections.Holding:
Preliminary agreements can create binding obligations of two types. In the first, the parties have reached complete agreement on all the issues perceived to require negotiation, and the contemplated formal document is only a memorial of an agreement already binding; either party may demand performance of the transaction.
In the second, the parties express mutual commitment to a contract on agreed major terms while recognizing that other terms remain to be negotiated. That agreement does not commit the parties to their ultimate contractual objective; it commits them to negotiate the open issues in good faith within the framework they have settled. It bars a party from renouncing the deal, abandoning the negotiations, or insisting on conditions that do not conform to the preliminary agreement, but it does not guarantee that a final contract will result.
Whether the parties intended to be bound is determined from their language, the context of the negotiations, the existence of open terms, partial performance, and the customary practice in the market. Id. at 497-99.
The commitment letter was a binding preliminary commitment of the second type. Offset accounting was not a condition of Tribune's obligation, and Tribune breached its duty to negotiate in good faith when it refused to proceed unless TIAA accepted that new condition. Tribune's refusal was primarily attributable to the decline in interest rates. Id. at 499-507.
sections.Judgment: Judgment on liability was entered for TIAA, with damages to be determined in further proceedings.
sections.Reasoning:
Judge Leval began with the risks on both sides. Courts must avoid trapping parties in surprise contractual obligations they never intended, because parties commonly exchange preliminary writings while reserving the freedom to walk away. But courts should also enforce commitments parties did intend, because giving legal recognition to preliminary binding commitments serves a valuable function in the marketplace, particularly for relatively standardized transactions such as loans. A borrower that obtains a firm commitment gains certainty about its financing and can plan around it; a lender that issues one forgoes other opportunities.
If either could walk away whenever the market moved, the commitment would be worthless. Id. at 497-99.
The first factor, the language of the agreement, strongly favored TIAA. The commitment letter called itself a binding agreement upon acceptance, and Tribune signed it as accepted and agreed. Tribune's reservations, board approval and satisfactory documentation, did not negate that intent. The board did approve the borrowing, and the court read the reservation of satisfactory documentation as consistent with a commitment on the major terms and a duty to negotiate the rest, rather than as a right to abandon the deal for any reason.
Id. at 499-500, 503.
The context of the negotiations pointed the same way. Tribune had sought a firm commitment by a deadline because it needed certainty about the financing for the building sale. Its lawyers warned it about the binding-agreement language, and Tribune signed anyway rather than risk losing the commitment, which showed that it understood the letter to bind it. Id. at 500-01.
The open terms did not defeat binding intent. The term sheet covered the major economic terms, including the amount, rate, and term of the loan. The terms left open were the kind of secondary provisions that a binding preliminary commitment contemplates the parties will negotiate. Open terms are fatal to a claim that the parties reached a fully binding final agreement, but they are consistent with a commitment to negotiate.
TIAA's partial performance, allocating $76 million of its lending capacity to the loan, and evidence that the financial community recognizes binding loan commitments, though not uniformly, supported the conclusion.
Id. at 501-03.
Tribune's principal defense was that offset accounting was an essential condition of the deal. The court rejected it. The commitment letter contained no basis whatever for the proposition that Tribune's obligation was conditioned on assurance that it could report the loan off its balance sheet. Tribune knew the importance of the accounting treatment and could have demanded such a condition, negotiated for a right to prepay if the treatment was disallowed, or paid for an option. It instead accepted a firm commitment without the condition, because it did not want to lose the commitment. Id. at 504-05.
Tribune breached its obligation. When interest rates fell, it refused to proceed unless TIAA agreed to a condition outside the scope of the preliminary agreement, and when TIAA declined, it abandoned the negotiations. The court found that Tribune's position was primarily attributable to the decline in rates, which had made the loan unattractive, rather than to its accounting concerns. Insisting on a condition the preliminary agreement did not contain was exactly what the duty to negotiate in good faith forbids. The court noted that Judge Weinfeld had reached a similar result in Teachers Insurance & Annuity Ass'n v. Butler, 626
F. Supp. 1229 (S.D.N.Y. 1986), where a borrower refused to negotiate a prepayment term within the scope of its commitment. Id. at 505-08.
sections.Separate Opinions: A single district judge decided the case after a bench trial. There is no separate opinion.
sections.Notes:
The two categories Judge Leval described are now commonly called Type I and Type II preliminary agreements; the labels come from later Second Circuit decisions applying this opinion and are standard vocabulary in the case law, although Leval described the categories without numbering them. The first type obligates the parties to the transaction itself; the second obligates them only to negotiate in good faith within the agreed framework, so the injured party's remedy is for the failed negotiation, and the measure of damages is contested. The opinion reserved damages, so it does not settle whether TIAA could recover the benefit of the lost loan or only its reliance losses.
The case connects to Sun Printing. Cardozo held that an agreement to agree on price and term left the seller free to refuse, but he noted that the buyer had not sued for an arbitrary refusal to negotiate. Tribune recognizes that claim when the parties intended to commit to negotiate. The limits matter: the duty does not require either party to accept terms it reasonably rejects, and a party may fail to reach agreement without liability if it negotiated in good faith. The breach lies in renouncing the deal, abandoning negotiations, or demanding terms outside the agreed framework.

briefs.title: Dixon v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
briefs.citation: Dixon v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 798 F. Supp. 2d 336 (D. Mass. 2011). United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Civil Action No. 11-10585, memorandum and order of July 22, 2011, by Judge William G. Young. The case concerns whether homeowners stated a promissory estoppel claim based on a lender's promise to consider them for a loan modification if they stopped making payments.

sections.Parties:
Frank and Deana Dixon, homeowners in Scituate, Massachusetts, were the plaintiffs. Wells Fargo Bank,
N.A., which held the mortgage on their home, was the defendant. The Dixons sought to stop the foreclosure of their home and to hold Wells Fargo to its promise; Wells Fargo moved to dismiss, arguing that no enforceable promise existed and that federal law preempted the claim.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts come from the complaint, which the court accepted as true on a motion to dismiss. On or about
June 8, 2009, the Dixons and Wells Fargo orally agreed to take the steps necessary to enter into a modification of their mortgage loan. Wells Fargo instructed them to stop making payments on the loan and told them that the unpaid payments would be added to the modified note. It also asked for financial information, which the Dixons promptly supplied. The Dixons stopped paying. Wells Fargo never completed the modification process. On or about December 8, 2010, the Dixons received notice from the Massachusetts
Land Court that Wells Fargo was proceeding with foreclosure. The value of their home exceeded the loan balance and any arrearage. 798 F. Supp. 2d at 339.
sections.Procedural History:
The Dixons sued in Massachusetts Superior Court, which issued a preliminary injunction against the foreclosure on February 14, 2011. Wells Fargo removed the case to federal court and moved to dismiss under
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), which tests whether the complaint states a claim on which relief can be granted. At a hearing on May 9, 2011, Judge Young dismissed the breach of contract claim as insufficiently pleaded and took the promissory estoppel claim and Wells Fargo's preemption defense under advisement. This opinion explains the ruling on those remaining issues. Id. at 338-39.
sections.Issue:
Does a lender's promise to consider borrowers for a loan modification if they stop making payments and provide financial information support a claim for promissory estoppel under Massachusetts law, even though the promise is too indefinite to create a contract to modify the loan? Is such a claim preempted by the Home
Owners' Loan Act and its regulations?
sections.Holding: Massachusetts enforces promises by virtue of reliance under Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90. The promise must be definite enough to show a commitment, but it need not be so comprehensive that it would qualify as an offer that could ripen into a contract. A promise to consider borrowers for a loan modification, conditioned on their defaulting and supplying financial information, is sufficiently definite when the borrowers took those steps in reasonable reliance and the lender then used the default to foreclose. Recovery is confined to the value of the borrowers' reliance, which avoids converting preliminary negotiations into a binding modification. The claim was not preempted, because it seeks to enforce a general duty to honor promises that applies to all businesses rather than to regulate lending. Id. at 340-59.
sections.Judgment: The court denied Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss as to the promissory estoppel claim and placed the case on the September 2011 trial list. The breach of contract claim had already been dismissed.
sections.Reasoning:
The contract claim failed because the Dixons alleged at most an agreement to enter into a loan modification whose terms were left for future negotiation, and such an agreement is too indefinite to be enforced. The
Dixons clarified that they did not seek a modification; they sought to hold Wells Fargo to its promise to consider them for one. Id. at 339, 341.
Massachusetts courts had avoided the label "promissory estoppel" since Loranger Construction Corp. v. E.F.
Hauserman Co., 376 Mass. 757 (1978), but they enforce promises by virtue of reliance and treat such a claim as equivalent to a contract claim without consideration. They have adopted § 90, under which a promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance, and that does induce it, is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. Some Massachusetts decisions required the promise to be definite and certain in its terms. Judge Young read § 90 and the Restatement's definition of a promise in § 2 to require a commitment, meaning a manifestation of intention to act or refrain from acting in a specified way, but not a promise comprehensive enough to be an offer, citing Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc. for the same point. Id. at 340-44.
Massachusetts cases had applied reliance-based recovery where one party's pattern of conduct kept the other on a string during negotiations, as in Pappas Industrial Parks, Inc. v. Psarros and Greenstein v. Flatley. A
Superior Court decision had allowed a similar claim where a bank encouraged a borrower to default to obtain a discounted payoff and the loan was then sold to a buyer who foreclosed. The Dixons' allegations fit that pattern. Wells Fargo told them that stopping payment and submitting financial information were the steps necessary to obtain a modification; it should have known, and must have intended, that they would take those steps expecting a modification. Its promise to consider them therefore carried, as a matter of fair dealing, an undertaking not to foreclose on the basis of the very default its promise had produced. Only because the
Dixons relied and stopped paying was Wells Fargo able to begin foreclosure, and foreclosing without warning was, the court wrote, unseemly conduct at best. Id. at 344-46.
The court addressed the concern that enforcing promises made during negotiations would restrict parties' freedom to negotiate by limiting the remedy. If the Dixons proved their allegations, their damages would be confined to the value of their expenditures in reliance on the promise. A footnote illustrated the idea: the
Dixons would be restored to their position before the default by resuming their original payments, with the missed payments added to the loan balance and amortized over the life of the loan; if they could not resume
payments, Wells Fargo could foreclose. The remedy protects reliance without imposing a modification the parties never agreed to. Id. at 346-47, 349 n.2.
The court then rejected preemption under the Home Owners' Loan Act (HOLA) and the Office of Thrift
Supervision regulation, 12 C.F.R. § 560.2. The Dixons did not seek a modification or any particular loan terms, so the claim did not purport to impose requirements on loan terms or servicing. Contract and tort law are presumptively not preempted, and promissory estoppel is not designed to regulate lending; all businesses owe the duty to honor promises made. Because HOLA provides no private right of action, Congress could not have intended to deny borrowers traditional state-law remedies for a lender's unfair conduct. Id. at
354-59.
sections.Separate Opinions: A single district judge decided the motion. There is no separate opinion.
sections.Notes:
The case separates two questions that indefiniteness can blur. The alleged promise to modify the loan was too indefinite to be a contract, because its terms were left for negotiation. The narrower promise to consider the
Dixons for a modification, together with the instruction to stop paying, was definite enough to support reliance-based recovery. The remedy tracks that distinction: the Dixons could not obtain the modification they hoped for, but they could be protected against the loss caused by defaulting at the bank's direction.
The decision arose on a motion to dismiss, so it holds only that the allegations stated a claim; the facts remained to be proved at trial. It also reflects the context of the post-2008 foreclosure crisis, which the court discussed at length. Compared with Cyberchron, Dixon relies more heavily on the lender's opportunistic conduct in using a default it induced, while Cyberchron emphasizes a buyer's demands for continued performance during a negotiation it then abandoned; both cases limit recovery to reliance.

briefs.title: Cyberchron Corp. v. Calldata Systems Development, Inc.
briefs.citation: Cyberchron Corp. v. Calldata Systems Development, Inc., 47 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 1995). United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, argued March 17, 1994, decided February 1, 1995. Judge Mahoney wrote the opinion for a panel that included Judge Walker and Judge Sprouse. The case concerns recovery by a supplier that produced goods at the buyer's urging while the parties failed to agree on ess

sections.Parties:
Cyberchron Corporation, a manufacturer of rugged computer equipment, was the plaintiff. Calldata Systems
Development, Inc., a subsidiary of Grumman Data Systems, was the defendant; the opinion refers to the defendant's side of the negotiations as Grumman. Cyberchron sought payment for equipment it built; Calldata denied that any contract existed.
sections.Material Facts:
Grumman held a Marine Corps contract for the Advanced Tactical Air Command Central, a combat command and control system. It negotiated with Cyberchron to supply rugged computer components: a video processor, a workstation, and a color monitor. The parties negotiated extensively but never agreed on the weight of the components or on penalties for exceeding weight limits. A May 15, 1990 purchase order specified a combined weight of 145 pounds and severe overweight penalties, terms Cyberchron never accepted. 47 F.3d at 40-42.
In July 1990 a Grumman representative told Cyberchron to proceed as if a new set of weights had been approved and said that the parties would work out the formal terms later; when Cyberchron asked for written confirmation, he declined but said Cyberchron should proceed. In August 1990, Grumman's director of material told Cyberchron that it had a responsibility and obligation to continue performing to maintain the schedule, and indicated that Cyberchron could assume it would be paid. Meanwhile Grumman was negotiating with another supplier, Codar Technology. On September 25, 1990, Calldata terminated the purchase order for default, no equipment having been delivered or paid for, and later bought heavier and inferior equipment from Codar. Between July 15 and September 25, 1990, Cyberchron spent $162,824.19 on labor and materials. Id. at 41-43.
sections.Procedural History:
Cyberchron sued in the Eastern District of New York. After a bench trial, Judge Spatt held that no contract had been formed because the parties never agreed on two essential terms, the weights of the components and the weight penalties, and he dismissed Cyberchron's contract and quantum meruit claims and Calldata's counterclaim. He awarded Cyberchron $162,824.19 on a promissory estoppel theory, consisting of
$53,588.40 for materials and $109,235.79 for labor incurred between July 15 and September 25, 1990, but excluded overhead, lost profits, and shutdown costs. Both parties appealed. New York law governed. Id. at
43.
sections.Issue: Where negotiations never produced a contract because essential terms remained unresolved, could the supplier recover under promissory estoppel for costs incurred after the buyer insisted that it continue performing? If so, what measure of reliance damages applies, and does it include overhead and shutdown costs?
sections.Holding: No contract exists where the parties never reached a meeting of the minds on essential terms, and the district court's finding to that effect was not clearly erroneous. Under New York law, promissory estoppel requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance by the party to whom the promise is made, and injury sustained by reason of the reliance. Grumman's July and August 1990 assurances and demands were such a promise, Cyberchron's reliance was reasonable and foreseeable, and its injury was unconscionable, so injustice could be avoided only by enforcing the promise. Recovery is limited to reliance damages, which include reasonable overhead where the claimant has a demonstrable history of ongoing business operations, and shutdown costs incurred because of reliance on the promise. Id. at 43-46.
sections.Judgment: The Second Circuit affirmed the judgment insofar as it allowed recovery on promissory estoppel, but vacated the judgment and remanded for a redetermination of damages consistent with its opinion, leaving the district court free to take additional proof.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first upheld the no-contract finding. The weights of the components and the penalties for exceeding them were essential terms, the parties never agreed on them, and the purchase order's termination-liability provision could not independently support recovery because it presupposed a valid purchase order. Id. at
43-44.
On promissory estoppel, the court applied the elements stated in Ripple's of Clearview, Inc. v. Le Havre
Associates, 88 A.D.2d 120 (2d Dep't 1982). The promise was clear and unambiguous: Grumman told
Cyberchron to proceed as if the new weights were approved, refused to put the assurance in writing but repeated that Cyberchron should proceed, and later insisted that Cyberchron was obligated to continue performing and could expect payment. Reliance was reasonable and foreseeable, because Grumman was demanding exactly the performance Cyberchron undertook. Some New York decisions required that the injury be unconscionable, and Calldata relied on Swerdloff v. Mobil Oil Corp. for a narrow view of the doctrine. The court concluded that Ripple's stated the New York rule and that, in any event, the injury here was unconscionable: Grumman pressed Cyberchron to produce at great expense while negotiating with a competitor, then abruptly terminated and bought heavier, inferior equipment elsewhere. Injustice could be avoided only by enforcing the promise. Id. at 44-45.
Recovery was limited to the period after the clear promise. Expenditures before July 15, 1990, when the parties were still negotiating without such assurances, were not recoverable. Id. at 45.
On damages, the court agreed that promissory estoppel recovery is limited as justice requires and here consisted of reliance damages rather than lost profits. It disagreed with the exclusion of overhead. Overhead is an actual cost of doing business, and nearly every business allocates it by standard accounting methods; the parties themselves had negotiated how overhead would be allocated. A claimant need not prove that an alternative project would have absorbed the overhead; a demonstrable history of ongoing operations suffices.
Shutdown costs incurred after termination were also recoverable to the extent they resulted from reliance on
Calldata's promises, but not to the extent they would have been incurred anyway. Id. at 45-46.
sections.Separate Opinions: The panel was unanimous. The reported decision contains no concurrence or dissent.
sections.Notes:
Cyberchron shows how definiteness and reliance divide the work. The failure to agree on weights defeated the contract claim entirely, because a court could not identify what Cyberchron had promised to deliver. The narrower promise, to pay for work done at Grumman's insistence during negotiations, was clear enough to enforce under § 90. The measure of recovery reflects that difference: Cyberchron recovered what it spent, not the profit it expected from a contract that never existed.
The case is also a statement of New York promissory estoppel law. The court read Ripple's's three elements as the governing test and treated the unconscionable-injury requirement found in some New York decisions as satisfied here rather than rejecting it outright, so later courts have divided over whether New York requires unconscionable injury outside the statute-of-frauds context. The timing limit is important for application:
only reliance after the clear promise is protected, so costs a party incurs while it knows terms are unsettled and no assurance has been given remain its own risk.

briefs.title: Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman
briefs.citation: Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman, 795 F.2d 291 (3d Cir. 1986). United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, argued January 7, 1986, decided June 30, 1986. Judge Becker wrote the opinion for a panel that included Judges Weis and Higginbotham. The case concerns whether a letter of intent's promise to negotiate exclusively and to take property off the market w

sections.Parties: Channel Home Centers, a home improvement retail chain operated as a division of Grace Retail Corporation, was the prospective tenant and the plaintiff. Frank Grossman, a real estate developer, and the entities through which he was acquiring a shopping mall were the defendants. Channel sought to enforce the letter of intent and to stop Grossman from leasing the space to a competitor; Grossman maintained that the letter was a nonbinding preliminary document.
sections.Material Facts:
Between November 1984 and February 1985, Grossman was acquiring the Cedarbrook Mall in Cheltenham
Township, Pennsylvania, and needed to show prospective tenants to lenders to obtain financing. Channel became interested in leasing space. On December 11, 1984, Channel sent Grossman a detailed letter of intent describing a 25-year lease of about 70,400 square feet, with a rent schedule and percentage rent. The letter stated: "To induce the Tenant to proceed with the leasing of this Store, you will withdraw the Store from the rental market, and only negotiate the above described leasing transaction to completion." Grossman had requested such a letter so that he could show it to "other people, banks or whatever," and he promptly signed and returned it. 795 F.2d at 292-93.
Both sides then worked toward a lease. Channel spent about $25,000 on measurements, plans, marketing, and equipment, and its parent approved the lease in February 1985. Grossman applied for zoning permits for
Channel's signs and exchanged draft lease documents. In late January 1985, Mr. Good Buys, a competitor of
Channel, contacted Grossman and toured the space. On February 6, 1985, Grossman terminated negotiations with Channel, asserting a 30-day deadline that did not appear in the letter, and on February 7 he leased the space to Mr. Good Buys at a substantially higher rent. Id. at 293-96.
sections.Procedural History:
Channel sued in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania under diversity jurisdiction and sought a preliminary injunction. The district court consolidated the injunction hearing with a trial on the merits under Federal Rule
65(a)(2) without clear advance notice, and it held the letter of intent unenforceable because it did not bind the parties, lacked consideration, and failed to satisfy Pennsylvania's statute of frauds for leases. It also rejected
Channel's alternative unilateral-contract and promissory estoppel theories. Channel appealed. Id. at 297-98.
sections.Issue: Under Pennsylvania law, is a landlord's promise in a signed letter of intent to take the premises off the market and negotiate the lease only with the prospective tenant an enforceable contract, even though the lease itself remained to be negotiated? Specifically, did the parties intend to be bound by that promise, was it supported by consideration, and was it sufficiently definite?
sections.Holding: An agreement to negotiate in good faith, if it otherwise meets the requirements of a contract, is an enforceable contract. Under Pennsylvania law, enforceability depends on whether the parties manifested an intention to be bound, whether the terms are sufficiently definite to be enforced, and whether there was consideration. The evidence would support a finding that the parties intended to be bound by Grossman's promise to withdraw the store from the market and negotiate exclusively with Channel; the promise was definite enough to enforce; and Channel's execution and delivery of the letter, which Grossman wanted in order to obtain financing, was consideration for it. The statute of frauds did not apply because Channel did not claim that the letter was a lease. Id. at 298-301.
sections.Judgment: The Third Circuit reversed the judgment of the district court and remanded for further proceedings, including a trial on whether the parties intended to be bound and on the duration of the obligation to negotiate.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first addressed procedure. Rule 65(a)(2) permits a court to consolidate a preliminary injunction hearing with trial on the merits, but parties must receive clear and unambiguous notice. The district court failed to give it, but because the court later offered a further hearing that Channel declined, the error did not by itself require reversal. The statute of frauds was irrelevant because Channel conceded that the letter was not a final lease and sought to enforce only the promise to negotiate. Id. at 297-98.
On intent, the court looked to the entire letter and the surrounding circumstances. Most of the letter described proposed lease terms that the parties plainly expected to negotiate further, but the exclusive-negotiation clause was unequivocal: Grossman would withdraw the store from the market and negotiate only with
Channel. The parties' conduct after signing, including Channel's planning expenditures, Grossman's zoning applications for Channel's signs, and the exchange of draft leases, was consistent with a binding commitment.
That evidence was sufficient to support a finding of intent to be bound, though it did not compel that finding as a matter of law. Id. at 299.
On definiteness, the court distinguished an unenforceable agreement to agree on the lease itself from
Grossman's promise to take the property off the market and negotiate exclusively with Channel. That promise was a specific, discrete undertaking whose breach a court could identify. Relying on decisions from other jurisdictions, the court held that an agreement to negotiate in good faith, if it otherwise meets the requirements of a contract, is enforceable. Id. at 299-300.
On consideration, the court rejected the argument that no money or thing of value supported the promise.
Grossman requested the letter so that he could show it to lenders, and Channel's signature, backed by its corporate parent, strengthened his financing position. Channel's execution and tender of the letter was therefore of substantial value to Grossman and constituted bargained-for consideration for his promise. Id. at
300.
On remand, the court identified at least two issues for trial: whether the parties in fact intended to be bound by the exclusive-negotiation promise, and how long the duty to negotiate lasted, including whether
Grossman's claimed 30-day limit had been agreed and, if not, what period was reasonable. Because it reversed on the contract theory, the court did not reach Channel's promissory estoppel and unilateral-contract arguments. Id. at 301.
sections.Separate Opinions: The panel was unanimous. The reported decision contains no concurrence or dissent.
sections.Notes:
Channel Home Centers enforces a narrow promise inside a letter of intent that was otherwise nonbinding.
The lease terms were not enforceable, and Channel could not obtain the lease; what Grossman promised was exclusivity and good-faith negotiation. That distinction matters for remedies. Damages for breach of a duty to negotiate are difficult to measure, because it is uncertain whether good-faith negotiation would have produced a lease, and courts have divided over whether the injured party may recover lost expectation or only reliance.
The case parallels the second category in Tribune: both enforce a commitment to negotiate while leaving the final transaction unenforced. The consideration analysis is distinctive. Channel's promise was not needed; its act of signing a letter Grossman could show to lenders supplied the benefit Grossman bargained for. Drafters now commonly include explicit statements that a letter of intent is nonbinding except for identified provisions, such as exclusivity or confidentiality, precisely to control the question this case sent to trial.

briefs.title: Sun Printing & Publishing Ass'n v. Remington Paper & Power Co.
briefs.citation: Sun Printing & Publishing Ass'n v. Remington Paper & Power Co., 235 N.Y. 338, 139 N.E. 470 (1923). New York Court of Appeals, decided April 17, 1923. Judge Cardozo wrote the opinion for a five-judge majority that included Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Pound, McLaughlin, and Andrews. Judge Crane dissented, joined by Judge Hogan. The case concerns whether a contract leaving price and the period for

sections.Parties:
Sun Printing and Publishing Association, a newspaper publisher, was the buyer and the plaintiff. Remington
Paper and Power Company, a newsprint manufacturer, was the seller and the defendant. The buyer sought damages for the seller's refusal to deliver paper during 1920; the seller maintained that its obligation for those months had never been fixed.
sections.Material Facts:
In September 1919 the seller agreed to sell and the buyer agreed to buy 1,000 tons of newsprint per month from September 1919 through December 1920, a total of 16,000 tons. The contract fixed the price for
September at $3.73¾ per hundred pounds and for October through December 1919 at $4.00 per hundred pounds. For the rest of the contract, it provided that "the price of the paper and length of terms for which such price shall apply shall be agreed upon by and between the parties hereto fifteen days prior to the expiration of each period for which the price and length of term thereof have been previously agreed upon," the price "in no event to be higher than the contract price for newsprint charged by the Canadian Export Paper Company to the large consumers." 235 N.Y. at 342-43.
The seller delivered and was paid for the paper due from September through December 1919. It then refused to agree on any price for 1920 and declined further performance, asserting that the contract was incomplete.
The buyer demanded delivery at the Canadian Export Paper Company's price, renewing the demand each month throughout 1920, and sued when the seller refused. Id. at 343.
sections.Procedural History: The case was decided on the pleadings. Special Term, the trial-level part of New York's Supreme Court, ruled for the seller. The Appellate Division reversed and certified a question to the Court of Appeals, which asked in substance whether the complaint stated a cause of action.
sections.Issue: When a sales contract leaves the price and the period for which each price will apply to future agreement, subject to a maximum price set by an external standard, is the seller bound to deliver at that maximum price if the parties fail to agree, or is the provision an unenforceable agreement to agree?
sections.Holding: An agreement that leaves essential terms to future agreement is not an enforceable contract as to those terms, and a court may not supply them by construction. Because the parties left open both the price and the length of the term during which each price would apply, and because agreement on time was as essential as agreement on price, the provision for 1920 was an agreement to agree. The seller was not bound to deliver at the Canadian price. The Court expressly did not decide whether the seller would have breached a duty by an arbitrary refusal to agree on a term after notice from the buyer, because the complaint did not rest on that theory. Id. at 344-47.
sections.Judgment: The Court of Appeals reversed the order of the Appellate Division, affirmed the judgment of Special Term for the seller, and answered the certified question in the negative, with costs.
sections.Reasoning:
The buyer argued that because the price for 1920 could not exceed the Canadian Export Paper Company's price, the seller was bound to deliver at that price if the parties failed to agree on a lower one. Cardozo agreed that the Canadian price was a maximum but held that the argument overlooked the second open term. The parties were to agree not only on a price but on the length of the period for which that price would apply, and the price, once fixed, would remain fixed during that period even if the Canadian price changed. Agreement on a maximum payable this month, he wrote, is not the same as agreement that it shall continue to be payable next month. Id. at 344.
Without an agreed period, a court could not determine which Canadian price governed which deliveries. If the buyer could invoke the Canadian price month by month, it would hold not one option but a dozen, able to take advantage of whatever price prevailed each month, while the parties had contemplated stability and certainty over agreed periods. The complaint therefore left no escape from the conclusion that agreement on time was as essential to a completed contract as agreement on price. Id. at 344-46.
The buyer also argued that the seller had a duty, in default of agreement, to accept a term reasonable in view of the nature of the transaction and the practice of the business. Cardozo rejected that standard. The seller reserved the privilege of doing its business in its own way and did not undertake to conform to the practice and beliefs of others; to hold it to a standard of reasonableness would be to make the contract over, and courts are not at liberty to revise while professing to construe. Id. at 345-46.
Cardozo closed by limiting the holding. The question whether the seller would have failed in a duty by an arbitrary refusal to reach any agreement on time after notice from the buyer was not presented. No such notice appeared in the complaint, and the action was not based on a refusal to negotiate and attempt to reach agreement. Id. at 346-47.
sections.Separate Opinions:
Judge Crane, joined by Judge Hogan, dissented. The parties were business people who used a formal contract, drafted by the seller, to bind themselves to buy and sell 16,000 tons of paper, and a court should presume they intended a binding agreement and give effect to it if possible. On December 15, 1919, a definite
Canadian Export price existed; if the buyer offered to pay that maximum, the seller was bound to deliver.
Crane offered several workable constructions: hold the seller to deliver the remaining paper at the Canadian price; apply the Canadian price in effect on the fifteenth of each month to that month's thousand tons; or fix a reasonable period in light of the circumstances and the practice of the paper trade. Letting the seller escape when any of these constructions would produce a practical and just result, he wrote, would give the sanction of law to a deliberate breach. Id. at 348-51 (Crane, J., dissenting).
sections.Notes:
Sun Printing is a leading statement of the common-law rule that an agreement to agree on essential terms is unenforceable, and its facts show why the rule has costs: a seller facing a rising market could escape a sixteen-month supply contract by refusing to agree. The Uniform Commercial Code rejects the premise.
Under § 2-305(1)(b), when the parties intended to be bound but leave price to be agreed and fail to agree, the price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery, and § 2-204(3) saves contracts with open terms when the parties intended to contract and a court has a reasonably certain basis for a remedy. The case might come out differently today, although § 2-305(4) preserves the result if the parties intended not to be bound unless the price was agreed.
The reservation at the end of the opinion links the case to the precontractual-liability materials. Cardozo left open a claim that the seller arbitrarily refused to negotiate after notice, the kind of claim later recognized in
Tribune and Channel Home Centers when parties commit to negotiate. Crane's dissent anticipates Oglebay
Norton's approach of honoring the parties' intent to be bound by filling the gap with a reasonable term.

briefs.title: Oglebay Norton Co. v. Armco, Inc.
briefs.citation: Oglebay Norton Co. v. Armco, Inc., 52 Ohio St. 3d 232, 556 N.E.2d 515 (1990). Supreme Court of Ohio, decided July 11, 1990. The opinion was issued per curiam, meaning by the court as a whole without a named author, and Chief Justice Moyer and Justices Sweeney, Holmes, Douglas, Wright, H. Brown, and Resnick concurred. The case concerns whether a court may enforce a long-term contract after both of

sections.Parties: Oglebay Norton Company, which operated a fleet of Great Lakes bulk vessels, was the carrier and the plaintiff. Armco, Inc., a steel producer, was the shipper and the defendant. Oglebay sought a declaration that the contract remained in force and a determination of the rate; Armco contended that the contract had become unenforceable because its pricing mechanisms had failed.
sections.Material Facts:
Under a 1957 long-term contract, Oglebay agreed to maintain vessel capacity sufficient to carry up to 7.1 million gross tons of Armco's iron ore per year on the Great Lakes, and Armco agreed to use that capacity.
Later amendments extended the contract through 2010, and a 1962 amendment gave Armco a contractual right to seek specific performance of Oglebay's obligations. The parties had a long and close relationship that included joint ventures, interlocking directorates, and Armco's ownership of Oglebay stock. 52 Ohio St. 3d at
233-35.
The contract set the rate through two mechanisms. The primary mechanism looked to the rate recognized by leading iron ore shippers, which in practice was the published rate for a leading shipper in Skillings Mining
Review. If no such rate existed, a secondary mechanism required the parties to agree on a rate taking into consideration the rates charged by leading independent vessel operators. The mechanism worked for decades, but in the mid-1980s, as the steel industry declined, it failed. For 1985 the published rate was $7.41 per gross ton, and Armco paid only $5.00. After 1985 the journal stopped publishing the rate, and information about independent carriers' rates could not be obtained. The parties could not agree on a rate, and Armco took the position that the contract was no longer enforceable. Id. at 234-35.
sections.Procedural History:
Oglebay sought declaratory relief in the Court of Common Pleas. The trial court found that the parties intended to be bound despite the failure of the pricing mechanisms. Relying on the parties' course of dealing, the detriment each would suffer, and market comparisons reflecting the depressed state of the steel industry, it set a reasonable rate of $6.25 per gross ton for the 1986 season. It also ordered the parties to negotiate a rate for each shipping season through 2010 and, if negotiations failed, to mediate, and it retained continuing jurisdiction. The court of appeals affirmed, and the Supreme Court of Ohio heard Armco's appeal. Id. at
235-36.
sections.Issue: When both pricing mechanisms in a long-term contract fail, did the parties still intend to be bound? If so, may the court determine a reasonable price, and may it exercise continuing equitable jurisdiction by ordering the parties to negotiate future rates and, failing agreement, to mediate?
sections.Holding:
Whether the parties intended to be bound despite the failure of their pricing mechanisms is a question of fact, and competent, credible evidence supported the trial court's finding that they did. When the parties intended to conclude a contract but the price is not settled, a court may determine a reasonable price, as Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 33 and its comments and UCC § 2-305(1), adopted in Ohio as R.C. 1302.18(A), recognize. The $6.25 rate fell within the range of reasonable rates the evidence established. Because damages for breach of a contract of this length in a volatile market would be speculative, the trial court could order the equivalent of specific performance and require the parties to negotiate and, if necessary, mediate future rates.
Id. at 235-38.
sections.Judgment: The Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed the judgment of the court of appeals.
sections.Reasoning:
On intent, the court deferred to the trial court's finding, which rested on the parties' long relationship, their course of dealing, and the importance of the contract to both. Armco needed dedicated capacity and Oglebay had maintained its fleet to supply it. Nothing in the record showed that the parties intended the entire arrangement to end if the published rate disappeared. Id. at 235.
On the rate, the court relied on Restatement § 33. Comment e recognizes that parties who intend to conclude a contract may leave the price unsettled, and a court may then supply a reasonable price; comment a notes that the parties' actions may show conclusively that they intended a binding agreement even though terms are missing. UCC § 2-305(1) states the same principle for sales of goods. Ohio precedent was consistent:
Normandy Place Associates v. Beyer enforced an agreement where the parties manifested intent to be bound and the terms were sufficiently definite, and Litsinger Sign Co. v. American Sign Co. held that a court should not frustrate the parties' intent to be bound if it is reasonably possible to fill gaps. Evidence of other carriers' rates, including $7.41 paid by another steel producer and $5.90 quoted by another carrier for 1986, placed the
$6.25 rate within a reasonable range. Id. at 236-37.
On the remedy, the court applied Restatement § 362, which permits specific performance when the terms are sufficiently certain to provide a basis for an appropriate order, allowing the court to use the usual aids, including usage and terms supplied by law. Damages were an inadequate remedy because the dramatic changes in Great Lakes shipping rates and the length of the contract would make it impossible to calculate
Oglebay's damages accurately. The parties' 1962 amendment had itself contemplated specific performance.
Ordering negotiation and, if it broke down, mediation neither added to nor detracted from the parties' obligations; it provided a practical means of carrying out a contract the parties had intended to last until 2010.
Id. at 237-38.
sections.Separate Opinions: The opinion was per curiam, and all seven justices concurred. There is no separate opinion.
sections.Notes:
Oglebay Norton is the modern counterpart to Sun Printing. In both, the parties left price to an external standard and to future agreement, and the standard failed. Cardozo treated the open terms as proof that no contract existed for the unpriced period; the Ohio court treated the parties' intent to be bound as controlling and supplied the missing term. The difference reflects the Code and Restatement principles in § 2-305 and §
33, the length and importance of the relationship, and the parties' decades of performance, which made intent to be bound much easier to find.
Two points about scope are important. The contract was for transportation services, so the court applied §
2-305 by analogy rather than directly. And the mediation remedy is unusual: courts rarely supervise ongoing negotiations, and the court justified doing so by the parties' unique, long-lasting relationship, the inadequacy of damages, and the parties' own provision for specific performance. The case also illustrates why §
2-305(1)(c) addresses the failure of an agreed market standard: when the index disappears, the question becomes whether the parties would have wanted the contract to continue at a reasonable price, and a long relational contract makes that answer more likely to be yes.

briefs.title: Scope of Article 2 and Firm Offers

sections.Sources:
UCC §§ 2-102, 2-104, 2-105, 2-205, and 1-103(b). Article 2 supplies special rules for transactions in goods;
the common law of contracts supplements those rules unless displaced. The casebook's discussion of firm offers explains why commercial assurances can become binding without the separate consideration ordinarily needed for an option. The provisions reproduced by Cornell are model UCC text; the applicable state's enacted version governs an actual dispute. § 2-102; § 2-104; § 2-105; § 2-205; § 1-103.
Scope
Article 2 generally applies to transactions in goods. Under § 2-105, goods are things movable when identified to the contract, including specially manufactured goods. Carpeting and steel coils therefore fit
Article 2 in Dorton and C. Itoh. Goods also include unborn animals and growing crops, subject to the Code's provisions concerning things attached to realty. Money used as the price, investment securities, and things in action fall outside the statutory definition. A sale of land or a contract solely for professional services ordinarily falls under other law.
A transaction need not involve two merchants to fall within Article 2. A consumer buying a refrigerator and a private owner selling a used refrigerator can enter sales contracts governed by Article 2. Merchant status matters only where a particular provision makes it matter. Section 2-205 requires the offeror to be a merchant; § 2-207(2)'s automatic incorporation of certain additional terms applies between merchants.
Sections 2-204 and 2-206 do not generally require merchant status.
Contracts combining goods and services require a further classification. Many courts ask whether the predominant purpose of the transaction is a sale of goods with incidental labor or a service with incidental goods. The contract's language, the supplier's business, and the relative significance of the goods and services help answer that question. A purchase of equipment with installation can be predominantly a sale; a painting service does not ordinarily become a sale of goods merely because the contractor supplies paint.
Jurisdictions differ in their treatment of mixed transactions. The uploaded casebook illustrates the predominant-factor approach through Bonebrake v. Cox, 499 F.2d 951, 960 (8th Cir. 1974), in its later discussion of Article 2's scope.
Merchant Status
Section 2-104 includes a person who deals in goods of the kind, a person whose occupation holds the person out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the practices or goods involved, and a person to whom such knowledge or skill is attributed through an agent or intermediary. The relevant expertise depends on the provision being applied. A business may possess expertise in ordinary commercial practices even when it does not regularly sell the particular goods involved in a transaction.
For firm offers, knowledge of commercial practices can suffice. A manufacturer selling used factory equipment therefore should not automatically be treated as a nonmerchant simply because selling that equipment is not its regular business. The casebook contrasts this broader inquiry with the implied warranty of merchantability, which § 2-314 ties to a merchant dealing in goods of the kind. Merchant status must be connected to the specific statutory rule, rather than treated as a universal label with identical consequences throughout Article 2.
Firm Offers
Section 2-205 protects an offer by a merchant to buy or sell goods when a signed writing gives assurance that the offer will be held open. No consideration is required for that assurance. If the assurance states a period, statutory irrevocability lasts for that period, subject to a three-month maximum. If no period is stated, it lasts for a reasonable time, also subject to that maximum. If the offeree supplies the form containing the assurance, the offeror must separately sign the assurance; a general signature on the form is insufficient for this special requirement.
An ordinary offer and an assurance against revocation perform different functions. A quotation must first be sufficiently definite and committed to count as an offer. Its identifying an acceptance deadline does not automatically establish every element of a firm offer. The writing must also communicate that the offer will be held open. Conversely, a qualifying firm offer remains only an offer until accepted. Section 2-205 binds the merchant's assurance without requiring the offeree to accept the proposed sale.
The three-month ceiling limits irrevocability supplied by § 2-205 without consideration. It does not impose a three-month ceiling on a separately supported option contract. It also does not necessarily make the underlying offer lapse when statutory protection ends. An offer that remains outstanding may still be accepted after that point unless it has expired, been effectively revoked, or otherwise terminated. A stated four-month acceptance period and a three-month period of statutory irrevocability can therefore coexist.
sections.Application:
Suppose a merchant signs an offer to sell 500 chairs for a specified price and promises to keep it open for sixty days. Section 2-205 can prevent revocation during those sixty days even if the buyer pays nothing for the assurance and never relies on it. If the buyer prepared a form containing that assurance, the seller must separately sign the assurance. If the same writing promises six months of irrevocability, § 2-205 alone supplies at most three months; additional legal grounds must support protection beyond that period.
The contrast with Drennan is central. Star Paving made an oral bid for construction work, and the court protected foreseeable reliance under common-law principles. Drennan does not depend on a merchant's signed assurance. Section 2-205 supplies an independent statutory route, with its own scope and formal requirements. Failure to qualify under that section is not itself proof that every possible consideration-based or reliance-based argument fails; those arguments require their own analysis under the governing law.

briefs.title: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 45 and 90

sections.Sources:
Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 45 and 90. The Restatement describes common-law principles and is persuasive authority unless adopted by the relevant court. Section 45 addresses beginning the performance invited by an offer that permits acceptance only through performance. Section 90 addresses promises inducing foreseeable reliance. Drennan applied the First Restatement's versions; the Second Restatement's wording should be distinguished from the language quoted in that 1958 opinion. The assigned casebook reproduces and discusses these rules. Online reproductions appear in Revocation of Offers and Promissory
Estoppel.
Section 45
Section 45 applies when the offer invites acceptance through performance and does not invite a promise as acceptance. An option arises when the offeree tenders or begins the invited performance, or tenders its beginning. The resulting protection limits the offeror's ability to revoke while the offeree has the opportunity to complete the requested performance. The offeror's duty to perform the proposed exchange remains conditioned on completion or tender of the invited performance according to the offer's terms.
The distinction between creating the option and earning the promised return matters. If A offers B $100 for walking across a bridge and the offer genuinely calls for completed performance rather than a promise, B's beginning the crossing creates protection against revocation. It does not ordinarily entitle B to the full $100 merely for starting. Completion remains the condition of A's duty to pay. B does not, merely by obtaining the option, promise to finish the walk and become liable for stopping.
The offeree must begin the performance that the offer actually requests. Buying walking shoes or traveling toward the bridge ordinarily amounts to preparation. Preparation can be costly and foreseeable without constituting the invited act itself. It may support a reliance argument on appropriate facts, but § 45 does not turn every expense incurred after hearing an offer into the beginning of contractual performance. The offer's wording and context determine where preparation ends and the requested performance begins.
Section 45 also must be separated from an offer that allows acceptance by either a promise or performance.
Under the Restatement's related § 62, beginning the invited performance in that setting can constitute acceptance and carry a promise to complete. Under § 45, the performance-only offer creates an option at the beginning, while the offeror's ultimate exchange obligation remains conditional. The classification therefore affects both parties' duties, not just the moment when revocation becomes ineffective.
Section 90
Section 90(1) recognizes enforcement when a promise foreseeably induces action or forbearance by the promisee or a third person and enforcement is necessary to prevent injustice. Its second sentence permits relief to be tailored as justice requires. The rule supplies a possible basis for enforcement even when the promise lacks bargained-for consideration. A person must identify a promise, the reliance it should reasonably have induced, the actual resulting change of position, and the injustice that enforcement would prevent.
Foreseeability and actual reliance require separate proof. A promisor may reasonably expect a contractor to use a bid, but a contractor who never used that bid has not established the same causal reliance. Conversely, a person may actually change position for reasons that the promisor could not reasonably anticipate.
Reasonableness also matters: reliance on an obviously mistaken price, an expressly tentative estimate, or an assurance outside its stated limits is more difficult to justify. Expenditures made before the promise ordinarily cannot have been induced by it.
The Second Restatement removes the First Restatement's express requirement that the induced conduct be definite and substantial, but the seriousness and reasonableness of reliance remain relevant to injustice and relief. It also expressly includes reliance by a third person and recognizes remedial flexibility. A successful §
90 claim therefore does not mechanically produce either full expectation damages or reimbursement of every expenditure. The court connects the remedy to the promise, the reliance, and the injustice shown.
Section 90(2) separately addresses charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements: the Restatement's rule does not require proof of induced action or forbearance for those promises. That qualification should not be generalized to ordinary commercial promises. Nor does the Restatement's treatment establish that every jurisdiction has adopted the same rule for charitable pledges.
Relationship to Drennan
Drennan used § 90 to protect reliance on an offer before conventional acceptance. The subcontractor could foresee that the general contractor would commit to the owner using the quoted price. The court treated that reliance as supporting a subsidiary promise to keep the bid available long enough for acceptance after the award. Section 45 supplied an analogy: the law already protected an offeree who began an invited unilateral performance. But using Star's price in the general bid was not itself an acceptance of Star's offer or the bargained-for performance that Star requested.
The Second Restatement later addresses this situation more directly in § 87(2), which treats an offer inducing the requisite preacceptance reliance as binding as an option to the extent necessary to prevent injustice. This helps explain why reliance can preserve an opportunity to accept without automatically establishing that both parties already promised the entire exchange. In Drennan, the general contractor then promptly sought performance at the quoted price; the case did not authorize indefinite delay or renewed bargaining while retaining the original bid as a fallback.
sections.Application:
Begin with the offer's invited method of acceptance. If a promise is invited and effectively given, ordinary formation may resolve the case. If only performance is invited, determine whether the offeree has begun that performance, bringing § 45 into play. If the conduct consists of preparation or another foreseeable change of position before acceptance, examine reliance under § 90 and, where relevant, § 87(2). Then identify the consequence actually justified: preservation of the offer, enforcement of a promise, or a remedy tailored to the reliance.
A signed merchant assurance under § 2-205 can be binding without any of this conduct. A qualifying New
York writing under General Obligations Law § 5-1109 likewise supplies its own basis for protection. These doctrines address overlapping practical problems through distinct elements; they should be applied independently before their consequences are compared.

briefs.title: Drennan v. Star Paving Co.
briefs.citation: Drennan v. Star Paving Co., 51 Cal. 2d 409, 333 P.2d 757 (1958). Supreme Court of California, decided December 31, 1958. Justice Traynor wrote the opinion. The appeal concerned whether reliance made a subcontractor's offer irrevocable before the general contractor communicated acceptance. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
William A. Drennan, a licensed general contractor, was the plaintiff and respondent. He sought the additional cost of obtaining paving work after the subcontractor refused to perform at its quoted price. Star
Paving Company was the defendant and appellant. It maintained that its bid was a revocable offer and that it withdrew the offer before acceptance. The school district awarded the principal construction contract to
Drennan but was not a party to this damages action.
sections.Material Facts:
On July 28, 1955, Drennan prepared a bid for the Monte Vista school project in the Lancaster school district.
Bids were due before 8 p.m. Local practice was for general contractors to receive subcontractor quotations by telephone on the bidding day and use them in calculating their own bids. Drennan's secretary received approximately fifty to seventy-five quotations, recorded them on forms, and gave them to Drennan for his master cost sheet.
Late that afternoon, Star's estimator telephoned a price of $7,131.60 for the paving work according to the project's plans and specifications. He repeated the figure at the secretary's request. Drennan listened on an extension and entered the quotation on his cost sheet. Star supplied the lowest paving bid. Drennan used it to calculate his own total bid of $317,385 and identified Star as the paving subcontractor. The bidding requirements called for identification of subcontractors responsible for at least one-half of one percent of the work and a bond equal to ten percent of the general bid. Drennan's bid was the lowest, and he received the principal contract.
The next morning, Drennan stopped at Star's office. Before he communicated acceptance, Star's construction engineer said the bid contained a mistake and could not be honored. Star demanded at least $15,000.
Drennan responded that he had used the original figure, was obligated to perform his own contract, and expected Star to perform at its quoted price. Star refused. After seeking replacement quotations for several months, Drennan hired L & H Paving for $10,948.60, the lowest replacement bid he obtained. 51 Cal. 2d at
411-13.
sections.Procedural History:
Drennan sued Star for the additional paving cost caused by its refusal to perform. The trial court found that
Star made a definite offer to perform the specified work for $7,131.60 and that Drennan relied on the offer in calculating his general bid and naming Star. It entered judgment for Drennan for $3,817, plus costs. The damages represented the difference between Star's bid and the reasonable replacement cost.
Star appealed.
