Its principal argument presented a formation problem: no consideration supported an option, no bilateral contract arose from Drennan's use of the bid, and Star communicated withdrawal before Drennan communicated acceptance. It also relied on its mistake and challenged the sufficiency of Drennan's damages allegations. The California Supreme Court reviewed the legal effect of reliance while accepting the trial court's supported factual findings.
sections.Issue: Did Drennan's foreseeable and reasonable reliance on Star's definite subcontract bid make the offer temporarily irrevocable, even though he had neither paid consideration for an option nor accepted the subcontract before Star attempted to withdraw? Could Star nevertheless escape liability because its bid resulted from mistake, and did Drennan adequately establish mitigation and resulting damages?
sections.Holding:
Reasonable, foreseeable reliance producing a prejudicial change of position can support an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke an offer, even without bargained-for consideration. Under the First
Restatement's § 90, Star's bid became irrevocable long enough to give Drennan a reasonable opportunity to accept after the general contract was awarded. Drennan's use of the figure alone did not establish a bilateral subcontract; reliance instead protected his later opportunity to accept.
Star's mistake did not defeat recovery because Drennan had no reason to know of it and had already committed himself on the strength of the bid. The evidence also established reasonable mitigation. The result was enforcement sufficient to recover the $3,817 additional cost. Id. at 413-17.
sections.Judgment:
The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's judgment for Drennan for $3,817 plus costs. Drennan prevailed on the reliance theory. The affirmance awarded damages for Star's refusal to honor the bid; it did not compel
Star to perform the paving work.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first rejected the easiest conventional contract theories. Star had not bargained for Drennan's use of its quotation in exchange for a promise to keep the bid open. Nor did using the quotation manifest an acceptance binding Drennan to award Star the subcontract if he obtained the principal contract. There was therefore neither a consideration-supported option nor an already formed bilateral contract. Identifying this gap was essential: the court's work was to explain why revocation could still be ineffective.
Section 90 supplied the answer. Star submitted the bid to obtain the paving subcontract. It could expect that a low bid would be included in Drennan's calculation, help him obtain the principal award, and improve Star's own prospects. Drennan's reliance was therefore commercially expected and beneficial to Star's objective.
Once Drennan committed himself to the owner, revocation would leave him bound to a price calculated from a quotation that Star now refused to honor. Protecting a reasonable opportunity to accept allocated that risk to the party that induced the commitment.
The court drew support from § 45's protection of an offeree who begins the performance invited by a unilateral offer. In that setting an implied subsidiary promise prevents revocation while the offeree completes the requested act. The court reasoned that foreseeable preacceptance reliance can justify comparable protection for an offer contemplating a bilateral contract. The analogy did not convert Drennan's bid calculation into the performance Star had requested. It explained why the absence of a completed exchange did not necessarily preserve unrestricted revocation.
The protection had limits. A general contractor cannot delay acceptance after the principal award while searching for a better price, or reopen negotiations with the subcontractor while continuing to insist on a right to accept the original bid. Drennan promptly told Star that he had used its bid and expected performance. His later search for replacement paving occurred after Star refused to honor the bid and served to mitigate the resulting loss; it was not the forbidden attempt to keep Star's offer in reserve while bargaining for a better original deal.
Mistake did not change the allocation. Drennan lacked notice of error, and paving quotations in the
Lancaster desert area commonly varied widely; the court referred to a 160-percent variance between the highest and lowest bids. A low price therefore did not itself make reliance unreasonable. Star's cited rescission cases involved circumstances in which the mistake was or should have been known and the other party could be restored to its former position. Drennan had already committed to the principal contract. The court placed the resulting loss on Star, which caused the mistake, rather than on the contractor who reasonably relied on it.
Finally, the evidence showed that Drennan sought quotations for months and accepted the lowest replacement bid. That conduct satisfied reasonable mitigation. His complaint alleged the amount he had to pay for substitute paving. Any uncertainty in that allegation could have been challenged through a special demurrer; Star's failure to raise the objection in that manner waived it. Id. at 413-17.
sections.Separate Opinions: Chief Justice Gibson and Justices Shenk, Schauer, Spence, and McComb concurred in Justice Traynor's opinion. The reported decision contains no separate concurrence or dissent.
sections.Notes:
Drennan distinguishes reliance from acceptance and reliance from consideration. The same act can reasonably induce commercial expectations without having been bargained for as the price of a promise. The court's solution was an implied commitment against revocation. Its discussion of a possible negligence duty in preparing bids reinforced the fairness of allocating the loss to Star, but the court expressly left unresolved whether negligence alone would support recovery on a case tried under that theory.
The opinion also stated that an offer expressly or clearly reserving revocation before acceptance would be treated accordingly. Its holding should therefore be connected to the definite, unqualified bid and justifiable reliance actually proved. The precise $3,817 recovery does not establish that every promissory-estoppel case receives full expectation damages. The Second Restatement's § 90 expressly permits a remedy limited as justice requires; § 87(2) more directly addresses protection of offers inducing preacceptance reliance.

briefs.title: UCC §§ 2-204 through 2-207

sections.Sources:
The provisions work in sequence. Section 2-204 asks whether the parties formed a sales contract. Section
2-205 protects certain offers against revocation. Section 2-206 identifies permissible methods of acceptance.
Section 2-207 addresses formation and terms when an acceptance or confirmation does not match the offer or earlier agreement. The section numbers should remain distinct: an irrevocable offer, an accepted offer, and an incorporated additional term are three different legal conclusions. § 2-204; § 2-205; § 2-206; § 2-207.
Section 2-204: Formation in General
A sales contract can arise in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties recognizing a contract. The precise instant of formation need not be identified. Open terms do not defeat formation if the parties intended a contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for an appropriate remedy.
Commercial conduct and objective intention therefore matter even when the parties' paperwork is incomplete.
This flexibility does not dispense with agreement. Negotiations that reserve commitment for later approval may remain preliminary. Nor does the Code supply every missing essential automatically. An open price can often be supplied under § 2-305, but the absence of an ascertainable quantity is a more serious problem unless a recognized arrangement, such as a requirements or output contract, supplies the quantity measure.
Formation also should be separated from enforceability under the statute of frauds in § 2-201, an independent inquiry where applicable.
For example, if a seller repeatedly ships identified goods and the buyer accepts and pays for them, the parties' conduct may demonstrate a sales contract despite uncertainty about which conversation completed the agreement. If their exchanged forms conflict, § 2-207 supplies the more specific analysis of which terms govern. Section 2-204 establishes flexibility; it does not let a court simply select whichever party's boilerplate seems preferable.
Section 2-205: Firm Offers
A merchant's offer to buy or sell goods is protected against revocation without consideration when a signed writing assures that the offer will be held open. Protection lasts for the stated time, or a reasonable time if none is stated, with a maximum of three months under this statutory mechanism. An assurance appearing on the offeree's form must be separately signed by the offeror. Only the offeror must qualify as a merchant for this provision; the offeree may be a consumer.
The section removes the need for consideration supporting the assurance, not the need for acceptance of the proposed sale. It also does not require the reliance that matters in Drennan. The detailed scope and examples appear in the opening notes. Its three-month limit concerns the particular statutory protection, rather than every option or every outstanding offer involving goods.
Section 2-206: Offer and Acceptance
Unless the offer's language or circumstances unambiguously indicate otherwise, an offer invites acceptance in any reasonable manner and by any reasonable medium. An order for prompt or current shipment can ordinarily be accepted through a prompt promise to ship or through prompt or current shipment. The offeror can specify a narrower method, but an exclusive requirement must be established from the actual language and circumstances.
Shipment of nonconforming goods ordinarily both accepts the order and breaches the resulting contract. The seller cannot automatically avoid a contract by sending the wrong goods. The exception is a seasonable notice that the nonconforming shipment is offered only as an accommodation. With that notice, the shipment functions as a proposed substitute transaction rather than acceptance of the original offer. The buyer can decide whether to accept the proposed accommodation.
Suppose a buyer orders 100 blue chairs for immediate shipment. A prompt promise to send them accepts the offer. A prompt shipment of 100 blue chairs also accepts. A shipment of 100 red chairs without a seasonable accommodation notice ordinarily accepts and breaches. If the seller seasonably explains that the red chairs are offered only as a substitute accommodation, the shipment does not accept the original order. These are formation consequences; the buyer's separate rights concerning rejection, cure, or acceptance of goods depend on other Article 2 provisions.
Where beginning the requested performance is a reasonable method of acceptance, § 2-206(2) protects an offeror who is not notified within a reasonable time: the offeror may treat the offer as having lapsed before acceptance. An offeree therefore should not assume that undisclosed commencement always binds an unaware offeror indefinitely. Also distinguish acceptance of an offer, which forms a contract, from acceptance of delivered goods, which concerns performance under a sales transaction.
Section 2-207: Additional or Different Terms
Subsection (1) first asks whether there is a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance, or a written confirmation sent within a reasonable time. Such a response can operate despite additional or different terms.
This displaces the traditional insistence that the acceptance mirror the offer. The response must still objectively express agreement; a fundamental disagreement over the transaction can show that no definite acceptance occurred.
The proviso in subsection (1) makes an exception where the response expressly conditions acceptance on the offeror's assent to the additional or different terms. Dorton interprets that language strictly: the response must clearly communicate unwillingness to proceed without the offeror's assent. Merely saying the response is subject to the seller's terms did not satisfy that standard there. A material alteration and an expressly conditional acceptance are distinct concepts. The importance of a term does not by itself prove that the seller expressly conditioned acceptance on assent to it.
If a contract arises through subsection (1), subsection (2) addresses additional terms. They begin as proposals. Where the transaction is not between merchants, inclusion ordinarily requires agreement to the proposed addition; the special rule for merchants does not automatically incorporate it. Between merchants, an additional term becomes part of the contract unless the offer expressly limits acceptance to its own terms, the addition materially alters the contract, or timely notice of objection has been given. An objection may already have been communicated or may be made within a reasonable time after notice of the proposed term.
Material alteration generally concerns a change that would produce surprise or hardship if incorporated without express awareness. The parties' practices, communications, and commercial setting can matter.
Dorton required factual findings about the arbitration clause rather than announcing that every arbitration term necessarily is, or is not, material. Failure to object is not enough to incorporate a material alteration under the merchant rule. Conversely, a term excluded from automatic incorporation can still become binding through actual agreement.
If the writings do not form a contract, subsection (3) asks whether both parties nevertheless act as though a contract exists. Shipment and the buyer's acceptance and payment can establish that conduct. The resulting terms are those on which the writings agree, together with supplementary terms supplied under the Code. A seller's unaccepted additional arbitration clause does not enter this contract merely because it appeared in the last form sent. C. Itoh applies this route after a genuinely conditional acknowledgment and subsequent performance without assent to the added clause.
The statute expressly mentions additional and different terms in subsection (1), but its model subsection (2) expressly discusses additional terms. Courts differ in their treatment of different terms where a contract forms under subsection (1). A common approach removes conflicting terms and supplies the applicable
Code rule; other approaches favor the offer's term or analyze differences through subsection (2). Do not present one approach as universal. This interpretive dispute is separate from subsection (3)'s express instruction to retain agreed terms and add the Code's supplementary provisions.
sections.Application:
Reconstruct the transaction before reading the boilerplate in isolation. Determine whether an oral agreement already existed, identify the offer and response, and locate the disputed term in each communication. If the response is an effective acceptance under subsection (1), apply subsection (2) to additional terms. If the response is genuinely conditional and the offeror does not assent, ask whether later mutual performance establishes a contract under subsection (3). If neither assent nor qualifying conduct exists, formation has not been established through either route.
This sequence explains the different outcomes of Dorton and C. Itoh. Dorton's acknowledgment was not expressly conditional in the required sense, so the court needed findings about earlier agreement and material alteration. C. Itoh's acknowledgment was expressly conditional, the writings did not form a contract, and subsequent performance supplied one under subsection (3). Receipt and payment proved commitment to the sale without necessarily proving assent to every printed term.

briefs.title: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp.
briefs.citation: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp., 453 F.2d 1161 (6th Cir. 1972). United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, decided January 6, 1972. Judge Celebrezze wrote the opinion. The case concerns whether an arbitration clause in a seller's acknowledgments became part of carpet sales under UCC § 2-207. Full judicial opinion.

sections.Parties:
Frank E. Dorton and his partners, doing business as The Carpet Mart in Kingsport, Tennessee, were the plaintiffs and appellees. They bought carpets for retail sale and claimed that the seller misrepresented the fiber content. Collins & Aikman Corporation, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in
New York and a carpet plant in Dalton, Georgia, was the defendant and appellant. It sought to enforce arbitration language in its printed sales forms. Both sides qualified as merchants for the transactions at issue.
sections.Material Facts:
During 1968 through 1970, the parties conducted more than fifty-five carpet transactions. Orders were telephoned to Collins & Aikman's Georgia order department, sometimes by a Carpet Mart partner and sometimes through the seller's visiting salesman. The parties disputed whether those communications themselves produced oral sales agreements. One buyer affidavit described employees or the salesman agreeing to sell the requested carpet during the ordering process. The seller's position and the wording of its forms suggested that written acknowledgment supplied acceptance.
After checking the price and the buyer's credit, Collins & Aikman sent a printed acknowledgment. The forms had several titles and variations. Their front sides stated that the transaction was subject to terms on both sides, including arbitration. They purported to bind the buyer through various acts, including signing, furnishing shipping directions, accepting delivery, or in some versions retaining the form for ten days without objection. The reverse contained a broad clause requiring arbitration in New York City of disputes connected with the contract.
The seller mailed the acknowledgment on the ordering day or the following day. Except for possible postal delay, it arrived before the carpets. The Carpet Mart accepted delivery and paid without objecting to the printed terms. In May 1970, a customer complaint led it to discover that some carpet supposedly manufactured entirely from Kodel polyester allegedly contained a cheaper, inferior fiber. The parties' agreement to buy and sell carpet was evident; the dispute concerned whether they had also agreed to the seller's arbitration mechanism. 453 F.2d at 1163-65.
sections.Procedural History:
The Carpet Mart sued in Tennessee state court for fraud, deceit, and misrepresentation, seeking $450,000 in compensatory and punitive damages. Collins & Aikman removed the action to federal district court on diversity grounds and moved under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act to stay the litigation pending arbitration. The district court concluded that no binding arbitration agreement existed. It applied § 2-207(3), treating the transactions as contracts established by conduct, and refused to include the seller's additional arbitration clause.
Collins & Aikman appealed the denial of the stay. Although the order was interlocutory, the Sixth Circuit held it appealable under the doctrine then governing stays pending arbitration and 28 U.S.C. § 1292. It noted that Georgia and Tennessee had both enacted the UCC before these transactions. The appeal required the court to review the district court's use of § 2-207, not to determine whether the alleged fiber substitution or fraud actually occurred.
The Sixth Circuit concluded that the existing findings did not permit a final decision on whether arbitration was a contractual term. It remanded for findings about formation during the oral dealings, whether arbitration had already been included, and, if arbitration was an added term, whether it materially altered the relevant offer or agreement. Id. at 1163-64, 1169-71.
sections.Issue: Did the seller's acknowledgments make acceptance expressly conditional on the buyer's assent to additional terms, so that the writings failed to form a contract and § 2-207(3) governed? If they instead were effective acceptances or confirmations under § 2-207(1), did the arbitration clause enter the contracts under subsection (2)? If it did, did the buyer's fraud claims nevertheless permit the court action to proceed without a stay?
sections.Holding:
An acceptance is expressly conditional within § 2-207(1) only when it clearly conveys that the offeree will not proceed without the offeror's assent to the additional or different terms. The seller's subject-to language and provisions treating various acts or silence as acceptance did not satisfy that requirement. The district court therefore could not bypass subsections (1) and (2) by applying subsection (3) on that basis.
If arbitration was additional to the oral offers or prior agreements, it had to be evaluated under subsection (2). Because the parties were merchants, the material-alteration inquiry was central. A material addition would require express agreement to become binding. The appellate court did not decide whether this arbitration clause materially altered these transactions; it required factual findings on remand. If the clause was part of the contracts, its breadth covered the asserted fraud claims and required a stay. Id. at 1168-71.
sections.Judgment: The court remanded to the district court for further findings consistent with its opinion. It did not finally order arbitration and did not finally hold that arbitration was excluded. The disposition required the trial court to use the correct formation and terms analysis before deciding whether the action should be stayed.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2-207 responds to the commercial practice of exchanging forms whose standard terms seldom match. Under the traditional mirror-image approach, a response adding terms could become a counteroffer, and subsequent performance could give the party sending the final form a substantial advantage. The Code permits a contract to exist despite differences in boilerplate and separately determines which added terms enter it. Treating every qualified acknowledgment as a counteroffer would undermine that statutory design.
The first factual question was whether the oral dealings already completed the contracts. If they did, the acknowledgments were confirmations of existing agreements. If they did not, the forms could be acceptances of oral offers. Section 2-207 applies in either situation; the dispute need not involve two competing written forms. The distinction nevertheless matters because it identifies the agreement against which the alleged addition must be compared. It also prevents a court from treating a later confirmation as if no prior contract existed.
The second question was whether arbitration was actually new. The district court had apparently assumed the oral orders contained no arbitration term. The Sixth Circuit required a finding. If the parties already agreed to arbitration, the printed clause would not need to enter as an additional term under subsection (2). If they did not, its inclusion depended on the statutory treatment of additions or on a later actual agreement.
The conditional-acceptance proviso required more than the seller's assertion that its terms governed. It required an express condition tied to the buyer's assent. The forms supplied several supposed ways to bind the buyer, including mere retention without objection. That language did not distinctly establish that the seller would refuse to proceed unless assured of assent to the added terms. Calling an acknowledgment subject to its reverse-side conditions therefore did not have the same effect as clearly conditioning acceptance on the offeror's agreement to them.
Once the acknowledgments were treated as acceptances or confirmations, subsection (2) governed an additional arbitration clause. The court left materiality to factual determination. If the addition materially altered the transaction, the buyer would not become bound without expressly agreeing. If it did not materially alter it, the merchant rule could incorporate it under the circumstances presented. The repeated transactions and receipt of forms supplied relevant context; they did not eliminate the need for the correct legal inquiry.
Finally, the court distinguished a challenge to making an arbitration agreement from a claim that the overall contract was induced by fraud. Under Prima Paint, a broad arbitration clause, if actually agreed upon, could cover the alleged fraud in carpet composition. The buyer attacked the underlying sale rather than asserting fraud specifically in procuring the arbitration clause. Thus, the court first had to decide whether the arbitration agreement existed. Only after an affirmative answer would the broad clause require a stay. Id. at
1166-71.
sections.Separate Opinions:
The reported decision contains Judge Celebrezze's opinion without a separate concurrence or dissent. Judge
Brooks participated in the decision but died before it was filed.
sections.Notes:
The holding concerns the meaning of expressly conditional acceptance and the need for proper findings.
Whether arbitration materially altered the particular bargains remained unresolved. A brief that says the
Sixth Circuit conclusively rejected arbitration would misstate the disposition. Likewise, the court's statement that a stay would be required if the clause was included is conditional on the formation issue being resolved for the seller.
Dorton also separates two provisions that are easy to conflate. The § 2-207(1) proviso asks what condition the responding party expressly communicated. Section 2-207(2)(b) asks what effect an added term would have on the bargain. A substantial alteration does not, merely because it is substantial, turn an otherwise effective acceptance into an expressly conditional counteroffer. C. Itoh presents the contrasting situation in which the seller's language did satisfy the proviso.

briefs.title: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. v. Jordan International Co.
briefs.citation: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. v. Jordan International Co., 552 F.2d 1228 (7th Cir. 1977). United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, decided April 4, 1977. Judge Sprecher wrote the opinion. This brief uses the judicial-opinion excerpt in the supplied Farnsworth casebook, seventh edition, printed pages 199-201, which includes an editorial statement of facts and procedure. The full onlin

sections.Parties: C. Itoh & Co. (America) Inc. was the buyer, plaintiff, and appellee. The Jordan International Company was the steel seller, defendant, and appellant. Itoh sought judicial relief for allegedly defective steel and late delivery. Jordan contended that the dispute had to be arbitrated under a provision in its acknowledgment and sought to stay the litigation pending arbitration.
sections.Material Facts:
Itoh sent Jordan a purchase order for steel coils. Jordan responded with its acknowledgment form. Its language expressly conditioned the seller's acceptance on the buyer's assent to the additional or different terms appearing in the form and on its reverse side. It also directed the buyer to notify the seller immediately if the terms were unacceptable. One reverse-side provision required arbitration. Itoh's purchase order contained no corresponding arbitration clause.
The writings therefore did not establish agreement on arbitration. Jordan nevertheless delivered the steel, and
Itoh paid for it. Itoh later complained that the steel was defective and had arrived late. The parties' performance showed that they were carrying out a sales transaction even though the seller had never obtained the assent required by its expressly conditional acknowledgment. The question became which terms governed the contract demonstrated by that performance.
sections.Procedural History:
Itoh filed suit against Jordan based on the alleged defects and late delivery. Jordan moved to stay the proceedings pending arbitration, relying on its acknowledgment. The trial court denied that motion. Jordan appealed the denial to the Seventh Circuit.
The appellate inquiry addressed whether the arbitration clause belonged to the sales contract under § 2-207.
The question did not require a final decision about the quality of the steel, the timeliness of delivery, or the amount of damages. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the denial of the stay on the ground that the contract created by conduct did not include the unagreed arbitration provision.
sections.Issue: When a seller expressly conditions acceptance on the buyer's assent to additional terms, the buyer does not assent, and both parties nevertheless perform, does § 2-207(3) create a contract? If so, can the seller's arbitration clause become one of that contract's terms through the buyer's receipt and payment or through the provision for supplementary Code terms?
sections.Holding:
The seller's acknowledgment satisfied the expressly-conditional proviso in § 2-207(1). The exchange of writings therefore did not itself create a contract; the acknowledgment operated as a counteroffer. The parties' subsequent performance nevertheless established a contract under § 2-207(3).
That contract included the terms on which the writings agreed and applicable supplementary Code terms.
The parties' writings did not agree to arbitration, and Article 2 did not supply arbitration as a gap-filling term. The unaccepted clause was therefore excluded. Delivery and payment established the sales contract without establishing assent to that additional clause.
sections.Judgment: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the denial of Jordan's motion to stay the proceedings pending arbitration. Itoh could continue litigating its claims in court. The decision resolved the asserted obligation to arbitrate; it did not establish that Itoh had proved breach or its claimed damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Jordan's form used the condition that Dorton's forms lacked: it expressly tied acceptance to the buyer's assent to additional or different terms. That language prevented contract formation through the writings unless the condition was satisfied. The seller could not rely on § 2-207(1)'s ordinary rule treating a nonmatching acknowledgment as an acceptance while simultaneously insisting that its acceptance was withheld pending further assent.
The failure of the writings to form a contract did not end the analysis. Section 2-207(3) expressly recognizes contracts demonstrated by both parties' conduct. Jordan delivered and Itoh paid. Those reciprocal acts supplied objective evidence of a sales relationship. The Code thus avoided treating a completed commercial exchange as legally nonexistent merely because the parties' forms had failed to match or form a contract on their own.
The same subsection determined the terms. Its agreed-terms rule excluded Jordan's additional arbitration provision because the buyer's purchase order did not agree to it. Requiring an express contradiction in the buyer's form would defeat that rule: a term present only in the seller's form still was not a term on which both writings agreed. Neither the seller's last word in the exchange nor the buyer's ordinary performance automatically made that provision binding.
Jordan also could not reintroduce the arbitration clause as a supplementary term. The court interpreted that language as referring to the standardized gap-filling provisions of Article 2. Such provisions can complete a contract by supplying applicable default obligations. They do not serve as a route for importing disputed boilerplate that the agreed-terms rule has just excluded. Arbitration was not a necessary missing term supplied by the Code. The sales contract could operate with disputes resolved through the ordinary judicial process.
The court also addressed fairness to a seller choosing an expressly conditional form. Before the buyer assents or the parties proceed with conduct creating a contract, the seller benefits from not being committed through the writings alone. If the additional terms truly are essential, it can withhold delivery until it obtains the required assent. If it elects to deliver without that assent, it accepts the risk that the conduct-based contract will omit its unagreed terms. Giving the seller both freedom from a contract when it wishes to withdraw and automatic inclusion of its boilerplate when it wishes to perform would distort the statutory allocation.
sections.Separate Opinions: The assigned excerpt presents Judge Sprecher's opinion and contains no separate opinion. It does not provide a basis for adding an unverified account of other opinions or of proceedings beyond the reproduced decision.
sections.Notes:
C. Itoh illustrates the cost of making acceptance expressly conditional. That drafting can prevent formation through the forms, but it does not guarantee that the seller's preferred terms will govern if the parties proceed anyway. If agreement to arbitration is essential, the seller must obtain the requisite assent before relying on the conditional language and performing.
The comparison with Dorton turns on the formation route. Dorton required further examination under subsections (1) and (2), including material alteration, because the acknowledgments did not clearly condition acceptance on assent. C. Itoh proceeded under subsection (3), where the additional arbitration term was excluded because it was not agreed upon and was not supplied by the Code. Its exclusion did not depend on deciding the material-alteration question that remained open in Dorton.

briefs.title: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1109

sections.Sources:
New York General Obligations Law § 5-1109, concerning written irrevocable offers. The statute removes lack of consideration as a basis for revoking a qualifying written offer during its protected period. Its opening exception preserves the operation of UCC § 2-205 for merchant offers to buy or sell goods. Official
New York statutory text.
sections.Rule:
An offer to enter a contract must appear in a writing signed by the offeror or the offeror's agent and state that it is irrevocable for a specified period or until a specified time. The assurance is protected despite the absence of consideration. If the signed writing says the offer is irrevocable but supplies no period or ending time, the statute treats it as irrevocable for a reasonable time.
The provision requires neither the reliance demanded by a promissory-estoppel theory nor, outside its UCC exception, merchant status. It is broader in subject matter than Article 2's firm-offer provision and can address offers involving services or land. It nevertheless presupposes an actual offer and the required written assurance; preliminary discussions, an unsigned draft, or an oral promise to keep an offer open do not automatically satisfy its conditions.
Relationship to Section 2-205
For an offer by a merchant to buy or sell goods, the statute expressly defers to what § 2-205 otherwise provides. Section 5-1109 therefore cannot simply be invoked to disregard the UCC's applicable three-month maximum or its rule about assurances on an offeree-supplied form. The first step is to classify the transaction and determine whether § 2-205 governs the merchant's assurance.
Outside that exception, § 5-1109 itself states no three-month ceiling. A qualifying signed offer concerning a service contract and expressly made irrevocable for four months therefore is not reduced to three months merely by importing the UCC rule. Other formation requirements and applicable defenses remain relevant.
The statute addresses the effect of absent consideration on irrevocability; it does not declare every written proposal an otherwise valid or fully formed contract.
sections.Application:
Suppose a New York service provider signs a definite proposal and states that the offer is irrevocable until a specified date. Even if the customer pays no option price and incurs no reliance expense, § 5-1109 can preserve the opportunity to accept until that date. If the signed proposal declares irrevocability without naming a date, a reasonable period is supplied. The customer still must accept effectively while the power of acceptance remains available before the service exchange itself becomes binding.
The assignment's doctrines therefore offer distinct routes to protection. A bargained-for option rests on consideration. Section 45 protects the beginning of invited performance under a performance-only offer.
Drennan protects qualifying reliance on a subcontract bid. Section 2-205 protects a merchant's signed assurance concerning goods within its limits. Section 5-1109 protects qualifying New York writings within its broader scope while respecting the UCC exception. Identifying the source of irrevocability explains both why the offer stays open and what still must happen to form the contemplated exchange.

briefs.title: Offer and acceptance: reading guide

sections.Preamble:
Offer and acceptance
Reading guide and governing framework
An offer gives its recipient the legal power to form a contract by accepting the proposed exchange in the invited manner. The person making the offer is the offeror; the person authorized to accept is the offeree. An offer exists when the words and circumstances reasonably communicate that the recipient's assent will complete the bargain. A statement that reserves a further decision for its maker ordinarily begins or continues negotiations. Acceptance expresses assent to the offered terms through the words or conduct that the offer invites or requires. These questions concern the parties' observable communications and the reasonable meaning of their conduct. Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 24, 26, 30, 50 (1981).
Lefkowitz concerns a definite advertisement and acceptance by complying with its terms. Wucherpfennig distinguishes a present commitment from continued negotiation. International Filter identifies the operative offer and the effect of a specified approval method. White examines whether preparations objectively communicate acceptance. In each case, the wording and circumstances determine what further action completes the bargain.
A promise can serve as acceptance when the offer seeks a commitment to perform; conduct can also express that promise. When an offer invites either a promise or performance, beginning the invited performance ordinarily accepts and carries a promise to finish. When the offer invites acceptance only through performance, beginning or tendering the invited performance can create an option protecting the opportunity to finish, while the offeror's duty remains conditional on completion according to the offer. Preparation, actual beginning, completion, and notice therefore require separate analysis. Restatement §§ 32, 45, 50, 54,
56, 62.
For goods, the applicable state's Uniform Commercial Code supplies additional rules. UCC § 2-206 ordinarily permits acceptance in a reasonable manner and medium unless the offer or circumstances unambiguously require otherwise. An order for prompt shipment generally invites either a prompt promise to ship or prompt shipment. These rules should be distinguished from the historical reasoning in the older opinions. The Restatement synthesizes common-law principles whose adoption depends on the jurisdiction.
UCC § 2-206.
The assigned names control this packet's coverage because the supplied book is the seventh edition and uses different pagination. In that scan, Lefkowitz appears on printed pages 134-135, PDF pages 184-185;
International Filter on printed pages 147-151, PDF pages 197-201; and White on printed pages 152-154,
PDF pages 202-204. The silence discussion is on printed pages 166-167, PDF pages 216-217. The antidiscrimination discussion is on printed page 156, PDF page 206. The termination section occupies printed pages 167-185, PDF pages 217-235, followed by the mailbox discussion and problem on printed pages 185-188, PDF pages 235-238. Reporter citations identify the decisions independently of casebook pagination. Full online opinions were consulted for Lefkowitz, Wucherpfennig, and White. The accessible online International Filter opinion ends during its reasoning; the remainder and precise disposition were checked against the supplied excerpt. Its complete unabridged text was therefore not independently verified online. Linked citations identify the opinion texts and statutory sources.

briefs.title: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc.
briefs.citation: 251 Minn. 188, 86 N.W.2d 689 (1957). Supreme Court of Minnesota. Murphy, J. Decided December 20, 1957.

sections.Preamble:
The Minnesota Supreme Court held that the store's advertisement for a specifically identified fur stole at a stated price, offered to the first customer to arrive, created an offer that Morris Lefkowitz accepted by satisfying those conditions. The store could not then add an eligibility restriction absent from the advertisement. Lefkowitz, the customer and plaintiff below, was the respondent on appeal and represented himself. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc., the merchant and defendant below, appealed an order refusing to alter the trial court's findings or grant a new trial. The Supreme Court affirmed, leaving
Lefkowitz's $138.50 damages award in place. 251 Minn. at 189-92, 86 N.W.2d at 690-91.
The full opinion concerns two newspaper advertisements published a week apart. On April 6, 1956, the store advertised three new fur coats for one dollar each, available at 9 a.m. the following Saturday on a first-come, first-served basis. The advertisement described the coats as worth up to $100. On April 13, the store advertised two pastel mink three-skin scarfs, described as selling for $89.50, and one black lapin stole, described as worth $139.50, for one dollar each. The second advertisement again specified Saturday at 9 a.m. and first-come, first-served availability. The lapin stole was the item that ultimately supported the damages award.
On each Saturday, Lefkowitz arrived first at the appropriate counter, demanded the advertised item, and indicated that he was ready to pay one dollar. The store refused both times. On the first visit, it told him that an internal house rule limited the offer to women. On the second, it relied on his knowledge of that rule from the previous encounter. Neither published advertisement stated the restriction. The trial court's supported findings established Lefkowitz's compliance with the advertised conditions; the Supreme Court therefore examined the legal consequences of that conduct.
Lefkowitz sued for breach of contract in the Municipal Court of Minneapolis. The trial court rejected his claim for the value of the coats because the only evidence of their value was the uncertain upper limit stated in the first advertisement. A statement that the coats were worth up to $100 did not establish what any particular coat was actually worth. The stole's advertised value was a definite $139.50, and the court accepted that figure as established on this record. It awarded that value less the one-dollar purchase price, producing $138.50. The store moved for amended findings or, alternatively, a new trial; the municipal court denied the motion, and the store appealed that denial. 251 Minn. at 189-90, 86 N.W.2d at 690.
The formation issue was whether the advertisement itself committed the store to sell on stated terms when a customer performed the requested acts, or instead invited customers to submit purchase offers that the store remained free to reject. The related acceptance issue was whether Lefkowitz's arrival and offer to pay satisfied the advertisement. The store relied on decisions treating advertisements as invitations to bargain and argued that its advertised proposal could be withdrawn without notice. It also argued that the house rule restricted which customers could obtain the bargain. Lefkowitz's position depended on the public advertisement's definite terms and his performance of the acts it requested.
The court recognized that ordinary advertisements often invite buyers to make offers. The legal character of a particular advertisement nevertheless depends on its language and surrounding circumstances. Here the advertisement identified a particular article, supplied an exact price, fixed the time, and identified the eligible purchaser through the order of arrival. Those provisions supplied a way to determine both the store's obligation and the person entitled to enforce it. The court treated a public advertisement as an offer when it was sufficiently definite and left no further negotiation necessary to complete the transaction. A customer's response then could form the contract without a further discretionary approval by the store. 251 Minn. at
190-92, 86 N.W.2d at 690-91.
Lefkowitz accepted by arriving first as requested and offering the stated purchase price. The opinion does not require that the merchant first take his money: the findings established his readiness and offer to pay, followed by the merchant's refusal. The store's requested conduct supplied an objective method of acceptance. Specifying one stole and first-come, first-served availability also made the extent of the promised sale ascertainable. As an analytical explanation of the holding, those terms address the concern that an advertisement might otherwise expose a merchant to obligations exceeding its stock. The court's actual holding rests on this advertisement and Lefkowitz's compliance with it.
The house rule failed because it added a condition after Lefkowitz had accepted the published offer. The court recognized an advertiser's ability to modify an offer before acceptance but held that the advertiser could not impose new or arbitrary conditions afterward. Lefkowitz's prior awareness that the store had asserted a women-only rule did not persuade the court to insert that restriction into the second published advertisement. The opinion resolved the dispute through the terms and timing of contract formation; it did not decide a statutory sex-discrimination claim. 251 Minn. at 192, 86 N.W.2d at 691.
The case also separates the existence of an obligation from proof of recoverable loss. The court's refusal to award the claimed coat value rested on uncertain valuation, while the stole award used the established value minus the amount Lefkowitz would have paid. That calculation gives him the economic value of the promised bargain. The opinion does not establish a universal rule that an advertiser's stated value conclusively fixes damages in every case. It accepts the stole's value on this record and treats the coats' stated maximum as insufficient proof.
For class analysis, identify the exact words that give the customer power to complete the bargain, the conduct those words require, and the time at which that conduct occurs. A later refusal to perform an already formed contract has different consequences from a timely withdrawal of an outstanding offer. In Lefkowitz, the advertised terms made that sequence decisive. The opinion contains no separate concurrence or dissent.
The full decision is available at Lefkowitz, 251 Minn. 188, 86 N.W.2d 689.

briefs.title: Wucherpfennig v. Dooley
briefs.citation: 351 N.W.2d 443 (1984). Supreme Court of North Dakota. Sand, J. Decided July 11, 1984.

sections.Preamble:
The North Dakota Supreme Court held that Donald Wucherpfennig failed to accept Elizabeth Dooley's offer to sell her interest in inherited farmland before she revoked it. The response sent through the estate's attorney expressed readiness to proceed and sought further information, but it did not communicate a definite present commitment to buy on the offered terms. The court affirmed dismissal of Donald's claim for specific performance, the remedy that would have required Elizabeth to convey her interest. Donald was the plaintiff and appellant; Elizabeth, his sister, was the defendant and appellee. Their sister Louise Grettum and persons claiming interests in the land were also named defendants, although the disputed sale concerned
Elizabeth's share. 351 N.W.2d at 443-45.
The siblings inherited a family farm consisting of four quarters of land after their father died in 1964 and their mother died in 1977. Donald received an undivided two-thirds interest in the quarter containing the farmstead, while Elizabeth and Louise each received an undivided one-sixth interest in that quarter. Each sibling received an undivided one-third interest in each of the other three quarters. The unequal fractional interests matter because the parties were negotiating over Elizabeth's total ownership interest, and a price per acre had to be translated into the amount due for that interest.
During probate of their mother's estate, Elizabeth indicated that she wanted to sell her share to Donald. On
January 4, 1979, she wrote Robert Case, the attorney handling the probate, offering to sell at $200 per acre if
Donald wanted to buy, provided the transaction was for cash and handled promptly. The parties did not dispute that this letter was an offer. Case replied on January 13 that Donald was interested in purchasing her interest. That expression of interest preceded the communication on which Donald ultimately relied as his acceptance.
On February 17, Case wrote that Donald had arranged financing through the Federal Land Bank and that they were ready to proceed with the transaction. He then asked Elizabeth to state the exact amount she expected for her interest in the land. He also asked whether she would sign an agreement relating to Special
Use Valuation and requested a response on both subjects. Elizabeth did not answer. On March 9, she revoked her offer to sell at $200 per acre. Donald contended that the February 17 letter had already created a contract and that the revocation therefore came too late. 351 N.W.2d at 443-44.
Donald sought specific performance of the alleged sale contract and, alternatively, partition of the jointly owned property. Partition would address the co-owners' interests independently of the claimed agreement to buy Elizabeth's share. By consent, the parties tried the specific-performance claim first. The district court found that Donald had not accepted Elizabeth's offer and that, even if an acceptance existed, the supposed contract could not be specifically enforced. It gave four independently sufficient grounds for dismissal. On appeal, Donald therefore needed to defeat every independent ground to obtain reversal. The Supreme Court agreed with the lack-of-acceptance ground and expressly declined to decide the remaining issues. Its affirmance concerned dismissal of specific performance; the reported decision does not resolve the alternative partition claim. 351 N.W.2d at 444.
The controlling question was whether the February 17 letter expressed assent that would itself complete the bargain on Elizabeth's terms, or whether it contemplated further negotiation before either side became bound. Applying N.D. Century Code § 9-03-21 and its precedents, the court required an absolute, unequivocal, and unconditional acceptance. The offer and acceptance had to concern the same bargain, and the response had to express an intention to create the contract through that response itself. The court drew that formulation from Cooke v. Blood Systems, Inc., Grossman v. McLeish Ranch, Greenberg v. Stewart, and Minnesota decisions including Markmann v. H.A. Bruntjen Co. and Minar v. Skoog.
The court read the letter as a whole. Arranging financing showed that Donald was preparing to buy, and readiness to proceed showed continued interest. The immediate request for the amount Elizabeth expected, however, indicated that a material aspect of the proposed exchange remained open. The court understood the letter as movement toward a future agreement. Donald had not unequivocally committed himself to the transaction described in Elizabeth's offer. The letter's additional inquiry concerning Special Use Valuation formed part of the correspondence, but the court did not announce a separate holding that such an inquiry automatically defeats acceptance in every transaction. 351 N.W.2d at 444.
Donald's own trial testimony strengthened that reading. When asked why the February 17 letter did not specify a total amount, he said the amount would have been $37,200 and acknowledged that Elizabeth would have expected more. He also said that she would not have signed a contract stating the figure he intended to pay. The court used that testimony as further support for its conclusion that the parties had not assented to the same terms. The problem was therefore more substantial than leaving out a mechanical calculation that both parties understood identically. Donald knew that the figure he intended to pay would not secure Elizabeth's agreement. 351 N.W.2d at 444-45.
The opinion should be applied with care to a response that both accepts and requests information. A response can accept an offer while also asking for a change or clarification, if assent is complete and does not depend on the offeror agreeing to the request. The Restatement expresses that distinction in §§ 59 and
61: a response conditioning assent on different terms is a counteroffer, while a completed acceptance may accompany a nonconditional request. In Wucherpfennig, the court found the threshold commitment missing.
It did not hold that every question following words of acceptance destroys the contract. Nor did it need to classify the February 17 letter as a definite counteroffer; continued negotiations were enough to explain why it was ineffective as an acceptance.
The transaction also illustrates the limit of reliance as a formation argument. Donald's financing arrangements showed preparation, but the court did not treat them as acceptance of Elizabeth's cash-sale offer. It resolved the case on the correspondence and supporting testimony, without deciding the district court's other grounds. The reported opinion contains no separate dissent; the other justices concurred. The full opinion is available at Wucherpfennig v. Dooley, 351 N.W.2d 443.

briefs.title: International Filter Co. v. Conroe Gin, Ice & Light Co.
briefs.citation: 277 S.W. 631 (1925). Texas Commission of Appeals, Section A. Nickels, J. Decided December 10, 1925; disposition adopted by the Texas Supreme Court.

sections.Preamble:
The court held that Conroe Gin's signed order authorized International Filter to complete the contract through approval by an executive officer at its Chicago office. The officer's dated approval satisfied that specified method, and the writing did not require separate notice of approval. The court also concluded that the company's subsequent acknowledgment sufficiently communicated approval if notice was required.
International Filter, an Illinois manufacturer of water-purification equipment with its principal office in
Chicago, was the plaintiff and party seeking review. Conroe Gin, a Texas company manufacturing ice in
Conroe, was the defendant. International Filter prevailed on the formation issues, but the case returned to the
Court of Civil Appeals for unresolved questions; the reviewing court did not enter a final damages award.
277 S.W. at 631-33.
On February 10, 1920, International Filter's traveling representative, W. W. Waterman, presented a written proposal to Conroe Gin's manager, Henry Thompson. The proposal described a No. 2 Junior steel-tank water softener and filter for $1,230, to be furnished f.o.b. Chicago and suitable for water whose characteristics would be determined from a sample. The decisive language provided that the proposal would become a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an executive officer of International Filter at its
Chicago office. The form also required modifications to be made through an approved supplementary agreement signed by both parties and stated that the proposal was submitted for prompt acceptance, with change without notice possible if prompt acceptance did not occur.
Thompson signed the paper for Conroe Gin on February 10, using an acceptance notation. The document also requested shipment by March 10. It then went to International Filter's Chicago office. On February 13,
P. N. Engel, identified in the opinion as the company's president and vice president, wrote a dated approval on the paper. On February 14, International Filter mailed a letter acknowledging and thanking Conroe Gin for the order, identifying the equipment and its electrical specifications, and referring to March 10 shipment.
The letter asked Conroe Gin to send a water sample promptly so the manufacturer could analyze the water before shipping the equipment. Conroe Gin received that letter in due course. 277 S.W. at 631-32.
Conroe Gin attempted to cancel the order in a February 28 letter and reiterated that position on March 4.
International Filter answered on March 2, denied a right to cancel, and insisted on performance. It then sued for breach. Conroe Gin argued that neither Engel's endorsement nor the February 14 letter constituted the executive approval contemplated by the proposal. It further argued that notice of approval was essential and had not been given. Thompson testified that, when he signed the order, he had told Waterman that prompt notification was required. The defense therefore relied both on its reading of the form and on a claimed oral instruction accompanying the signature.
The trial court heard the case without a jury and entered judgment for Conroe Gin, finding in its favor on the formation issues and other material issues. The Court of Civil Appeals affirmed at 269 S.W. 210. That court nevertheless agreed that Engel's endorsement was an approval within the document's terms; the principal remaining obstacle was the asserted need for notice. International Filter sought further review. The
Commission of Appeals recommended reversal of the intermediate appellate judgment and remand to that court for questions properly presented but not previously decided. Chief Justice Cureton, for the Texas
Supreme Court, adopted that disposition. This procedural endpoint matters because a favorable ruling on contract formation did not resolve every issue in the breach action.
The first analytical step is to identify who made the legally operative offer. International Filter prepared the form and called it a proposal, while Conroe Gin signed beneath language of acceptance. Even so, the form reserved a further act of approval for International Filter's executive officer. Conroe Gin's signature therefore supplied the offer to purchase on those terms. The company became the offeree with authority to accept through the reserved approval. The court expressly treated the signed paper sent to Chicago as
Conroe Gin's offer. Drafting the form and making the operative offer were separate roles. 277 S.W. at 632.
The court agreed that Engel's dated endorsement constituted approval by an executive officer at the designated place. No additional ritual was necessary to make that endorsement an approval. The remaining question was whether the contract also required communication of that approval to Conroe Gin. Although notice ordinarily protects an offeror who seeks a return promise, the offeror may dispense with it by authorizing a particular act as sufficient acceptance. Drawing on Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., the court reasoned that the offeree completes the required acceptance by following the specified method when the offer makes that method sufficient.
The signed writing said that the proposal became a contract upon the executive officer's approval in
Chicago. Requiring notice to arrive in Conroe would add another condition and change both the designated time and place of formation. The separate prompt-acceptance provision addressed the timing of the required approval; it did not prescribe an additional form of acceptance or a notice requirement. The court treated the writing as unambiguous and judged the offer by those written terms despite the claimed oral demand for notification. Its reasoning supports a contractual waiver of notice in this transaction, while leaving the ordinary notice rule applicable when the offer does not dispense with it. 277 S.W. at 632-33.
The court supplied an alternative ground concerning the February 14 letter. Approval had already occurred through Engel's endorsement; the letter's possible role was to notify Conroe Gin of that existing act. A notice can communicate acceptance by reasonable implication without repeating a particular formula. The acknowledgment thanked the buyer for the specified order, identified the planned shipment, and requested the water sample needed for performance. The court concluded that a reasonable recipient in Conroe Gin's position would understand it to communicate approval. Its additional observation that reliance on the letter could have prevented International Filter from denying approval was hypothetical; the reported facts do not establish that Conroe Gin actually changed position in such reliance.
The narrow formation holding depends on the particular approval clause and the occurrence of the required executive act. An offeree's unexpressed decision to agree would not satisfy the prescribed act merely because the offer waived notification. Engel made an observable written endorsement of the document itself.
This explains the comparison with White: the controlling question in each case is whether the offeree performed an act that the offer and circumstances made sufficient to express assent. In International Filter, the writing expressly selected the act that completed the bargain; in White, the builder's general preparations did not communicate acceptance of the proposed job.
The case concerns common-law formation in a 1920 transaction and should be stated in those terms. A modern sale of equipment would also require attention to the applicable UCC provisions and to whether the language unambiguously restricts the means of acceptance. The available online opinion text is linked at
International Filter, 277 S.W. 631; that public text ends during the reasoning. The later reasoning and remand described here appear in the supplied seventh edition, printed pages 149-151, PDF pages 199-201.

briefs.title: White v. Corlies & Tifft
briefs.citation: 46 N.Y. 467 (1871). Court of Appeals of New York. Folger, J. Decided November 20, 1871. Also reported as White v. Corlies; the supplied casebook spells Tift with one final f.

sections.Preamble:
The New York Court of Appeals held that White's private decision to accept a proposed office-fitting job, followed by buying and working on general-purpose materials, did not sufficiently manifest acceptance to the merchants who proposed the job. The trial judge had incorrectly instructed the jury that White could bind the merchants by acting on their note and beginning the job without indicating assent to them. The
Court of Appeals reversed the judgment for White and ordered a new trial, with costs to depend on the eventual outcome. White was the builder, plaintiff, and respondent on appeal; Corlies and his associates were the merchants, defendants, and appellants. 46 N.Y. at 467-70.
White operated his building business on Fortieth Street in New York City. The merchants conducted business on Dey Street and wanted a suite of offices at 57 Broadway fitted up. In September 1865, they gave
White specifications and asked him to estimate the cost. He delivered his estimate on September 28, after which the merchants were to consider it and communicate their decision. They changed the specifications that day and sent the revised version to White to obtain his assent under the estimate. White signed his assent to the changes and returned the specifications. That preliminary agreement about specifications formed part of the negotiations; the Court of Appeals found no completed agreement before the later note.
The next day, the merchants' bookkeeper sent White a note dated September 29. It stated that, upon an agreement to finish fitting up the offices within two weeks from that date, he could begin at once. The writer also said he would probably call again between five and six that afternoon. White did not reply. Immediately after receiving the note, he bought lumber and began working on it. The merchants countermanded the proposal the following day. White sued for damages on the theory that his conduct had accepted the undertaking before the countermand arrived.
The supplied casebook adds details from White's testimony in the record on appeal. The merchants had initially wanted the offices finished in black walnut within twenty-one days; White said he could not do that hardwood work within that period. They then requested an estimate for white pine. White's September 28 estimate did not specify a completion time. The subsequent countermand requested another estimate for black walnut. Those record details help explain why agreement about specifications and price did not necessarily settle the entire undertaking. They supplement the published opinion and are identified here as casebook reporting of the appellate record. The opinion itself refers once to a September 30 communication;
the casebook notes that the court apparently meant the September 29 note.
At trial, the judge told the jury that White did not have to return to the merchants and state that he had begun, and that he could act on the note and commence the job. The defendants took an exception to that instruction, preserving the claimed legal error. The jury found for White. The General Term of the First
Judicial District affirmed the trial judgment, and the defendants appealed to the Court of Appeals. The issue on that appeal was whether the instruction treated White's decision and preparations as sufficient acceptance when his conduct had not communicated assent or been placed in an appropriate course of communication.
The disposition was a new trial, rather than a final appellate award to either party. 46 N.Y. at 467-70.
The court first treated the merchants' note as a proposal requiring White's acceptance. It found no earlier contract in the evidence or the jury's findings. The court then stated that an offer made when the parties are apart requires acceptance through an appropriate outward act. The act need not always have reached the offeror's actual knowledge before a contract forms. It must, however, be placed in a proper course of communication so that it will ordinarily reach the offeror within a reasonable time. A mailed acceptance illustrates the distinction: dispatch may complete the contract even before delivery because the offeree has taken an objectively communicative step. 46 N.Y. at 469.
White's conduct failed that test. The lumber he purchased was suitable for other comparable jobs, and the work he performed on it resembled the work he would do for those jobs. His acts therefore did not identify this proposed undertaking as the one he had accepted. His private intention could explain the acts to himself, but it did not give the merchants an outward indication of assent. The court found nothing in his conduct that communicated acceptance, set such communication in motion, or would necessarily result in communication to the merchants. His expenditures and labor thus established preparation without establishing the acceptance required on this record. 46 N.Y. at 469-70.
White's strongest argument arose from the note's permission to begin immediately: a builder could reasonably understand an instruction to start as inviting responsive conduct. The court nevertheless examined what White actually did and how those acts would manifest assent. It did not establish a rule that conduct can never accept an offer. Nor did it hold that actual receipt of notice is always essential, since its mailed-letter example expressly recognized formation before receipt. Its conclusion was that these general preparations, accompanied by an uncommunicated intention, were insufficient under this proposal.
The casebook identifies a genuine interpretive question concerning the note's opening phrase. It could require White to agree to the newly stated completion period before starting, or it could refer to the proposed work while authorizing commencement. The Court of Appeals treated the note as an offer but did not develop every possible reading of that phrase. Work at the specified offices, an unequivocal return message, or other conduct objectively directed to this job could present a different acceptance question. Those are analytical variations; the court did not decide them. The brief's holding should remain tied to the generic lumber and uncommunicated work in the actual record.
Under the later Restatement framework, the initial inquiry would be whether the offer invited a promise, performance, or either. Section 62 may make the beginning of invited performance an acceptance carrying a promise to complete; § 45 may protect an offeree who begins performance when only completed performance is invited as acceptance. Both inquiries require identifying the work actually requested and distinguishing its beginning from preparation. Sections 54 and 56 separately address notice. These later provisions help organize a modern analysis of similar facts, but the 1871 court did not apply them.
The decision supports an objective account of assent: an act must obtain its contractual meaning from the communication and circumstances, and a hidden intention cannot supply the missing outward meaning. The justices concurred in reversal, with Justice Allen not voting. The opinion is available at White v. Corlies, 46
N.Y. 467. The fuller factual statement and the appellate-record note appear in the supplied casebook at printed pages 152-154, PDF pages 202-204.

briefs.title: Silence not ordinarily acceptance
briefs.citation: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 69; casebook printed pages 166-167, PDF pages 216-217.

sections.Preamble:
Silence acquires contractual significance when the circumstances reasonably give it the meaning of assent.
An unsolicited offer, standing alone, ordinarily leaves the recipient free to do nothing. The offeror cannot impose a duty to reject merely by announcing that silence will count as acceptance. This rule protects the recipient's control over whether to enter a bargain and avoids making every uninvited proposal a demand for action. The assigned discussion uses an offer declaring acceptance automatic after forty-eight hours of silence to illustrate that limit. Restatement § 69; casebook at 166.
Section 69(1)(a) addresses the knowing acceptance of services. An offeree who takes the benefit of offered services, has a reasonable opportunity to reject them, and has reason to know that the provider expects compensation may accept through that conduct. For example, a person who knowingly permits requested paid work to continue for that person's benefit can communicate assent without a spoken promise. The opportunity to reject and the reason to understand that payment is expected are essential. If someone provides an unavoidable benefit without giving the recipient a meaningful choice, those facts require a different analysis; liability cannot be inferred simply from the existence of a benefit.
Section 69(1)(b) concerns an offeror who gives the offeree reason to understand that assent may be expressed through silence or inaction. In this situation, silence operates as acceptance only when the offeree intends to accept. The offer can authorize silence as a convenient way of accepting, but it cannot force an unwilling recipient into a bargain. The offeree's intention therefore has a specified role within this exception.
The requirement differs from a general rule under which an offeror could impose contractual consequences by setting an arbitrary deadline for rejection.
Section 69(1)(c) concerns previous dealings and other circumstances that make it reasonable for the offeree to notify the offeror if the offeree intends to decline. A repeated practice can establish what an unspoken response means between these parties. If a supplier regularly sends goods of an agreed kind and the buyer regularly accepts and pays, the supplier may reasonably understand the same pattern to continue unless the buyer objects. The relevant question is the meaning created by the parties' relationship and current conduct.
A party's undisclosed intention to reject may fail to overcome conduct that objectively communicates acceptance under that established practice.
The casebook's principal illustration is Hobbs v. Massasoit Whip Co., 158 Mass. 194, 33 N.E. 495 (1893).
Hobbs sought $108.50 for 2,350 eel skins sent to a whip manufacturer. He had sent skins in the same manner four or five times before, and the manufacturer had accepted and paid for them. In the disputed transaction, the company retained the skins for months without giving Hobbs notice that it declined them, and the skins were eventually destroyed. Justice Holmes explained that the established dealings and retention could support a jury finding of acceptance. The prior transactions gave the shipment an understood commercial context, and prolonged retention without objection reinforced that meaning. The court overruled the defendant's exceptions, leaving the plaintiff's recovery intact. 158 Mass. at 196-97, 33 N.E. at 495.
The precise significance of Hobbs is evidentiary: those circumstances permitted the jury to infer assent. The decision does not establish that delivery of any unrequested goods automatically produces a contract. The defendant's established relationship with Hobbs and its handling of the shipment supplied the additional facts. The opinion's objective approach also explains why a recipient cannot always avoid liability by asserting that it silently meant to refuse. When conduct reasonably indicates assent in the relationship the parties have created, an undisclosed reservation may carry little weight. The opinion is available at Hobbs,
158 Mass. 194.
The casebook gives a second illustration involving a seller's response to orders. In American Bronze Corp. v.
Streamway Products, 8 Ohio App. 3d 223, 456 N.E.2d 1295, 1300 (1982), the parties had used a practice for more than twenty years under which the buyer telephoned orders, followed with written purchase orders, and the seller began production. When the seller refused three orders, the appellate court reversed and remanded after the buyer's claim had been denied. The established method of filling orders supported the buyer's belief that production had begun absent notice of rejection. The court relied on UCC § 2-204(1), which recognizes formation through conduct demonstrating agreement. This account follows the assigned casebook note; it illustrates how prior practice can supply meaning to a seller's silence as well as a buyer's.
Casebook at 167.
Section 69(2) separately addresses the exercise of ownership over offered property. An offeree who acts inconsistently with the offeror's ownership can become bound on the offered terms unless those terms are manifestly unreasonable. If the act is wrongful against the offeror, it operates as acceptance only if the offeror ratifies it. Using or disposing of offered property may thus carry a contractual consequence, while simple possession requires attention to the circumstances. A court must also consider any statute that changes the common-law result.
For merchandise mailed without the recipient's prior expressed request or consent, federal law provides a specific protection: qualifying unordered merchandise may be retained, used, discarded, or otherwise treated as a gift without an obligation to the sender. That statute prevents a sender from turning an unsolicited mailing into a bill merely because the recipient keeps or uses it. A subscription arrangement the recipient has already accepted presents a different consent question, because a later delivery may occur under that existing agreement. Whether a particular renewal arrangement is lawful also depends on applicable consumer-protection rules. 39 U.S.C. § 3009(a)-(d).
In applying this topic, specify which facts make silence meaningful: knowingly taking paid services, intending to use a permitted silent method of acceptance, an established course of dealings, or exercising ownership over offered goods. Then identify what the recipient could reasonably have understood and whether a governing statute changes the result. That method ties the conclusion to consent and conduct rather than treating silence as having the same meaning in every transaction.

briefs.title: The significance of contract formation for antidiscrimination law
briefs.citation: Casebook printed page 156, PDF page 206; 42 U.S.C. § 1981; Perry v. Command Performance and Hampton v. Dillard Department Stores.

sections.Preamble:
Contract formation can determine the existence and scope of a protected civil right. Section 1981 guarantees equal rights to make and enforce contracts and reaches racial discrimination in private contracting. Its current definition covers formation, performance, modification, termination, and enjoyment of the contractual relationship's benefits, privileges, terms, and conditions. A claimant may therefore challenge interference with an existing contract or discriminatory obstruction of a proposed contract. The analysis must identify the contractual activity or right affected and connect its impairment to intentional racial discrimination. 42 U.S.C. § 1981(a)-(c).
The casebook's example, Perry v. Command Performance, 913 F.2d 99 (3d Cir. 1990), arose under an earlier interpretation of § 1981. In Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, 491 U.S. 164 (1989), the Supreme
Court limited the statute's protection concerning the making of contracts and generally excluded discriminatory conduct occurring afterward during performance. That interpretation made the instant of formation decisive in some service transactions. Congress subsequently expanded the statute through the
Civil Rights Act of 1991. The chronological distinction is necessary to understand both the 1990 decision and the rule applicable today.
Edith Perry, a Black woman, had used the Command Performance salon in Pennsylvania's King of Prussia
Mall more than five times. On October 12, 1987, her husband telephoned the salon and arranged a noon appointment for her wash and set. The full opinion identifies her husband as the caller, although the casebook compresses that detail. When Perry arrived, Helene Kugler, who had previously styled her hair, explained that she had a bad cold and asked whether another hairdresser could do the work. Perry agreed.
According to Perry's complaint and deposition, the substitute, Beth Abbott, loudly refused because Perry was Black and made explicitly racial statements about whom she would serve. Perry became distressed, summoned mall security, and left with her husband. Perry, 913 F.2d at 100.
Perry sued the salon under § 1981 and Pennsylvania's law of intentional infliction of emotional distress. The district court granted summary judgment for the salon because it assumed the telephone appointment had already created a contract on racially neutral terms. Under its reading of Patterson, the subsequent refusal therefore constituted conduct outside the statute's contract-making protection. Perry appealed. The Third
